# Word groups

Cards teach one word at a time. This is the part they can't do: what a word looks like standing next to its neighbours.


---

## Meaning clusters

*Words that crowd the same patch of meaning. The definitions overlap; the nuance is what separates them.*


<a id="meaning__a-group-splitting-apart"></a>
### A Group Splitting Apart

All of these words live around the same event: one thing that was supposed to be whole comes apart into opposed sides. They differ on what exactly splits (ideas, opinions, an institution), whether the split is a process, a completed fact, a tendency, or merely a climate, and how much hostility is baked in. The trap is that they sit at different stages of the same story and in different parts of speech, so they almost never substitute for one another.

- **dichotomy** — The only one here that divides **ideas**, not people — nobody has to be angry, or even present. **Dichotomy** names the either/or frame itself (mind/body, art/commerce) and insists the two options are exhaustive; that insistence is why it so often appears with *false* attached.
- **polarize** — The verb for the **process**, and the only one that tracks the moderates: **polarize** describes people migrating toward the extremes until nothing is left in the middle. It takes an agent — an issue, a leader, a policy *polarizes* a population — so it says less about the two camps than about the vanishing space between them.
- **factious** — An adjective describing a **disposition**, not an event — a bloc that is **factious** keeps generating sub-groups, split or no split. It is a hostile judgment delivered from the standpoint of the whole, and its specific accusation is self-interest: they put their faction above the body. It never describes one person's temper.
- **schism** — The **completed, formal** break, and the only word here that leaves you counting two bodies where there was one. Its cause is doctrine — each side claims to be the true church, party, or movement — so calling a split a **schism** frames it as a war over orthodoxy rather than tactics, and implies it will not be sewn back up.
- **strife** — Names no division at all — only the bitter **climate** that persists. **Strife** has no count of sides, no doctrine, no resolution; it settles over a country or a marriage for years (*civil strife, marital strife*). Elevated and faintly biblical, it is too large for two people and one argument.

> **On the exam:** Watch the part of speech and what is doing the splitting: sentences about opinions hardening want *polarize*, sentences about a conceptual either/or want *dichotomy*, and *strife* is the decoy when the sentence describes ongoing bitterness but never actually divides the group in two.


<a id="meaning__a-mixture-of-sources"></a>
### A mixture of sources: praised, dismissed, or merely measured

All three describe something made of unlike parts pulled from different origins — no single style, school, or kind runs through it. What separates them is the verdict attached and whether anyone is credited with doing the mixing. One assumes a chooser with taste, one insists no one was choosing at all, and one refuses to say. The mixture is identical; the judgment is the whole difference.

- **eclectic** — The only one that **compliments**, and it compliments a *person*: **eclectic** implies a selector who ignored genre boundaries and picked each item on its merits. It attaches to taste, collections, and influences — and quietly concedes the person borrowed rather than invented.
- **hodgepodge** — The only **noun**, and the only one that says nobody was steering: a **hodgepodge** accumulated by accident. Informal and lightly contemptuous, it calls the result incoherent rather than rich — a policy described this way is being told to start over.
- **heterogeneous** — The lab-report word: **heterogeneous** states composition and awards nothing, which is why it often signals trouble — such data won't pool, such a class can't be taught at one level. Note the grammar trap: it describes only the whole, never a single member of it.

> **On the exam:** Context tone decides the answer — approving sentences take *eclectic*, dismissive ones *hodgepodge*, clinical or statistical ones *heterogeneous*; and a blank needing an adjective rules out *hodgepodge* outright.


<a id="meaning__a-settled-leaning-toward"></a>
### A settled leaning toward

All of these name a leaning that is already there before any particular choice comes up — a settled tilt rather than a decision made on the spot. They differ on three axes: how respectable the thing leaned toward is, who is doing the describing (a friend, a novelist, a prosecutor, a statistician), and whether the leaning is a lasting trait or just today's lean. Miss those axes and they look interchangeable; catch them and each one is nearly forced by its context.

- **penchant** — The indulgent one: **penchant** attaches to a pleasure you enjoy having, usually a small or slightly frivolous one (loud ties, gossip, good champagne). It's what friends would list about you with a smile, never what a report would record about you.
- **predilection** — The *pre*- is load-bearing: a **predilection** is already formed before the case arrives, so it colours judgement rather than just describing taste — a judge's predilection for lenient sentences. It's the most formal of the set and the most useful for quiet editorialising (*a predilection for lost causes*), and it stays mild: never a passion, only a standing preference.
- **proclivity** — The vice word. A **proclivity** is toward *doing* something disreputable — gambling, brawling, lying — and it implies the leaning is settled and characteristic, part of who you are. Attach it to something harmless and it turns arch or sounds like an accusation.
- **propensity** — The clinical, measurable one: a **propensity** is a trait you've been assessed as having, which is why lawyers, psychologists and statisticians own the word. Unlike the others, it applies to things as readily as people — steel has a propensity to fracture in cold — and it names a rate of acting, not a taste.
- **affinity** — The only member that needn't involve behaviour at all. An **affinity** claims a built-in match: an affinity *for* something is attraction (elements for oxygen, a person for jazz), an affinity *with* or *between* things is plain resemblance (Sanskrit and Latin) with no feeling involved. Nothing here is a fault, and nothing here is indulgence.
- **inclined** — The only adjective, and the only one that isn't a standing trait: to be **inclined** is to lean on *this* question, right now (*inclined to agree*), which is why it's committee-speak — the exit door stays open. Everything else in this group is something you carry around; this is a position you're halfway to taking.

> **On the exam:** The trap is valence: the sentence supplies a harmless pleasure and offers proclivity/propensity, or supplies a vice and offers penchant — read the object of the leaning, not the leaning itself.


<a id="meaning__a-situation-with-no-clean-exit"></a>
### A Situation With No Clean Exit

All five name trouble you cannot simply walk away from — a knot, a bind, a mess with no tidy resolution. They split on three axes: whether the difficulty is *intellectual* or *practical*; whether it describes the **person stuck** or the **situation itself**; and how big the trouble is, from a scandal that ends careers down to a spilled drink at a state dinner. Several of them also say something about the speaker — how amused, how dry, how far above the mess they wish to sound.

- **conundrum** — The only one that's a **puzzle rather than a plight** — the difficulty is in your head, not in your circumstances. It's the only member of this group you can hand to someone else to solve, and the only one that's neutral enough to attach to an abstraction ("the pricing **conundrum**") rather than to a person in trouble. Nothing bad has happened to anyone yet.
- **quandary** — Describes the **person mid-deliberation**, not the situation — you are *in* a **quandary**, turning it over, and the costs are still prospective because you haven't chosen yet. Unlike a conundrum, the answers are all sitting right there; you just hate every one of them. Faintly hand-wringing: the speaker is stuck and slightly embarrassed to be dithering.
- **predicament** — The trouble has **already landed** — a quandary is deciding, a **predicament** is being in it. Names the situation rather than the state of mind, and carries a whiff that you walked into it yourself, which is why "got himself into a right **predicament**" is idiomatic and no other word here substitutes.
- **imbroglio** — The only one that requires **multiple parties and bad blood** — not a bind you're in but a snarl several people are tangled in, acrimonious, public, and faintly scandalous. The others can happen to one person alone; an **imbroglio** cannot. It's the dry, formal word a journalist reaches for when "scandal" would sound excitable.
- **contretemps** — The **smallest** thing here, and deliberately so — a mistimed mishap or a petty snapping-match, beneath the level of real trouble. The word is an act of minimisation: calling something a **contretemps** shrinks it and advertises that the speaker is far too composed to be rattled. Applied to genuine disaster, it reads as sarcasm or spin.

> **On the exam:** The exam banks on you flattening these into one blob called "problem" — so the correct choice usually turns on the axis, not the severity: puzzle-in-the-head (conundrum) vs. person-deciding (quandary) vs. situation-already-happened (predicament), with imbroglio requiring warring parties and contretemps requiring triviality.


<a id="meaning__make-it-stand-out"></a>
### Accentuate / Underscore / Amplify — turning up what's already there

All three take something that already exists and raise its salience — none of them invents, and none of them distorts. That shared honesty is why they get swapped: each one leaves the underlying fact intact and only changes how much it registers. The differences live in *what* gets raised: the sharpness of a feature, the perceived importance of a fact, or the sheer magnitude of a thing.

- **accentuate** — Works on a **feature** and sharpens its contrast against everything around it — a cheekbone, a curve, a hairline crack, a class divide. Nothing gets bigger or louder; the edges just get harder to miss, which is why it's the only one of the three at home in descriptions of clothing, faces, and design.
- **underscore** — Changes nothing about the thing itself — only your recognition that it **matters**. Its object is abstract and evaluative (a need, a risk, a fragility, a point), and its subject is usually an event or a statistic rather than a person: the crash underscores; the editorial merely stresses.
- **amplify** — The only one that increases actual **magnitude** — louder, stronger, further-reaching — which is why it alone governs sound and signals, and why panic, tension, and rumour are its natural objects. It also has a sense the others lack entirely: "amplify that point" means *say more about it*, not *say it more forcefully*.

> **On the exam:** Sentence Equivalence loves this trio because all three fit "made X more noticeable" — decide first whether the sentence needs the thing to grow (**amplify**), to be recognised as important (**underscore**), or to be thrown into sharper contrast (**accentuate**); then check the subject, since only **underscore** is routinely driven by an event or statistic rather than a person.


<a id="meaning__achieving-nothing"></a>
### Achieving nothing

All three point at the same empty result: work goes in, nothing comes out. But they locate the emptiness in different places — in the attempt itself, in the thing that was supposed to produce, or in the dreamer who aimed too high. They also differ sharply in what the speaker feels about it, ranging from weary dismissal to open affection. Getting one right means asking *what is being blamed* and *how warm is the tone*.

- **futile** — The only one that is a **verdict on the attempt itself** — it says the effort could never have worked, so the tone is weary and faintly superior, with an implied *stop trying*. Attaches to actions and gestures (**futile** resistance, a **futile** search), never to soil or a womb, and never with admiration.
- **barren** — Blames the **producer, not the attempt** — a field, a womb, a decade, a round of talks that ought to have yielded something and didn't. It's the most physical and the coldest of the three, and the only one with an organic, fertility-based root, which is why aimed at a person it lands as an accusation.
- **quixotic** — The only word here that can be **warm**. It grades the dreamer's *aim*, not the outcome: noble, chivalrous, self-sacrificing, and hopeless against reality. A campaign can be **quixotic** and still command respect — call the same campaign futile and you've withdrawn it.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating **quixotic** as a pure synonym for doomed — it needs the idealism and the sympathy; if the passage sneers, the answer is **futile**, and if something failed to *yield*, it's **barren**.


<a id="meaning__acting-before-thinking"></a>
### Acting before thinking

All four condemn action that outruns deliberation — the gap between wanting and doing collapses, and judgment never gets its turn. The disapproval is real but never moral: nobody here is malicious, just unbraked. What separates them is *what* is missing — the pause, the composure, the fear, or the right moment — and how much credit the speaker gives the actor for nerve.

- **impulsive** — The mildest and the only one that names a **temperament** rather than an act — the person is like this on Tuesdays too. Crucially, the risk was never *considered and dismissed*; the thought simply never got that far. Warm enough to be affectionate about a friend.
- **impetuous** — Adds heat and forward motion: passion is doing the driving, not mere absence of thought. It's the word for someone who **charges**, which is why it attaches to the young and the in-love — and why the criticism carries a flicker of admiration for the fire.
- **foolhardy** — The only one that requires a **visible, obvious danger** to be ignored. It concedes genuine courage and then rules it wasted — you'd use it for the unroped climber, never for someone who impulsively bought a couch. Judgment on a specific act, with a strong hint it ends badly.
- **precipitate** — About **timing**, not psychology: the action came before the situation was ripe. No heat, no danger, no temperament — just a formal, cool rebuke that the thing was undercooked. And its dominant GRE sense is verbal: to *trigger* a latent crisis early, where the subject is often an event, not a person.

> **On the exam:** The trap is **precipitate**: tested as a verb about events ("the arrest precipitated riots"), where no rashness is implied at all — and among the adjectives, only **foolhardy** requires a danger the actor could plainly see.


<a id="meaning__actively-harmful"></a>
### Actively harmful

All four label something as actively damaging rather than merely bad — a force, substance, condition or utterance that works to injure whatever it touches. They differ on three axes: whether the harm is *toxic* or merely *unfavourable*, whether any *opposition* is implied, and whether the damage *spreads*. All four are formal, and all four condemn. Roughly ascending in severity as listed.

- **adverse** — The only one with no poison in it — the harm is purely relational, measured against some named interest (an **adverse** ruling, market, headwind). Weakest of the four: an adverse outcome can be a mere setback, and it attaches to conditions and results, never to a person's temper.
- **inimical** — Harm framed as *thwarting*: it comes with **to** and names what cannot survive it (**inimical** to growth, to free speech). Where *adverse* merely loads the dice against you, this says the whole environment is set against the thing's flourishing — structural opposition with nobody doing the opposing.
- **noxious** — The only one where the injury is literally toxic to bodies — fumes, weeds, chemicals that damage lungs, not smells that merely offend. It poisons what it touches but sits still doing it; applied to an ideology, the medical metaphor is the point, not decoration.
- **virulent** — Takes **noxious**'s poison and adds speed and contagion: aggressively destructive and *spreading*. It is also the only one that works on hostility coming out of a mouth — a **virulent** attack, virulent racism — where the venom, not just the damage, is being named.

> **On the exam:** Two traps: **adverse** vs. *averse* (conditions vs. your reluctance — only *averse* describes a feeling), and **inimical**, dangled beside *hostile* to see if you'll demand a hater; usually the answer is an environment, not an enemy.


<a id="meaning__airily-unconcerned"></a>
### Airily unconcerned

All three describe a conspicuous absence of concern in a situation that seems to call for some — the person is light where you expected weight. They differ in what supplies the lightness: coolness, dismissiveness, or cheer. They also differ in who is being judged. One can be pure style, one is always an accusation, and one indicts the smile more than the act.

- **nonchalant** — The only one of the three that can be a compliment. **Nonchalant** reports on visible manner — the composed face, the unhurried exit — and says nothing about what the person actually feels or neglects. It attaches to bearing (a nonchalant shrug, a nonchalant reply), not to a duty being shirked.
- **cavalier** — Always a charge, and it names a power relation: **cavalier** is unconcern waved down from above, by someone entitled to find the stakes beneath discussion. It attaches to the treatment of other people's risks, rules, or facts — cavalier about safety, about the evidence — and the fault is the lordly attitude itself, not any error it produced.
- **blithe** — Supplies the missing ingredient the others lack: actual cheerfulness. **Blithe** convicts by contrast — sunniness that only stays sunny because the person never looked. Literary in register, and in GRE prose it is nearly welded to a noun of neglect: blithe disregard, blithe assumption, blithely ignored.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable "carefree"; the sentence usually names the missing element — a cool exterior wants **nonchalant**, dismissal of someone's legitimate concern wants **cavalier**, and a happy obliviousness (or a following noun like *disregard*) wants **blithe**.


<a id="meaning__an-unrepentant-scoundrel"></a>
### An unrepentant scoundrel

All three are elevated, faintly old-fashioned labels for a person of bad character — and all three are softened by that elevation. Each keeps the speaker at a comfortable distance: you reach for these words when you disapprove but are not actually frightened, which is why none of them lands on a murderer without sounding arch. What separates them is what each one is actually judging: whether the man can be reformed, what specific appetites he indulges, or how far beneath the speaker he stands.

- **reprobate** — The verdict is on his **reformability**, not his particular vice — he has been tested and abandoned as past saving. It's the only one of the three that implies a permanent condition rather than a set of deeds, and the only one that turns fond: *the old reprobate* is a shrug at someone who will never change and never intended to.
- **libertine** — The only one that names the appetite — sex and drink, pursued as a creed rather than a lapse. It describes a whole style of life, complete with wit and money and a defence he'd deliver over wine, so it carries a flicker of glamour the others lack; a candlelit drawing room, never a dock.
- **miscreant** — Measures the **speaker's altitude**, not the offender's depth. It comes down from headmasters, magistrates and narrators onto small fry — the boys who egged the car — and its faint archaism is a way of refusing someone the dignity of a serious word.

> **On the exam:** Offered as interchangeable in an all-that-apply item: pick by the clue — irredeemable/beyond reform → reprobate, pleasure-seeking or dissipation → libertine, petty mischief scolded from above → miscreant.


<a id="meaning__annul-by-authority"></a>
### Annul by Authority

All four end something's force from a position of higher standing: what was binding, in effect, or under way stops counting. The register is formal and institutional — courts, legislatures, treaties, official documents — and the result is total, not a reduction. What separates them is *what* gets cancelled and *how*: the instrument itself, its practical effect, a live event, or its standing relative to a newer version.

- **abrogate** — The only one that destroys the **instrument** rather than its effect: the object must be something formally enacted (a law, treaty, clause, right) and the subject must be the body empowered to unenact it. It concedes the thing was validly in force — it is being struck off, not exposed as void — and the word usually arrives loaded with someone's grievance.
- **nullify** — Attacks the **effect**, not the document — the thing may sit on the books and simply count for nothing. Uniquely in this group it needs no authority at all: inflation, a counterweight, an offsetting clause can **nullify**. Reach for it when two forces meet and the net is exactly zero.
- **quash** — Its object is **live and moving** — a rebellion, a rumour, a rising hope — or a pending legal act (a subpoena, an indictment) still capable of doing something. One decisive stroke from above, and the thing does not resurface; nothing here is repealed or replaced, it is stopped.
- **supersede** — The only cancellation performed by a **successor**: the old edition, model, or regulation loses authority because a newer one has arrived, not because anyone moved against it. Bloodless and procedural — no grievance, no struggle, no scheming (that would be *supplant*); the old text just becomes waste paper.

> **On the exam:** Sentence-equivalence traps hinge on the object: only **abrogate** takes a formally enacted instrument, only **supersede** requires a replacement to exist, only **quash** needs something still in motion, and only **nullify** works with an impersonal cause like inflation or a counterforce.


<a id="meaning__argument-you-can-t-resist"></a>
### Argument you can't resist

All four rate how much an argument, story, or claim earns your belief — and all four describe the thing being judged, not the person judging. They differ on two axes: how *much* belief is compelled (from irresistible down to merely not-yet-dismissed), and *what earns it* — the structure of the reasoning, the surface impression, or the raw force of the evidence. The trap is that they look like synonyms on a scale of "convincing," when two of them quietly decline to say anything is true.

- **compelling** — The strongest, and the only one that works on stories as well as arguments — **compelling** exerts *pressure*: you can't refute it, or you can't look away. Where the others let you weigh and decide, this one removes the option.
- **cogent** — **Cogent** praises the architecture of the reasoning, not its effect on you — tight logic, well-evidenced, hard to answer. It's the coolest and most formal of the four (judges, examiners, reviewers), and it's the only one that can be true of an argument nobody happened to find moving.
- **credible** — **Credible** is about the *source* clearing a bar of trustworthiness — a witness, a threat, a candidate, an attempt. It says you lean toward believing, without claiming proof; it's the word professionals use precisely because it commits to seriousness, not truth.
- **plausible** — **Plausible** rates only how something *sounds on first hearing* — the weakest of the four and the only one that can turn hostile. "A plausible enough story" is what a skeptic says when he doesn't believe a word; the others cannot be used that way.

> **On the exam:** The exam tests whether you know **plausible** and **credible** stop short of truth while **cogent** and **compelling** don't — sentence-completion cues like *merely*, *superficially*, or a following *but* signal the weak end; *irrefutable* or *left no room to disagree* signal the strong end.


<a id="meaning__asleep-but-not-dead"></a>
### Asleep but not dead

All four describe a state of inactivity that is a pause rather than an ending: the thing still exists, its capacity is intact, and resumption is expected or at least possible. Each stands opposed to words that close the door — *extinct*, *defunct*, *barren*, *cancelled*. The differences are not about how inactive the thing is, but about **why it stopped and who stopped it**: an internal cycle, a lull between bouts, deliberate rest for recovery, or an authority pressing pause pending a condition. Register splits them too — two are everyday, two belong to clinics and committees.

- **dormant** — The unmarked, all-purpose member: nothing and nobody paused it — it's sleeping on its own internal clock, waiting on a season, a trigger, or nothing in particular. It's also the only one you'd use freely of seeds, volcanoes, bank accounts, and untapped talent alike, in ordinary conversation.
- **quiescent** — A clinical observer's word for the lull *between bouts* of something that has flared before and will flare again — a disease in remission, a market between shocks. Where **dormant** implies a nap, **quiescent** implies a history of activity and a technical register: you meet it in medicine, geology, and physics, rarely about a person.
- **fallow** — The only one that frames the idleness as **restorative**: the field is ploughed and deliberately unsown so the soil can recover, and the yield afterwards should be better for it. Applied to a career or a writer's decade, it's a generous verdict — it insists the ground is still good and something is replenishing underneath.
- **abeyance** — A noun, and the only member with an **agent and a condition**: someone with authority parked this, and a specific event — a ruling, a vote, an heir — is expected to restart it. Stiffly institutional (law, parliaments, HR letters) and effectively frozen into *in abeyance* / *held in abeyance*.

> **On the exam:** The exam separates these by the *cause* of the pause, not the depth of it: look for an agent-plus-condition ("pending the ruling") → abeyance, soil/productivity or a creative drought → fallow, a clinical or geological passage → quiescent, and plain sleep-with-a-comeback → dormant; also note abeyance is a noun, so the sentence slot alone often decides it.


<a id="meaning__wanting-nothing-more"></a>
### At ease — and whether that ease is earned

All three describe a person at rest: no craving, no alarm, no impulse to push for more or do more. What separates them is what the calm is aimed at — what you already possess, what you expect to happen, or how you rate yourself — and whether the writer thinks the calm is justified. On the GRE they cluster because each can sit in the same "despite the mounting problems, he remained ___" frame, but each makes a different claim about the person and carries a different verdict.

- **content** — Points backward and inward at what you already have — an absence of appetite, not a prediction about anything. It makes no claim that the future is safe and no claim about your own merit; its only vulnerable edge is that accepting what you've got can look like settling for it.
- **sanguine** — The forecast word: it's about how things will turn out, not about what you hold now, and it takes *about* a specific trouble — the deficit, the diagnosis, the quarter. Formal and temperamental rather than momentary, and deliberately unresolved: the writer may mean steady nerves or may mean the danger hasn't registered.
- **complacent** — The only rebuke of the three, and the only one aimed at the self — the calm is smug and unearned, and its consequence is named: you stop checking, stop training, stop improving. Where the others merely fail to worry, **complacent** says the failure is yours and the threat is still live.

> **On the exam:** The giveaway is the writer's verdict, not the calm itself: an approving or neutral clause takes **content**, a hedged forecast about a looming risk takes **sanguine**, and an explicit warning (the threat that goes unwatched, the effort that stops) takes **complacent**.


<a id="meaning__at-home-everywhere"></a>
### At home everywhere

All three praise what wide exposure does to a person: the rawness is gone, nothing startles them, and they can move through unfamiliar rooms without friction. Each names a different asset the exposure bought — geographic breadth, social smoothness, or acquired discrimination — and each takes a different opposite: narrow, boorish, naive. The GRE keeps them apart by what they attach to and what they quietly withhold.

- **cosmopolitan** — **Cosmopolitan** is about *range* — the absence of the provincial flinch at anything foreign. It's the only one here that describes a *place* (a cosmopolitan port, a cosmopolitan faculty) by the mix it contains, and it says nothing about whether the person has manners or taste; a blunt, badly dressed traveler can be cosmopolitan.
- **urbane** — **Urbane** is about performance in a room — the smooth, lightly witty ease that keeps a difficult dinner table talking. It's the narrowest of the three: only people, usually male and older, and only their manner. Praising a man as urbane compliments his surface while pointedly saying nothing about his depth or his sincerity.
- **sophisticated** — **Sophisticated** is about acquired discrimination — enough exposure to stop being impressed, to catch fine distinctions. Alone in this group it also goes to *things*, where it means intricate rather than worldly (a sophisticated algorithm, a sophisticated fraud). Its shadow is loss of innocence: sophistication is always worked up, never natural, so the word can chill where the other two only flatter.

> **On the exam:** The trap is the non-human sense: only **sophisticated** can modify an algorithm, an attack, or an argument's machinery — if the blank sits before an inanimate noun, **urbane** and **cosmopolitan** are dead on arrival.


<a id="meaning__attack-a-reputation"></a>
### Attacking a reputation

All five damage standing rather than refute substance: they go after the person's good name, not the merits of what the person said. All are formal, all are negative, and — importantly — nearly all tilt the reader's sympathy toward the target, quietly marking the attack as undeserved and the attacker as the one at fault. What separates them is the mechanics of the damage: how loud it is, whether it's a campaign or a single thrust, what specifically is being attacked (worth, honesty, or identity), and who does the branding — one accuser, a whisper network, or the whole society.

- **vilify** — The loudest of the group and the most public: **vilify** needs an audience — print, a podium, a pile-on. Where the others can be done quietly or in passing, this one is sustained character assassination, painting the target as wicked and worthless rather than merely inferior.
- **malign** — The quiet one. **Malign** is done behind the back — a steady drip of ill-speaking that never has to be public or organised, which is exactly why it's hard to answer. It also uniquely doubles as an adjective (*a malign influence*), where it means evil in effect and has nothing to do with speech at all.
- **denigrate** — Attacks *worth* rather than character: **denigrate** talks someone or their achievements down, belittling competence and value, and it can take an impersonal object — you can denigrate a book, a discipline, a whole body of work. Milder than vilify: it makes the target small, not monstrous.
- **impugn** — A single frontal thrust, not a campaign, and it lands specifically on **honesty** — motives, integrity, the credibility of a witness or the validity of a claim. It also stops short of proving anything: to **impugn** is to cast doubt, which is why the accuser often looks like the one overreaching. The natural habitat is courtroom and legislature.
- **stigmatize** — The disgrace is social and collective — **stigmatize** is what a whole society does, not what one speaker does, and the mark sticks to an identity or condition (addiction, poverty, mental illness) rather than to a rival's name. Alone in the group, its object is usually a class of people, and it lives in the passive with no attacker named.

> **On the exam:** The trap is the object: impugn takes motives and claims, stigmatize takes conditions and groups, denigrate takes achievements — so check what the sentence is attacking before you pick the word whose *tone* feels right.


<a id="meaning__back-a-claim-with-evidence"></a>
### Backing a Claim with Evidence

All of these belong to the formal language of proof — courtrooms, audits, newsrooms, research — where a statement is not accepted until something outside it does work on its behalf. They differ on *what the evidence does*: strengthen an existing story, discharge the burden on the person who told it, prop up a shaky structure, or settle a question that was still open. Three of them presuppose a claim already on the table; one of them is what you do before there is any claim at all. The GRE lives in that gap.

- **corroborate** — **Corroborate** demands a *second, independent* source agreeing with the first — the emphasis is on the separateness, not the strength. A witness corroborates another witness; you can never corroborate yourself, no matter how much evidence you pile up. The other three have no independence requirement at all.
- **substantiate** — **Substantiate** puts the burden on the speaker: you asserted it, now make it hold up. It attaches to things under suspicion — allegations, rumours, charges — and "unsubstantiated" is its natural home, an accusation left dangling. When someone asks you to substantiate a claim, they are challenging you, not helping you; corroboration, by contrast, is help arriving from outside.
- **buttress** — **Buttress** is the metaphor word, and the metaphor still bites: outside support, deliberately added, to a thing that would otherwise lean. It attaches to a position, argument, case or regime — never to a person, and never to a fact. Where *corroborate* is about the source's independence and *substantiate* about the speaker's burden, **buttress** is about the argument's structural weakness.
- **ascertain** — **Ascertain** is the outlier: it does not back a claim, it *settles a question*. There is no prior assertion to strengthen — you went looking and now you know for certain. Police ascertain the cause of a fire; they do not corroborate it. If the sentence has no claim already on the table, this is the only one of the four that fits.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating all four as interchangeable "prove" words: watch whether the sentence already contains a claim (substantiate/buttress), a *second* source (corroborate), or only an open question (ascertain).


<a id="meaning__sorry-after-the-fact"></a>
### Bad conscience, bruised pride, and the twinge before

All three name a private, uncomfortable feeling triggered by your own conduct or your own showing — the inward wince rather than anger at someone else. They split on two axes: **when** the feeling arrives (before the act or after it), and **what is injured** (your conscience or your dignity). Because all three are polite, restrained, formal-register words, English speakers reach for them interchangeably when they shouldn't — one of them involves no wrongdoing at all.

- **qualm** — The only one that arrives **before** the deed, and the only one small enough to be overridden — a flicker you can act straight through. It's also the only one usually measured by its absence: "had no qualms about firing them" grades someone's scruples, not their feelings.
- **contrite** — The only one that concedes actual fault and faces outward, toward the person wronged — defences down, excuses withdrawn. It's the strongest of the three and the one others read off you (you *look* contrite), which is why it can be faked and why "suitably contrite" is nearly always sardonic.
- **chagrin** — The only one where nothing wrong was done — your **pride** took the hit, not your conscience: outclassed, proved wrong, publicly wrong-footed. It's swallowed rather than displayed, and in its home phrase "much to my chagrin" the speaker is usually being wry about their own vanity.

> **On the exam:** The classic trap is treating **chagrin** as a guilt word: GRE sentences use it where the subject is merely embarrassed at being outdone, so a guilt/remorse answer choice fits the mood but not the meaning — and watch **qualm** appear negated, where the sentence is characterizing a person's ruthlessness, not their emotion.


<a id="meaning__utterly-baffled"></a>
### Baffled: fogged, stumped, stalled, outmatched

All four describe a mind that has stopped working on the problem in front of it. The differences are in *where the failure sits*: in the head (a fog), in the puzzle (a wall), in the response (a blank), or in the contest (a defeat). They also split hard on tone — two are informal and faintly comic, two are formal and let the confused party keep their dignity.

- **befuddled** — The fog is **inside the head** — the faculties themselves are dulled, so the person isn't tracking anything, not just this one problem. It's the only one that routinely comes from an agent that muddles you (drink, jargon, a lawyer's cross-examination), and the only one that quietly implies the subject is slow.
- **flummoxed** — The wits are fine; the **specific puzzle** beat them. You know exactly what you're looking at — the flat-pack instructions, the error message — and have no move. It's the most visible of the four (it shows on your face) and the one people cheerfully apply to themselves, because the joke is on the problem as much as on them.
- **nonplussed** — You may understand perfectly — what fails is the **reply**. It's a stall in the response system after something socially unaccountable, and it exonerates you: the world was strange, not you. Formal, and the only one about being struck speechless rather than about not comprehending.
- **confound** — The only **verb**, and the only one where something *wins*. It takes abstract objects the others can't — predictions, critics, expectations — and carries two senses beyond bewilderment: to defeat what was forecast, and to conflate two things that should stay apart.

> **On the exam:** Two traps: **nonplussed** is baited with the popular-but-wrong "unfazed" sense (it means the opposite — stalled, not unbothered), and **confound** shows up on the test far more often as "defeat expectations" or "conflate" than as plain "bewilder."


<a id="meaning__bare-and-comfortless"></a>
### Bare and comfortless

All four say: nothing extra here — no ornament, no cushion, no indulgence. They separate on *what* is stripped and *why*. Some describe only a surface (nothing was added), some describe conditions (nothing is provided), and one describes a will (everything was refused). They're ordered below by how much self-denial they imply, from purely decorative plainness to a whole life built on renunciation.

- **unadorned** — **Unadorned** is the only one that judges nothing but the surface — it says nothing was *added*, not that anything is lacking, so an unadorned room can still be warm and comfortable. It's also the one that goes on facts and prose (the *unadorned truth*), where it means no flattering trim rather than no comfort.
- **austere** — **Austere** is the only one that reaches the face and manner: an austere man is unsmiling and unbending, not merely under-furnished. It's also the word for policy and money — austerity budgets, austerity measures — where it means the perks were cut, and it chills when applied to a person in a way the others don't.
- **spartan** — **Spartan** rates the *conditions* — the thin blanket, the cold barracks, the one bare bulb — and implies toughness in whoever puts up with them. It attaches to quarters, camps, and rations rather than to a face or a prose style, and it's the likeliest of the four to double as a dry complaint about what wasn't provided.
- **ascetic** — **Ascetic** is about the will, not the furniture: it names a program of renouncing pleasure, usually for religious or moral reasons, so it says what a person has *refused* rather than what he lacks. It's the only one that's also a noun for such a person, and the only one that can tip into a charge of extremism.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable synonyms for "plain": sentence-equivalence pairs turn on evidence of *choice* (ascetic, spartan) versus mere absence of decoration (unadorned), and only austere fits a person's demeanor or a national budget.


<a id="meaning__beg-from-below"></a>
### Begging, from dignified to abject

All four describe approaching someone who holds power over you and trying to move them — by asking, by kneeling, by apologising, by flattering. What separates them is not the request but the **dignity**: how much of it the asker keeps, whether the surrender is chosen or merely witnessed, and whether the observer respects the person or is embarrassed for them. The list runs from composed pleading down to self-abasement. Two of them can only be said *about* someone, never *by* them.

- **entreat** — The only one where dignity survives intact. **Entreat** is what the powerless say with their posture unchanged and their manners on — the force comes from affection or respect, not desperation, and the observer thinks no less of them. It's also the only word here you can apply to yourself without irony ("I entreated him to reconsider").
- **supplicate** — Adds the **body**: kneeling, hands out. The abasement is deliberate and often ritually correct — this is the word for prayer, for petitioning a king, for the defeated asking mercy, where lowering yourself is the proper form. Contempt enters only when the setting is ordinary; "supplicated for a raise" is withering precisely because no altar was involved.
- **grovel** — The abasement is the **observer's verdict**, not a ritual. **Grovel** attaches to one occasion and usually to an apology that overshot — you grovel for forgiveness, for an extension, after a screw-up. No one claims it for themselves except as a joke, and it makes the reader wince on the person's behalf.
- **fawn** — The only one that isn't a request. **Fawn** is ongoing courtship of favour — hovering, agreeing, laughing too hard — with nothing specific being asked for, aimed at a boss, a celebrity, a rich uncle. Doggish and physical, and it takes *over* or *on*: you fawn over someone, whereas you entreat or supplicate them directly.

> **On the exam:** The exam hides a register swap: a courteous, respected plea needs **entreat**, but the tempting wrong answers (**grovel**, **fawn**) drag in contempt the sentence never earned — and **fawn** fails outright whenever something specific is actually being asked for.


<a id="meaning__belonging-to-a-dead-era"></a>
### Belonging to a dead era

All four say: this belongs to a time that has passed, and the present has moved on. They part company on *why* it's stranded. One turns on nobody using it anymore, one on something better replacing it, one on it sitting in the wrong century, one on it being a shrunken leftover of something larger. Sorting them means asking what evidence the speaker is pointing at: disuse, a successor, a mismatch, or a remnant.

- **archaic** — **Archaic** is about *disuse* — the form still exists, but nobody reaches for it. It needs no successor and no absurdity, just abandonment, which is why it's the default word for language and manners (**thou**, a courtly bow). Uniquely in this group it has a clean technical register ("Archaic Greek"); the insult only switches on when the target is a live institution or someone's opinions.
- **obsolete** — **Obsolete** is the only one that requires a *replacement* — something better came along and the world routed around it. That makes it the standard word for technology and skills, and the cruelest one for people: not behind, but roleless. It's also the only member that verbs (a firm **obsoletes** its own product line), which is business register, not literary.
- **anachronistic** — **Anachronistic** is the only one built on *mismatch with surroundings* — it needs a frame it doesn't fit, so an observer catches it: a wristwatch on a gladiator, a dueling statute still on the books. It's a verdict on placement rather than on usefulness, and applied to institutions it carries a dry contempt the others don't: not merely old, but *ridiculous* that it lasted.
- **vestigial** — **Vestigial** is the only one implying *shrinkage from a larger whole* — the thing was once bigger and load-bearing, and what's left is a stub that still exists but does nothing. Borrowed from biology, it stays clinical: calling a board's veto power vestigial is a diagnosis, not a jab, and unlike the others it says nothing about whether anyone should get rid of it.

> **On the exam:** The GRE's giveaway is the trigger phrase: "superseded by" → obsolete, "out of place in its period" → anachronistic, "no longer in use" → archaic, "surviving remnant of" → vestigial; wrong answers work because all four fit a bare "old and useless" blank.


<a id="meaning__devoted-follower"></a>
### Below the Master: Server, Student, Newcomer

All three name someone standing *below* somebody else inside a faith, school, or movement — defined not by what they do but by their position relative to a master or an established inner circle. Every one comes out of religious life and drags that incense into secular use, so applying one to a CEO's staff or an economist's followers is always a small rhetorical choice. The differences are axis differences: one is about **service**, one about **transmitted doctrine**, one about **arrival date**. They stop being interchangeable the moment you ask whether the person is learning, fetching, or merely new.

- **acolyte** — The one who **attends**, not the one who understands — the function is service, and the loyalty has outrun independent judgement. It is an outsider's word, usually plural and faceless ("the founder and his acolytes"), and the sneer targets the flattery, not the inexperience: an acolyte can be fifty and hold a title.
- **disciple** — The only one here that implies **absorbed content and onward transmission** — a named master, a doctrine, a duty to carry it. Where the word above marks servility, this one can be genuine tribute ("a disciple of Keynes"); the raised eyebrow, when it comes, is for repeating the master too faithfully, not for hovering near him.
- **neophyte** — Says nothing about devotion, service, or a master — only about **how recently the person was let in**. Time alone cures it, which is not true of the other two, and the condescension concerns competence under the gaze of the already-initiated. Its threshold can be a field, craft, or firm, not just a faith.

> **On the exam:** The trap is **neophyte**: it joins this cluster by religious origin, not by devotion — its antonyms are *veteran, adept, old hand*, so a sentence about zeal or servility wants one of the other two.


<a id="meaning__beyond-argument"></a>
### Beyond argument

All four say the same thing at first glance: there is nothing left to argue about. The differences lie in *why* the argument is over — because the evidence answered the question, because the proof cannot be attacked, because the claim was never up for debate to begin with, or because the thing has no seam to pry open. Three of them are verdicts reached after examination; one is a premise granted before it. And one describes a structure rather than a truth.

- **conclusive** — **Conclusive** is about a *pending question being closed*. It attaches to evidence, tests, results — things produced to settle something specific — and marks the moment inquiry can stop. Hence its natural home in the negative: *inconclusive*, *no conclusive evidence*, meaning the question is still open.
- **incontrovertible** — **Incontrovertible** grades how well the proof withstands attack, not whether it answered anything. A fact can be incontrovertible and completely beside the point, where *conclusive* always implies it resolved the matter at issue. It's also the heaviest register of the four — documents, data, DNA — and in ordinary speech it can sound pompous.
- **axiomatic** — **Axiomatic** is the odd one: no evidence has been offered at all. It sits *before* the argument as a granted starting point, where the others are earned at the end. Watch for the rhetorical move — "it is axiomatic that…" fences a claim off from dispute rather than proving it.
- **ironclad** — **Ironclad** describes a structure, not a truth — an alibi, a contract, a guarantee, a rule: things with seams that someone is actively trying to pry open. It promises no loophole exists, so it's the only one here you'd apply to a document or an arrangement rather than to a claim about the world. Aimed at a person's principles, it can turn cold.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating these as interchangeable degrees of certainty: a completed-sentence blank about *unproven assumptions* wants **axiomatic**, one about *contracts and alibis* wants **ironclad**, and only a blank about evidence answering a question takes **conclusive**.


<a id="meaning__boil-it-down"></a>
### Boil it down

All four involve taking something large and rendering it in reduced form — the long paper, the two-hour lecture, the decade of work, made small enough to hold at once. They diverge on *what the reduction is for*: pulling the idea off the particulars, going back over ground in order, gaining altitude over the whole, or burning off everything that isn't essential. Three describe an act of compression; one of them is really about a vantage point. The GRE cares about which axis the sentence is pointing at.

- **abstract** — The only one here with a life outside summarizing: as an adjective it means *unattached to the concrete*, which is a claim about the idea's nature, not its length. As a noun it names a specific artifact — the fixed block of text at the head of a paper. As a verb it is bare extraction: you abstract a principle from cases with no promise that the result is ordered, broad, or potent, only that it has been lifted free.
- **recapitulate** — The only one that requires the material to have been covered already — the *re-* is load-bearing. It is retrospective and sequential: you walk the same path again, in the same order, faster. It adds nothing new by definition, and it lives at the end of things, where the other three can open a work.
- **synoptic** — Not an act but a vantage — an adjective for the view, not the labor of shortening. Its axis is width, not brevity: a synoptic treatment can be long, so long as every part is visible in relation to the others. It carries quiet approval of altitude gained, and it stays formal — meteorologists, theologians and strategists use it straight.
- **distill** — The only one where the product is *stronger* than the source. Its axis is purity: everything inessential is discarded, so what remains is concentrated rather than merely brief. It flatters the person doing it — distilling implies patience and the judgement to know what to throw away, which recapitulating pointedly does not.

> **On the exam:** The exam treats these as interchangeable synonyms for "summarize" and lets one clue decide: "again, in order, at the close" → recapitulate; "the whole seen at once, breadth" → synoptic; "purer and more potent than the original" → distill; "away from the particular case" → abstract.


<a id="meaning__bought-and-paid-for"></a>
### Bought and paid for

All four describe people or arrangements in which profit has crowded out an obligation — to a cause, an office, a rule, or another person. Each is an accusation, and each locates the rot in a different place: in the actor's motive, in the sale of a duty, in the absence of internal restraint, or in the shape of the relationship itself. They are confusable because a single villain can be all four at once; the exam separates them by asking which element the sentence actually supplies. Note also that only some of them require money at all.

- **mercenary** — Names the **motive and nothing else** — the only one of the four that describes no wrongdoing. A **mercenary** consultant may follow every rule and serve you well; the charge is that the fee is the entire reason. It stings precisely where affection or conviction was expected (a friend, an artist, a doctor), which is why it needs no victim and no broken duty to land.
- **venal** — Requires **an office and a bribe**. **Venal** attaches to someone holding a public trust — a judge, an inspector, a customs officer — and says the trust itself has a price list. Where mercenary describes a private motive, **venal** describes a betrayal that is usually criminal, and the formal register makes it a charge levelled from outside; nobody calls themselves venal.
- **unscrupulous** — The only one that says nothing about money. **Unscrupulous** names a missing brake, not a goal: the person would lie, cheat, or cut the corner for any prize at all. It describes **method**, and it quietly concedes effectiveness — the unscrupulous operator wins, which is the point of the warning. A venal official is unscrupulous about one specific thing; an **unscrupulous** one is that way by default.
- **exploitative** — Judges the **arrangement, not the person** — a wage, a lease, a contract can be **exploitative** while everyone involved is perfectly sincere. It alone demands a power imbalance: someone with no other option is being used up. The verdict is already rendered by the speaker, so it appears in argument (op-eds, reports), where the other three appear as character sketches.

> **On the exam:** The trap is swapping **venal** for **mercenary** — check whether the sentence gives you an office being sold (venal) or merely a fee-driven motive (mercenary); and remember **exploitative** modifies the deal while **unscrupulous** modifies the dealer.


<a id="meaning__break-the-rule-openly"></a>
### Breaking rules: the breach, the text, the line, the deed

All four sit at the moment a rule is broken, and all four are unfavourable — but they answer different questions. Two are about *how* the breach happens (with contempt on display, or as a bare procedural conflict), one is about *what kind of line* was crossed (moral, not merely administrative), and one is not about a rule at all but about the badness of the deed itself. Register also splits them: three come from statutes, courtrooms and press releases, one from scripture and conscience.

- **flout** — The only one that describes **manner**: the rule is known, the breach is deliberate, and the offender wants an audience. Strip away the visible contempt and you can no longer use it — an accidental or hidden breach is never flouting.
- **contravene** — The coolest of the four and the only one indifferent to intent: it merely records that an act conflicts with a written provision, so it works fine for an honest mistake. It wants a document as its object — an article, a clause, a treaty — and its second sense has no wrongdoer at all, since evidence can contravene a hypothesis.
- **transgression** — The moral one, and the only noun here — it names the completed act, not the doing of it. It presumes a boundary with real authority behind it (conscience, God, the community), which is why it sounds too heavy for a parking ticket and why shrinking it to a trivial offence reads as a joke.
- **perpetrate** — Attaches to the **deed**, not the rule: a hoax, a fraud, an atrocity — things that need no statute to be bad. The disapproval lives in the verb itself, so it cannot take a neutral or good object the way *commit* can in "commit to a plan."

> **On the exam:** The traps are near-homophones, not meanings: **flout** ≠ *flaunt* (display proudly), **perpetrate** ≠ *perpetuate* (keep going) — and watch the part of speech, since **transgression** is the lone noun in a set of verbs.


<a id="meaning__open-opposition-to-authority"></a>
### Breaking with the official line

All five describe a public break with something authoritative — a ruling, a regime, an order, a creed, a reputation everyone treats as settled. Each is defined by the thing it pushes against, so none of them mean much in isolation; you need an establishment for them to work. The splits are three: what is opposed (an official position, a punishing power, a chain of command, a doctrine, a sacred cow), whether the break is speech, belief, or action, and whether the label flatters the person it lands on.

- **dissent** — The only one that names the *act* rather than a person or a standing disposition — a discrete, on-the-record disagreement, usually filed inside the same body that overruled it (a dissenting opinion, a dissenting vote). It costs you nothing but your position on the record; the machinery it argues with is procedural, not punitive.
- **dissident** — Names the *person*, and the only one where the price is personal — exile, prison, a career ended. Its weapon is still just speech, but it presumes a government, church, or party with the power to retaliate, which is why it never fits a critic of something harmless. The label is also contested: the regime uses it to mark a problem, everyone else to mean brave.
- **mutiny** — The only crime in the group, and the only one that requires a prior oath and a chain of command — subordinates rising against their own commanders. It is action, not argument: a crew seizes the ship, it does not file a brief. Borrowed for offices and teams, it does the work of casting the boss as a captain and the staff as insubordinate.
- **heterodox** — Belief only, and measured against a *doctrine* rather than an authority that can punish — the deviation is intellectual and the deviator is still inside the tent, arguing with the creed rather than renouncing it. It carries a faint respectability that none of the others do: rival economists get called heterodox, and are happy to take the name.
- **iconoclastic** — Targets what is *revered*, not what is official — reputations, sacred assumptions, untouchable institutions. It requires scale (nobody is an iconoclast for questioning the seating plan) and it arrives with admiration attached, the word obituaries and profiles use as praise for someone whose demolition was worth it.

> **On the exam:** The trap is target-swapping: **heterodox** deviates from a doctrine while still inside it, **iconoclastic** demolishes what's venerated, and **dissident** requires a power that can punish — the GRE builds sentences where only one of those conditions is actually present in the context.


<a id="meaning__bring-into-being"></a>
### Bring about vs. draw out

All five stand between an act and a result: something comes into existence, or comes to the surface, because of what someone or something did. They divide on two axes. First, is the result **new** or was it **already there, latent**, waiting to be pulled out? Second, what is the manner of the causing — an unintended by-product, a laid path, a premature tipping-over, a direct request, or a suggestion?

- **engender** — The one with **no intention behind it**: a situation throws off trust, resentment, debate as a by-product, and no one is doing the engendering on purpose. Its object is an abstract condition or climate, never a person's specific reply and never a physical thing — and the register is editorial/judicial, where *cause* would sound blunt.
- **induce** — The only one that takes **a person plus an infinitive** — *induced him to sign* — with an inducement (money, a discount, a threat softened into an offer) doing the work; the subject still walks in on their own feet. In its other sense the result is deliberately **artificial or early**: a drug induces sleep, a doctor induces labour, and neither would have arrived on its own.
- **precipitate** — Says the outcome was **already loaded** and you merely tipped it over — you didn't build the crisis, you dropped it ahead of schedule. Alone in this group it is reliably **negative and premature**, and as an adjective it turns on the actor: precipitate action is rash, not decisive.
- **elicit** — **Transactional and targeted** — you ask, prompt or provoke, and one specific latent thing comes back: an answer, a confession, a laugh, a groan. It requires a person on the receiving end and a deliberate act on yours; nothing gets elicited by accident or by atmosphere.
- **evoke** — Works by **association and suggestion**, not by asking: a smell, a chord, a photograph summons a mood or memory that was sleeping, with no request made and often no one addressed. It is the standard verb of **criticism** — a novel *evokes* an era, meaning it conjures without stating.

> **On the exam:** The exam leans on elicit vs. evoke (a specific response pulled from a person vs. a mood conjured by suggestion) and hides precipitate behind clue words like *suddenly*, *prematurely*, or *tensions already mounting*.


<a id="meaning__there-by-nature"></a>
### Built in — by nature, birth, place, or habit

All four say a quality is a permanent part of something rather than a passing or superficial addition — it won't wash off, and you can't separate it from the thing without changing what the thing is. The confusion is that they agree on *fixed* and differ entirely on *how it got there*: from the thing's own essence, from birth, from long residence in a place, or from years of repetition. Two of them also carry a verdict — one indicts an institution, one concedes defeat — while the other two are purely descriptive.

- **intrinsic** — The analytical one, and the only one defined by a contrast rather than an origin story: it answers "what's left when you strip off everything added from outside?" — value vs. price, motivation vs. bonus. It says nothing about when the quality appeared, and it applies happily to objects, arguments, and abstractions, not just living things.
- **inborn** — The only word pinned to a moment in time — birth — and the only one that needs a creature to be born. Plain and human where *intrinsic* is clinical: you use it of a real person's instincts, gifts, or defects, not of gold's value or a ministry's corruption.
- **endemic** — The only one that locates the trait in a *place or population* rather than in an individual: a disease, a species, or a vice that lives there permanently instead of visiting. Its force comes from the contrast with *epidemic* — no surge, no passing — and turned on an institution it becomes an accusation that the rot is structural.
- **ingrained** — The odd one out on origin: nothing here came with the thing, it was worked in by repetition over years. And it's the only one you reach for as a concession — saying a prejudice or a stain is ingrained is admitting you expect to fail at removing it.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable "natural/inherent" synonyms: **ingrained** is acquired (habit, not birth), **endemic** attaches to a place or population rather than an individual, and **intrinsic** contrasts with *extrinsic*, not with *learned* — GRE sentences usually hinge on exactly that contrast word.


<a id="meaning__burning-with-feeling"></a>
### Burning with feeling: ardent, fervent, fervid, zealous, fervor

All of these describe feeling at high temperature — devotion, conviction, or enthusiasm burning hot enough to be visible from outside. The shared image is literal heat (Latin *ardere*, "to burn"; *fervere*, "to boil"), applied to belief, love, or commitment to a cause. What separates them is not how much heat but who is holding the thermometer: whether the speaker admires the intensity, quietly distrusts it, or is just reporting the temperature. One is a noun; the rest are adjectives.

- **ardent** — The flattering one, and the only member that comfortably covers romantic love — an **ardent** suitor, an **ardent** admirer. Its heat is directional: it points toward what you're devoted to, so you can be an ardent opponent of a bill but never ardent with rage.
- **fervent** — The sincerity word. **Fervent** vouches for the feeling as genuine and unembarrassed, and it attaches to quiet inward states — a fervent hope, prayer, wish, belief — where *ardent* wants a beloved and *zealous* wants a campaign.
- **fervid** — Same root as *fervent*, one degree hotter and pointed the other way. Choosing **fervid** over *fervent* is a deliberate signal that the writer is standing outside the emotion and finds it overheated: a fervid nationalist, a fervid denunciation. Literary; nobody calls their own convictions fervid.
- **zealous** — The only one that requires a mission and visible effort — something is being *served*, tirelessly. **Zealous** describes conduct, not temperature: a zealous prosecutor is out doing things, and the word concedes he may be doing too many of them.
- **fervor** — The noun, and the name for the heat itself rather than for a person who has it — the emotional temperature of a crowd or an era. It keeps famous company (*religious*, *patriotic*, *revolutionary* **fervor**), which is exactly why it can either praise sincerity or hint that a mob has stopped thinking.

> **On the exam:** The exam rarely tests the shared "intense" sense — it tests the tilt, so watch for a sentence whose context word ("mob," "excess," "blindly," "admirable," "sincere") decides between fervent/ardent (approving) and fervid/zealous (raised eyebrow); it also uses fervid as a lookalike trap for fervent.


<a id="meaning__calm-and-untroubled"></a>
### Calm and untroubled

All four mean nothing is stirring — no ripple, no agitation, no disturbance. What separates them is *what* is undisturbed and how the writer feels about it: a visible face or sky, a whole setting, a surface that nothing can ruffle, or a process that has simply stopped for now. Approval is not shared either — one is admiring, one is warm, one is double-edged, one is coolly indifferent. And only one of them implies the calm is temporary.

- **serene** — The only one with dignity — calm that is *displayed*, unclouded and faintly luminous, which is why it survives in **Your Serene Highness**. It's also the group's word for composure held while things go badly: a serene face in a collapsing room. Nobody is ever serene by accident.
- **tranquil** — The scene-setter: it attaches to places and moments — a village, a lake at dusk, an afternoon — far more readily than to a person under strain. It implies nothing ever disturbed the thing, so it can't describe calm recovered after an upset, and it is always warm and approving.
- **placid** — The only one that can be an insult. It describes a surface nothing ruffles — water, a face, a disposition — with no claim about inner life, so unflappable slides straight into unexcitable, incurious, bovine. If the sentence sounds faintly condescending about a person, this is the word.
- **quiescent** — Not a mood at all — it rates *activity*, not feeling, and can take a volcano, a tumour, a market, a feud. Uniquely it means paused rather than peaceful: the thing is expected back. Clinical and cold; a quiescent disease is nobody's idyll.

> **On the exam:** Sentence equivalence loves pairing these as if interchangeable — decide on the noun (a place → tranquil, a process that will resume → quiescent) and the writer's attitude (admiring → serene, faintly dismissive → placid).


<a id="meaning__can-be-made-to-work"></a>
### Can Be Made to Work

All four give a plan, claim, or arrangement a passing grade — it holds up, it can go forward. But each tests a *different* stress. One asks whether you can get it off the ground; one whether it stays alive afterward; one whether it withstands an attacker; one whether it has a crack in it. All four are verdicts of inspection rather than admiration, which is why they cluster: none of them means *good*, and three of them are famous for faint praise.

- **feasible** — **Feasible** is the only one of the four measured against *resources* — the time, money, labor, and physics you actually have. It rules on the front end, before anything exists, and it is indifferent to whether the thing should exist: a scheme can be feasible and monstrous. Nobody defends a feasible plan; they cost it out.
- **viable** — **Viable** starts where feasible stops — the thing has been launched, and the question is whether it survives on its own without life support. Alone in this group it carries the literal biological sense (a viable fetus, a viable seed), and that origin sets its bar: not thriving, just not dying. "A viable option" is the standard damning-with-faint-praise construction.
- **tenable** — **Tenable** presupposes an *opponent* — it is the only one that needs someone attacking. It attaches to positions and claims you must hold under cross-examination, and it grants only that the attack hasn't succeeded yet, not that the claim is true. It also shows up far more often in the negative: **untenable** is the live form, and it means "you cannot keep standing here."
- **sound** — **Sound** looks *inward* at structure rather than outward at attackers or resources: no defect, no crack, nothing rotten at the foundation. It applies to things a scan or an audit could clear — buildings, arguments, sleep, minds — and it deliberately withholds any claim of brilliance ("sound, if unexciting"). It is also the group's only word with a second life as a verb: to **sound** is to measure depth, hence *sound out* and *sound the depths*.

> **On the exam:** The exam works two angles: negatives (**untenable** = indefensible, **unsound** = broken at the root — both harsher than their positives are warm), and tone questions where **viable** or **sound** is the correct *lukewarm* answer against a flattering-sounding trap.


<a id="meaning__cancel-out-a-plan-or-force"></a>
### Cancel Out a Plan or Force

All five describe something's intended effect failing to land: a plan doesn't come off, a prediction doesn't hold, a movement doesn't spread, a force doesn't register. The split is in *what gets cancelled* and *who does the cancelling* — a scheme mid-execution, an expectation, a rising challenge to authority, an opposing force, or an instrument that had legal standing. A second split is manner: interception, humiliation, suppression from above, exact counterbalance, or voiding.

- **foil** — **Foil** needs a specific plot already in motion and an opponent who intercepts it at the last moment — you foil a heist, never a force or a statute. It leaves the schemer looking inept rather than crushed, which is why it lives in headlines and adventure plots.
- **confound** — **Confound** is the only one whose object can be a *mind* or an *expectation*: it defeats forecasters, critics, and doctors, and the defeat is embarrassing to them. It also uniquely carries the "mix up two things that should stay apart" sense — correlation with cause.
- **quash** — **Quash** requires authority pressing downward — a court, a general, a government — on something rising: a revolt, a rumour, an indictment. Alone in this group it insists on one decisive stroke; anything that resurfaces was never quashed.
- **neutralize** — **Neutralize** cancels a force that is still there — a striker, an acid, a threat — by balancing it, not removing it. Its clinical flatness is the point: it's the word bureaucracies choose when they don't want to name the violence.
- **nullify** — **Nullify** strips a thing of force so it counts as if it never had any — a verdict voided, a raise eaten exactly by inflation. Where **neutralize** offsets an active opponent, **nullify** works on standing and arithmetic: the net is zero, and there's nothing to keep opposing.

> **On the exam:** Watch the object: schemes are foiled, expectations confounded, uprisings quashed, opponents neutralized, instruments nullified — and **confound** is planted where "confuse" feels right but "defeat" is meant.


<a id="meaning__careful-to-the-last-detail"></a>
### Careful to the last detail

All five praise work done with more care than the minimum — nothing skimped, nothing waved through. They diverge on *what the care is measured against*: the fineness of each detail, the hours of grinding labour, the conscience of the person doing it, the completeness of the process, or the completeness of the coverage. Swap one for another and you praise the wrong thing — you credit patience when you meant precision, or workmanship when you meant honesty. The GRE builds sentences whose surrounding clue picks exactly one of those axes.

- **meticulous** — The **finest grain** of the five: it judges the quality of attention paid to each small detail, not how long it took or how much ground was covered. Alone in the group it carries a faint anxious edge — the fourth recheck — so it can tip into fussiness in a way *thorough* and *exhaustive* never do.
- **painstaking** — Credits the **labour**, not the result — patience and stamina rather than precision or conscience. It needs slow, fiddly work to sit on (a painstaking reconstruction, a painstaking translation); attach it to a quick job and it reads as sarcasm, which is not a risk with the others.
- **scrupulous** — The only one about **conscience**. It describes a person refusing a shortcut nobody would catch, not a person catching every decimal — a meticulous accountant balances the columns, a scrupulous one won't cook them. Even in its "exact" sense (*scrupulous attention to detail*) the care is felt as an obligation, something owed.
- **thorough** — Praises the **process, plainly** — went everywhere, checked everything — with no implication of cleverness, no fussiness, and no moral weight. It is the workmanlike middle: less fine than *meticulous*, less absolute than *exhaustive*. Uniquely, it also works as a bare intensifier before a noun, and there it turns hostile: *a thorough scoundrel*.
- **exhaustive** — Measures **coverage, not effort or care** — every case on the list eliminated, nothing left to check. A thorough search was done properly; an exhaustive one is finished by definition. Its only shadow is excess: an exhaustive reply to a simple question is more than anyone asked for.

> **On the exam:** Sentence completions plant a moral clue (honesty, temptation, a bribe refused) to force **scrupulous** where students reach for *meticulous*, and pair *exhaustive* with completeness language (\"every case,\" \"nothing remained\") where *thorough* would be merely adequate.


<a id="meaning__cautious-foresight"></a>
### Caution That Counts as Good Judgment

All four describe caution that counts as *good judgment* rather than nerves — the actor has surveyed the risks and deliberately chosen to go slow, use less, or say nothing. They are the vocabulary of lawyers, bankers, editors and policy memos: formal, approving, faintly bloodless. The confusion is that English lets them share the same sentence frame, while each actually points at a different stage of the act — deciding, proportioning, watching, withholding.

- **prudent** — Aimed at **future consequences to your own position** — the risk you are managing is one you will personally have to pay for. It is the word of savings, insurance, reserves and contingency plans, and it judges the *decision* as sound rather than the actor as skillful.
- **judicious** — The only one about **proportion rather than risk**. Praise for hitting the right *amount* — a judicious edit, a judicious dose, a judicious silence — so a judicious act can be bold, even aggressive, as long as it stopped at the correct point. Nothing here implies danger was avoided.
- **circumspect** — Literally *looking around*: the caution is **outward-facing and pre-emptive**, a scan of who is watching and what could go wrong before you commit or speak. It attaches to conduct and speech under scrutiny, and it is the one that can tip into criticism — too circumspect means too slow to commit.
- **chary** — The only one about **withholding a supply**. It takes *of* or *about* — chary of praise, chary of lending — and rates how little you hand over, not how carefully you move. Neutral to mildly unflattering: caution here shades toward tight-fistedness in a way the other three never do.

> **On the exam:** The exam splits them by grammar and object: a blank followed by *of* wants **chary**; a blank about *how much* of something was used wants **judicious**; a blank about protecting future assets wants **prudent** — and **circumspect** shows up where the sentence mentions observers, scrutiny, or what someone declined to say.


<a id="meaning__cheat-someone-out-of-something"></a>
### Cheat someone out of something

All four describe getting the better of someone by trickery rather than force — the victim is talked into it, not overpowered. The differences are about where the sentence's weight falls: on the loot taken, on the credulous person taken in, on the technique used, or on the smooth talk that produced a yes. They also differ in what they grammatically attach to — a sum of money, a person, a whole style of conduct, or an action the victim performs themselves.

- **swindle** — The only one that requires **property actually changing hands** — a **swindle** that nets nothing is just a lie. It's also the group's tabloid word: big scheme, plausible cover story, named sum of money, and a victim the writer plainly pities.
- **dupe** — Nothing has to be stolen — the payoff is **belief**, not money, so you can be **duped** into voting, signing, or simply thinking something false. The word convicts the victim of credulity rather than the trickster of a crime, which is why it alone doubles as a noun for the sucker.
- **chicanery** — The abstract one: an uncountable noun for a **method**, not an act done to a named person. **Chicanery** works through the rules — loopholes, quibbles, fine print, procedure — so it needs an institutional setting and can't describe a lie told over a handshake.
- **inveigle** — The victim does the deed themselves; **inveigle** produces a **yes**, extracted by flattery and charm rather than by a fabricated story. It's the only one that's about tone of voice — smooth, coaxing — and the only one built on *into*: inveigle someone into lending, or inveigle your way into a room.

> **On the exam:** Watch the frame: only **inveigle** takes a person + *into* + an action, only **chicanery** is a mass noun with no direct victim, and **dupe** vs **swindle** splits on whether anything was actually taken.


<a id="meaning__cheeky-disrespect-upward"></a>
### Cheeky disrespect upward

All four accuse someone of failing to stay in their place. They require an implied hierarchy — a superior, an elder, a host, an expert — and the offence is not cruelty or crudeness but **presumption**: acting as though the rank difference weren't there. Because the accusation only makes sense from above, each says as much about the accuser (who expected deference) as about the accused, and all four carry a starched, slightly old-fashioned air.
