Where *peripheral* moves something to the edge and *extraneous* throws it out, **incidental** grants full membership and denies only importance (hence *incidentals*: real costs, small ones).

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating these as interchangeable synonyms for "irrelevant" — sentence completions hinge on the connection axis: **extraneous** requires an outside source, **incidental** requires the thing to arise from the main event, and only **digression** is a countable stretch of talk rather than a judgment.


<a id="meaning__wandering-off-the-subject"></a>
### Off the point — or just going on too long

All four describe talk or writing that gives a subject more room than the listener wanted. Two axes are tangled here: **direction** (does the speaker leave the main road?) and **duration** (does the speaker stay on it too long?). Most of these words criticize, but each aims at something different — the shape of the detour, the tedium of the drift, the relevance of the remark, or the sheer volume of words. Confusing them means mistaking a length complaint for a relevance complaint.

- **digression** — The only one that is a **countable, bounded unit** with a return trip built in — you can have three digressions in a lecture and still arrive at the point. It's also the only one a speaker cheerfully commits on purpose ("but I digress"), which is why it stays mild: it presumes a main argument competent enough to come back to.
- **ramble** — Presumes no destination at all — where a digression leaves a road, **rambling** never had one. The charge is tedium and drift, not error or irrelevance, and it's the bluntest insult of the four. It's also the only word here with a genuinely warm sense: a **ramble** through the hills is a pleasure, because aimlessness is the point of a walk and the flaw of a speech.
- **tangential** — The only **adjective**, and the only one judging relevance rather than length — a single sentence can be **tangential** while a forty-minute answer isn't. It's the reviewer's and the lawyer's verdict: it concedes the connection is real, then rules it out of bounds, which makes it politer than *irrelevant* and just as final.
- **expatiate** — The outlier: the speaker never leaves the subject — they stay on it far past necessity. Takes *on* or *upon* plus a topic, and describes volume, never wandering. It's the writer's word for someone holding forth, delivered with a raised eyebrow and never applied to oneself.

> **On the exam:** The trap is **expatiate**: it belongs to length, not wandering, so any answer treating it as \"stray off-topic\" is wrong — and **tangential** grades relevance where the other three grade duration.


<a id="meaning__offending-against-good-form"></a>
### Offending against good form

All four condemn something said or done that shouldn't have been — and none of them condemns it as *wrong*. No one is harmed, no law or moral rule is broken; what's been violated is an unwritten code about how a person in that position, on that occasion, ought to behave. The speaker is judging form, polish, or calculation, which is why every one of these words is cooler and more fastidious than *rude* or *disgraceful*. The differences lie in which code was broken and who pays for breaking it.

- **indecorous** — The narrowest and most literal: the **occasion** sets a required register and the act missed it — too jolly, too loud, too familiar for a funeral, a ceremony, a courtroom. Pure etiquette-column vocabulary, so it usually sounds gently arch rather than truly scandalised.
- **unseemly** — Turns on **how it looks given who you are** — a judge shouting, ministers bickering on camera, relatives circling an inheritance before the burial. Unlike *indecorous*, it can hint at an ugly motive showing through, and it's the word institutions reach for: the raised eyebrow of someone embarrassed *for* you.
- **gauche** — The fault sits in the **person, not in the act's fit to the occasion** — they lacked the polish to know better. It's a verdict from above about breeding rather than a description of a breach, so it convicts the speaker of snobbery as much as the subject of clumsiness.
- **impolitic** — The only one where **your manners were fine and the damage lands on you**. It faults calculation, not propriety: a perfectly courteous remark that weakens your own hand. Understated and strategic — a diplomat's substitute for *stupid*.

> **On the exam:** **Impolitic** is the trap: it sits among manners words but means *badly judged*, and the classic stem describes someone scrupulously polite who still wrecked his own position — where *unseemly* or *gauche* would be wrong.


<a id="meaning__on-watchful-guard"></a>
### On watchful guard

All four describe a guard that hasn't been lowered — attention held because something might go wrong. They split on four axes: what the watching is pointed at (a specific party, a general threat, your own next move, nothing in particular), whether it's sustained or a reflex, whether it stops you acting, and whether the speaker admires you for it or is quietly mocking you. Two are compliments, one is neutral, one is a put-down.

- **wary** — The only one with a named object — you are wary **of** someone, of an offer, of a clause in the contract. It's distrust of a particular party, and it doesn't stop you: you sign the deal, wary, watching his hands.
- **vigilant** — Not a reaction to any one suspect but a **post you hold** — sustained indefinitely, scanning for threat that may never come. It's the only member that's outright praise, and the only one that describes a duty rather than a feeling: sentries, auditors, night nurses.
- **circumspect** — The watching is aimed at **your own conduct**, not at an external threat — you survey the consequences and hold your tongue or your signature. Alone in the group it brakes action, and alone in the group it's formal: a diplomat is circumspect, a horse never is.
- **skittish** — The only involuntary one — a hair trigger, not a judgement, and the reaction is **out of proportion** to what caused it. Calling investors skittish says they're flinching rather than reasoning; the word belittles, and it drags along a whiff of the barnyard it came from.

> **On the exam:** Sentence equivalence loves pairing **wary** with **circumspect** — check whether the caution is pointed outward at a suspect thing or inward at your own next move; and check the sentence's tone, since **skittish** sneers where **vigilant** praises.


<a id="meaning__one-stands-in-for-another"></a>
### One stands in for another

Every word here covers the case where one thing occupies the place of another and the arrangement still works. The split that matters is symmetry. Two of them describe **mutual** substitutability — a pool of equivalents where no member is the original and swapping runs in either direction. The other two describe **one-way** substitution — there is a specific absent original, and the stand-in is measured against it.

- **fungible** — **Fungible** things aren't just swappable, they're *not individually tracked* — nobody asks which dollar or which barrel, because the units have no identities to distinguish. It's the legal-financial term of art (contracts, commodities, ledgers), so aiming it at people is the insult: they've been reclassified as countable stock.
- **interchangeable** — **Interchangeable** is the plain-English functional claim: these two particular items are distinguishable — different brand, different wording — but either fills the slot with no loss. Unlike *fungible*, you're comparing named things and finding the difference immaterial, not denying that differences exist.
- **surrogate** — A **surrogate** fills a *role that rightfully belongs to a specific someone else* — mother, father figure, decision-maker, campaign spokesman. The original is present as an absence: everyone knows who was supposed to be there, and the stand-in carries a faint second-best tinge that the symmetric words can't.
- **proxy** — A **proxy** is substitution by *grant* — the authority was openly delegated (she holds my proxy), which is what separates it from an impostor and from a merely drafted surrogate. It also owns a sense none of the others have: a measurable stand-in for something unobservable, as tree rings are a proxy for rainfall.

> **On the exam:** The trap is symmetry: a sentence with a named original ("stood in for the senator") wants **surrogate**/**proxy**, while one about undifferentiated units wants **fungible**/**interchangeable** — and only **proxy** can mean an indirect measure.


<a id="meaning__only-just-begun"></a>
### Only just begun

All four describe something at the bottom of its development curve — present, but not yet the full version of itself. The confusion comes from the fact that "undeveloped" splits four ways: recently started, not yet shaped, inexperienced but functioning, or stuck at the bare minimum. Two of these are claims about time, one is a claim about form, and one is a verdict on quality. Getting the group right means asking what exactly is missing — the years, the shape, the experience, or the substance.

- **nascent** — The only one that is purely a claim about **timing**: it marks the moment of coming-into-being and says nothing about whether the thing is coherent or any good. **Nascent** leaves the future deliberately open — the analyst's word for "this exists now, watch it" — and it attaches to abstractions and trends (a nascent movement, a nascent rivalry), never to a person's skill.
- **inchoate** — The complaint here is **shapelessness, not youth** — an **inchoate** grievance can be twenty years old and still have no outline. It's the word for things too formless to be stated: rage, longing, an argument that never resolves into a claim. Used of someone's reasoning it's a quiet insult, which is never true of *nascent*.
- **fledgling** — Alone in the group, **fledgling** describes something already **operating** — out of the nest and flying, just badly and without a safety net. It's the sympathetic option: it grants potential and survival odds (a fledgling airline may well make it), and it's the only member that works as a noun for a beginner.
- **rudimentary** — Not about beginnings at all but about **level** — it measures what's there against what full development would look like and finds it minimal. **Rudimentary** carries no promise of growth; rudimentary sanitation or rudimentary French may stay that way forever, which is why it lands as a polite downgrade rather than encouragement.

> **On the exam:** The classic trap is swapping *nascent* for *inchoate* — one dates the thing, the other faults its shape; *rudimentary* is the distractor slipped into sentences about a permanently low level, not about starting out.


<a id="meaning__overdecorated-style"></a>
### Overdecorated style

All of these describe something built up out of added detail — decoration, flourishes, extra parts, extra clauses — and all of them raise the same question: was the addition earned? They sit on a sliding scale from neutral admiration for craft, through polite complaint, to open contempt for ornament that has swallowed the substance. The trap is that most of them can swing either way depending on what they attach to and who is speaking, and two of them carry a completely separate second sense the GRE prefers to test.

- **elaborate** — The only one measuring **effort and number of parts** rather than surface prettiness — an elaborate scheme has no decoration at all, just many carefully fitted pieces. It is also the only word here that turns suspicious rather than tasteless: an *elaborate alibi* isn't ugly, it's over-engineered, and nobody works that hard on the truth.
- **ornate** — Strictly **surface**: carving, gilding, adjectives laid on top of a thing that already existed. It is the one that can still be straightforwardly admiring — of a cathedral screen or a Fabergé egg — and only curdles into complaint when applied to modern things, above all prose. Its constant implication is that someone couldn't stop adding, not that they went mad.
- **baroque** — Here the ornament has stopped being surface and become **structure** — the decoration is now load-bearing, fussy and showy at once. It's the only word in the group with a straight technical use (capital B, the 1600–1750 period), which is why it can be neutral in art history and a jab everywhere else. Reserve it for complexity that *shows off*; tangled bureaucratic complexity is byzantine, not baroque.
- **florid** — The only one with **no admiring reading at all** — it's a flat verdict that the flourishes have crowded out the sense. It's also the only member that applies to a **body**: a florid complexion is red and flushed from heat, drink or blood pressure, and in medicine a florid symptom is one that has bloomed into full, undeniable view.
- **embellish** — The only **verb of adding**, and the one whose GRE sense leaves decoration entirely: to pad a true story with invented detail. Its charge is deliberately mild and half-forgiving — it presumes a real core, which is exactly how it differs from *fabricate*. Saying a witness embellished casts doubt without calling her a liar.

> **On the exam:** The GRE rarely tests the decorating sense head-on — it hides the answer in the second senses (**florid** = flushed face / fully manifest symptom, **embellish** = exaggerate a true account) and forces you to read whether the sentence's tone is admiring, neutral, or damning to choose among the rest.


<a id="meaning__overstate-past-the-truth"></a>
### Overstate past the truth

All four describe an account that has been pushed beyond what the facts support — the size inflated, the details enriched, the shape bent, the drama cranked up. They differ on three axes: whether anyone is meant to be fooled, whether the starting material is real, and whether the charge is aimed at the content or at the effect on the audience. Some are named rhetorical devices; others are accusations. Only one of them names a technique that is openly, harmlessly false.

- **hyperbole** — The only one that isn't deceptive: the excess is visible on purpose, so no listener is meant to believe it. It's also the only noun here — it names a device ("that's hyperbole"), whereas the others name something being done to material.
- **embellish** — The mildest accusation, and the forgiving one: the core story is true and the invented details are added as ornament. Reserved for storytellers, anecdotes, and testimony — you're saying someone improved a tale, not that they lied.
- **sensational** — Judges the effect on the audience, not the content's fidelity — the aim is a gasp, and accuracy is collateral damage. It attaches to coverage and presentation (a headline, a trial, a tabloid), and it's the word that carries a live positive sense the GRE ignores.
- **distort** — The hardest charge: every element stays genuine, only the arrangement is falsified — the real quote, the real number, warped until it means something else. It also has a fully neutral technical use (lens, signal, waveform) where nobody is being accused of anything.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as one intensity scale — **hyperbole** deceives nobody, **embellish** softens the charge, and **sensational** may be praise, so context words like *lurid*, *accurate*, or *literal* decide the answer.


<a id="meaning__parading-your-own-virtue"></a>
### Parading your own virtue

All four live in the gap between virtue displayed and virtue actually held. Each is a way of saying *the moral show exceeds the moral substance* — but they indict different things: the smug tone, the empty costing-nothing gesture, the person's failure to live their own rule, or the pose adopted purely for leverage. Three are pure accusations; one can still be a compliment. The trap is that they overlap heavily in bad-faith contexts and almost not at all in good-faith ones.

- **sanctimonious** — Indicts the **tone**, not the conduct: moral superiority aimed downward at the listener. You can be sanctimonious about a virtue you genuinely have — the offence is the sighing lecture, not the failure. It's the only one of these that describes a manner of speaking.
- **pious** — The only word here that can be sincere praise — it alone describes real religious devotion. Its sneer is conditional, switched on by the noun it modifies (*pious hope*, *pious platitude*), which lets a writer disparage while keeping deniability. The others announce their hostility immediately.
- **hypocrite** — The only person-noun, and the only charge about **conduct** rather than performance: professing a standard you don't live by. No display, tone, or audience required — a quiet hypocrite still qualifies. It's also the harshest of the four, because it convicts the whole person as counterfeit rather than criticising one behaviour.
- **posturing** — Secular and strategic — often not about morality at all. It fits a threat, a negotiating stance, or a party's position, and what it denies is any **intention to act**, not any claim to goodness. The posturer wants leverage; the sanctimonious want to look good.

> **On the exam:** The classic bait is offering *hypocritical* when the sentence only establishes an insufferable tone (→ **sanctimonious**), or *sanctimonious* when the sentence establishes an empty gesture with no moral preaching (→ **posturing**); watch for **pious** in ironic pairings like *pious hope*, where the neutral gloss is the wrong reading.


<a id="meaning__persistent-to-the-end"></a>
### Persistent to the End

All of these describe someone who keeps going: effort sustained past the point where a normal person would stop, in the face of difficulty, tedium, or discouragement. They differ on three axes the GRE cares about. First, whether the speaker approves — most are praise, one is a complaint. Second, what the persistence pushes against: opposition and failure, physical tiredness, or the sheer grind of detail. Third, what the word attaches to — a person's character, a long campaign, or an inanimate nuisance that will not go away.

- **dogged** — The plain-English, working-class member of the group — no polish, no grandeur. It praises the unglamorous grunt: the one still knocking on doors in month nine, not the one who solved it cleverly. Where the others are formal, **dogged** is the word you'd actually say out loud, and it implies the work was boring as well as hard.
- **pertinacious** — The only insult here. **Pertinacious** tells you the speaker wants this to stop — the grip is aimed at something not worth gripping, and it has outlasted everyone's patience. It's also the one that attaches comfortably to non-persons: a pertinacious cough, a pertinacious rumour, a pertinacious creditor. Nobody claims it about themselves.
- **indefatigable** — Alone in the group, this names what's *absent* — fatigue — rather than the obstacle overcome. There need be no adversity at all; the marvel is the sheer un-tiring output, sustained over years by a campaigner or advocate. It's the grandest compliment on the list, and slightly hyperbolic: literally, cannot be worn out.
- **sedulous** — The only one about **care**, not endurance against resistance. What a sedulous person outlasts is the tedium of detail — every footnote checked, every entry verified — and the praise is for thoroughness, never for defying opposition. Unhurried where *industrious* is energetic; you can be sedulous at a task nobody is fighting you over.
- **perseverance** — The group's only noun, and the one that requires actual setback: **perseverance** presumes you already failed, were discouraged, and kept going anyway. Take away the obstacle and the word has nothing to describe. It names the virtue abstractly — the quality itself, awarded credit — rather than characterizing a person the way the adjectives do.

> **On the exam:** The trap is tonal: **pertinacious** looks like a fancy upgrade of *dogged* or *tenacious*, so it gets slotted into admiring sentences where only a negative word fits — check for a "though/regrettably" signal or an exasperated speaker before choosing it.


<a id="meaning__plot-together"></a>
### Plotting together

All of these describe people acting together on something they would rather not be seen doing: joint action plus concealment plus, usually, someone outside the arrangement who gets hurt by it. They differ on the shape of the partnership — equal partners in a plan, rivals with a quiet understanding, or a principal and the helper who eggs him on. They also differ on where the wrongdoing comes from: some carry it in the word itself, while others are perfectly innocent until the context (a war, a court, an occupied city) turns them.

- **collude** — The damning part is *who* the parties are: people who are supposed to be at arm's length — two bidders, an auditor and his client, a referee and a team. No plan and no meeting is required, only a shared understanding, which is why regulators and antitrust lawyers reach for it; the agreement itself is the offence.
- **conspire** — Needs an actual plot with a target — accomplices, an object, and a plan of attack — and the agreeing is itself the crime, chargeable before anyone acts. It is also the only word here that takes inanimate subjects: *the weather and the traffic conspired against us*, half-joking fatalism about a world that seems organised against you.
- **abet** — Asymmetric where the others are mutual: there is one wrongdoer and you are the second fiddle who supplies the push, the cover, or the nerve. You abet a *person*, not a plan, and the word is welded to wrongdoing — there is no innocent abetting, which is why it survives mostly inside the courtroom formula *aid and abet*.
- **intrigue** — Names scheming as an atmosphere rather than a single act — a court, a cabinet, a boardroom can be full of intrigue with no one crime to point at. It is also the only word here whose commonest sense is flattering (*the offer intrigued her*); in the plotting sense it typically takes *against*: he intrigued against the king.
- **collaborate** — Neutral-to-praiseworthy by default — a paper, an album — and it turns sinister only when the partner is an occupying enemy and the betrayed party is your own country. The guilt is imported entirely by context, and *collaborator* carries the stain more heavily than the verb does.

> **On the exam:** The GRE reaches for the buried sense — *collaborate* as treason, *intrigue* as plot — and tests collude vs. conspire on whether a plan existed: colluders need only an understanding between supposed rivals, conspirators need a scheme and a victim.


<a id="meaning__poise-under-pressure"></a>
### Poise under pressure: inner calm vs. visible style

All four describe not being rattled when the situation would rattle most people — the blow lands, and the person stays level. The pressure is built into every one of them: none is usable to describe someone merely relaxed on a quiet afternoon. What separates them is **where the steadiness lives** — inside the mind, in the fixed temperament, in the visible body, or in the style of the performance — and whether you are *enduring* something or *pulling something off*.

- **equanimity** — The purely **inner** one: evenness of mind, which nobody can see directly and which you infer from how someone took the news. It attaches to things done *to* a person — a verdict, a diagnosis, a demotion — so it measures endurance, not performance, and it is the one word here that implies the blow was genuinely felt.
- **imperturbable** — The group's only adjective, and the only one describing a **standing temperament** rather than conduct on one occasion: a claim that this person *cannot* be flustered, ever, not that they weren't today. Because it's a trait and not a response, it's the only one that can turn cold — unflappable enough that you wonder if anything registers.
- **poise** — Composure with a **body** attached: steady voice, unhurried hands, nothing fidgeting. It's the least formal of the four and carries a whiff of grace and breeding, so it's what you praise in a dancer, a diplomat, or a teenager fielding a hostile question. It alone has the coiled sense — *poised to spring* is balance held for a leap, not calm at all.
- **aplomb** — The only one that requires a **feat**: you don't take bad news with aplomb, you land the joke, the operation, the hostile press conference with it. It rates the ease of the execution, not the steadiness of the nerves — visible strain kills it outright, and there's nothing to praise if the task was easy.

> **On the exam:** The classic swap is **equanimity** vs. **aplomb** in a "with ___" slot: if the sentence gives the person a hard thing to *do*, it's aplomb; if it gives them a hard thing to *receive*, it's equanimity — and if the blank is an adjective, only **imperturbable** fits at all.


<a id="meaning__present-in-great-quantity"></a>
### Present in great quantity

All four say *there is a lot of it* — enough that the quantity itself becomes the point worth remarking on. They split on three axes: what the quantity attaches to (a place teeming, a supply produced, a stream pouring, a magnitude observed), whether the amount is merely ample or has tipped past what's wanted, and whether the speaker is reporting or reacting. One is a verb and cannot be swapped in as a modifier at all.

- **abound** — The only verb here, and never an adjective — you cannot have *abound resources*, you have *resources abound* or *a region abounding in copper*. It describes saturation of a **scene or setting**: the plentiful things are the subject, and the effect is "everywhere you look," not "a large amount was produced." Its tone is borrowed entirely from what abounds — wildflowers, or errors.
- **copious** — The mildest of the three adjectives and the only one with no edge of too-much: it measures **output and supply** — notes taken, tears shed, rain fallen, coffee drunk. It answers "how much was generated or consumed," so it fits poorly on static bulk (a copious mountain is wrong) and never implies the speaker is startled or uncomfortable. The well kept giving; nobody flinched.
- **profuse** — Adds **flow past the point of control** — the quantity is pouring, not merely present. It attaches to things that stream (bleeding, sweating, apologies, thanks) and, applied to a person's manner, carries the speaker's judgement that it was overdone: *profuse gratitude* is embarrassing in a way *copious* never is. Excess is in the word, not in the context.
- **prodigious** — Shifts from supply to **sheer magnitude, plus the onlooker's astonishment** — it is a reaction as much as a measurement. A prodigious appetite is one people remark on; a prodigious output seems barely human. It leans admiring and sits high in register, and it can modify size or degree, where the others need an amount: prodigious strength, yes; copious or profuse strength, no.

> **On the exam:** Sentence equivalence loves pairing **copious** with **profuse** as if interchangeable — check whether the sentence signals excess or discomfort (profuse) or just generous supply (copious); and **prodigious** is a trap for \"amazingly large,\" not \"plentiful,\" so it fails wherever a countable supply is meant.


<a id="meaning__prop-up-and-strengthen"></a>
### Prop up, add to, turn up

All four take something that already exists and make it more — more solid, more numerous, more intense. None of them creates from scratch, and none of them is negative. The split inside the group is between **support** words (the object was wobbling and needed help standing) and **increase** words (the object was fine, you just added to it or turned it up). The second split is *what* gets added: reinforcement, quantity, or intensity.

- **bolster** — The propping word that works on **morale and confidence** — flagging spirits, a sagging economy, a shaky case. It concedes that the thing was weak; the other three don't have to. Alone in this group it can take a person or a mood as its object: you bolster the troops, you never augment or buttress them.
- **buttress** — Formal and **structural**: support added from outside to a load-bearing position — a claim, a thesis, a regime. It attaches to arguments, not feelings, and comes with a fixed collocation (*buttress a claim **with** evidence*). Where **bolster** cheers something up, **buttress** keeps it from collapsing under challenge.
- **augment** — Pure **quantity added to a base** — a salary, a force, a collection, a staff. It carries no hint that the original was lacking or under pressure, which is exactly what separates it from the two propping words; you augment things that are already doing fine. Formal register, and the addition is typically brought in from outside.
- **amplify** — **Intensity, not quantity** — you turn the existing thing up rather than add more of it: a signal, an effect, a rumour, tension. Nothing new is introduced, so it stays neutral on truth (unlike *exaggerate* or *embellish*). Second GRE sense: to **expand on** a point — *amplify that* means *say more*.

> **On the exam:** Sentence completions hinge on whether the sentence admits weakness: a blank after "though the evidence was thin" wants **bolster/buttress**, while a neutral "already substantial holdings" wants **augment** — and if the object is a signal, effect, or point being elaborated, it's **amplify**.


<a id="meaning__provoked-anger"></a>
### Provoked anger: grievance and who it makes look bad

All four describe anger that comes with a claim attached: someone was wronged, slighted, or treated unfairly, and the feeling is the response to that offence. None of them is raw temper — each presupposes a trigger and a grievance. They split on whose side of the offence you're standing on, how long the feeling lasts, and whether the writer thinks the grievance was worth having.

- **ire** — The only one that names anger **from the offender's side of the transaction**: you don't feel ire, you *draw* it. Locked into set phrases (*drew/sparked/raised the ire of*) with an institution or crowd as the angry party — regulators, fans, the board. It reports anger from outside; it never describes an inner state you're sitting with.
- **umbrage** — The only one that quietly **discredits the person feeling it**. *Take umbrage at* implies the slight was small and the reaction over-ready — wounded vanity, not injury. Right for someone bristling at a tone or a seating chart; applied to real cruelty it reads as mockery.
- **indignant** — The **moral posture** word: not merely hurt but claiming a violated right — *how dare you*. The only member that can be wholly admirable (righteous indignation at injustice), and it points outward at the wrongdoer rather than inward at the wound. Describes a person mid-protest, usually audibly.
- **resent** — The only one with **duration and silence built in**. The others are reactions with a visible moment; resentment is what's still there months on, unspoken and nursed. It's also the only one you can aim at an impersonal thing you must keep living with — a duty, a rule, a colleague's promotion.

> **On the exam:** The trap is duration and sympathy: **indignant** is a hot public protest of unfairness while **resent** is cold and stored, and **umbrage** is the one that makes the offended party look petty — so a sentence endorsing the reaction as justified rules it out.


<a id="meaning__publicly-take-back"></a>
### Publicly Taking It Back

All four describe cutting yourself loose from something you were previously attached to, and doing it out loud, on the record, with witnesses. None of them works for a quiet change of heart — the break has to be *announced* to count. What separates them is the object of the break (a possession, a vow, a sentence you uttered, a bond you were party to), and whether you're stepping away by choice or being made to say the words.

- **renounce** — The plain-vanilla member, and the only one that can be pure sacrifice with no wrongdoing implied. What you **renounce** is something you *hold* and are giving up going forward — a throne, a fortune, a citizenship, violence as a tactic. It says nothing about having been wrong; the prince who renounces the crown isn't confessing, he's paying.
- **abjure** — **Abjure** is renouncing *under oath* — the ceremony is baked into the word. Its home turf is the formula recited before an authority: the heretic before the tribunal, the naturalizing citizen swearing off foreign princes. It attaches to allegiances and beliefs you were *bound* by, and it usually smells of someone standing over you making sure you say it.
- **recant** — Alone in this group, **recant** takes back *words*. There must be a prior public statement — a theory, a testimony, an accusation — and recanting declares that statement false, so it's the one that implies *I was wrong* (or that someone squeezed me until I said so). Galileo recanted; he did not repudiate or renounce.
- **repudiate** — **Repudiate** points *outward* at a tie and severs it: a debt you won't honour, a treaty you won't keep, an endorsement you disown, a supporter you cast off. It's the only one here that can take a *person* or someone else's act as its object — you repudiate the ally whose remarks embarrass you — and it's often aggressive rather than penitent.

> **On the exam:** The exam picks by object, not vibe: a prior *statement* wants recant; a prior *bond, debt, or person*, repudiate; an *oath*, abjure; a *possession or right surrendered*, renounce.


<a id="meaning__push-to-the-edges"></a>
### Push to the edges

All four locate something away from the centre — the edge of a society, an argument, a hierarchy, a movement — rather than destroying or denying it. Nothing here is banned or refuted; it is simply put somewhere it can be ignored. The differences are who does the pushing, what gets pushed, and whether the edge means powerless, demoted, secondary, or disreputable.

- **marginalize** — The only one about **power and voice**: its object is people, and the harm is being left present but unheard. Uniquely agentless — institutions and defaults do it with nobody deciding to, which is why you almost always meet it as *marginalized*, with no named villain.
- **relegate** — The one that requires a **doer and a destination**: someone relegates X *to* the bench, the basement, a footnote. A single, deliberate, downward move with a shrug attached — the thing wasn't worth the better spot — and it lands on tasks, ideas and traditions as readily as on people.
- **peripheral** — Not an act but a **claim about status**, and the polite one. It concedes your point is real while sliding it off the table — softer than *trivial* (contemptuous) or *irrelevant* (flatly disconnected). Watch for it as a debater's move; also the only word here that means a printer or mouse.
- **fringe** — Position measured against **legitimacy**, not importance: it says the centre is where the sensible people are (*lunatic fringe*, *fringe theory*). Attaches to groups and beliefs rather than tasks, and flips to a compliment — daring, unofficial — when the centre is the establishment (*fringe theatre*).

> **On the exam:** Sentence-equivalence traps swap **relegate** for **marginalize** — but *relegate* wants an explicit agent and a *to*-destination, while *marginalize* wants a passive subject and no villain; and **peripheral** is the answer when the sentence grants the point exists, where *trivial* or *irrelevant* would overshoot.


<a id="meaning__fake-a-feeling"></a>
### Putting It On: from a fake feeling to a fake institution

All of these cover a gap between what is shown and what is real: a face, manner, stance, or form put on for an audience. None requires an outright factual lie — the deceit lives in presentation, not in statements, and in every case the speaker using the word is claiming to see through the performance. What separates them is *scope* and *grammar*: a single passing emotion, a whole concealed inner self, a small habitual mannerism, a public stance, or an entire institution going through empty motions.

- **feign** — **Feign** manufactures something you don't have and puts it outward — it takes an inner state as its object (surprise, ignorance, illness, sleep, indifference). It's momentary and bounded: you feign interest for one dinner party, and nothing about your deeper character is on trial.
- **dissemble** — **Dissemble** runs the opposite direction: not adding a false feeling but covering a real one — fury, contempt, ambition — that already exists. It reaches deeper than *feign*, to motives and beliefs rather than a passing mood, and it's the genteel way to call someone deceitful without the word *lied*.
- **affectation** — **Affectation** is the artifact, not the act — a small, stylistic, repeated tic (a drawled vowel, a cigarette holder, a borrowed accent) adopted to seem a certain *kind of person*. It hides no secret and gains no advantage; that pettiness is why it reads as ridiculous rather than dangerous.
- **posturing** — **Posturing** is public and instrumental: the pose is a *position* — a threat, an ultimatum, a principled stand — and the charge is specifically that no action will follow it. Unlike the others, it predicts a failure to act, and it usually assumes the posturer is angling for leverage.
- **sham** — **Sham** is the only one that indicts a whole structure rather than a person's face: a trial, an election, a marriage that observes every correct procedure and means nothing. The complaint is emptiness inside a legitimate-looking form, not a performer managing an expression.

> **On the exam:** The trap is direction and scope: a context about *hiding* a real feeling wants **dissemble**, not **feign** (which supplies a fake one), and a context about an empty institution wants **sham**, not **affectation** (a personal quirk) or **posturing** (an unbacked stance).


<a id="meaning__quick-light-handed-skill"></a>
### Quick, light-handed skill

All five praise skill of the quick, economical kind — competence that shows up as speed and ease rather than force, depth, or genius. The compliment is for *how* something is done: neatly, without visible strain, faster than the difficulty seemed to allow. They separate mainly by *where* the skill lives — in the fingers, in the whole body, in the talk, or in years of accumulated command — and by how warm the praise is.

- **dexterous** — The one still attached to the **fingers** — fine motor control and speed at a physical task. It says nothing about the doer's character: a **dexterous** pickpocket is being praised for the hands, not accused of slyness. Its mental extension exists but is secondary and pale.
- **deft** — The praise is specifically for **economy** — the move used exactly the effort it needed and no more, so it looked easy. **Deft** rates the aesthetics of execution, which is why critics live on it ("a deft touch"); it can't describe a person's standing career, only a touch, a stroke, a scene, a sidestep.
- **nimble** — The only one about **evading rather than executing** — slipping the punch, sidestepping the objection. It also scales beyond a person to a whole body or organization (a nimble company, a nimble market), which none of the others do, and it's the warmest and least technical of the five.
- **adroit** — The skill is **under pressure from other people** — the awkward question, the hostile negotiation, the moment that could go wrong. **Adroit** admires the manoeuvre more than the person, so the praise is cool and faintly wary; lean on it and it tips into *slick*. Almost always social or verbal, rarely manual.
- **adept** — The only one that describes no single moment — it's **accumulated command of a domain**, earned by practice, and it takes a complement (*adept at/in*). Consequently it's the only one that can be a **noun** (an adept = an initiate of a difficult art), and the only one with no speed component at all.

> **On the exam:** The shared "quick and skilful" gloss is the trap: sort by domain (fingers = dexterous, pressure and people = adroit, evasion = nimble, economy of touch = deft) and remember adept is the odd one out — durable mastery, no quickness implied, and the only member that takes *at/in* or works as a noun.


<a id="meaning__tender-backward-looking-sadness"></a>
### Quiet sadness: the mood, the longing, and the thing that stings

All three name sadness in its soft, refined register — nothing loud, no wailing, no grudge. The feeling is quiet, tinged with tenderness, and usually tied to distance: something absent, past, or slipping away. The differences are structural, not just intensity. Two of them describe a *person's* inward state; one describes the *thing* that produces the state in someone watching. And they differ in whether the sadness has an object at all: a vague grey mood, a specific lost thing longed for, or a precise detail that pricks.

- **pensive** — The only one that is primarily about **thinking**; the sadness is a tint on the thought, not the point. Crucially, it needs **no object** — a pensive person is lost in thought about nothing you can name, whereas the others require a lost thing or a piercing detail. It is also the most *external*: you call a face, a silence, or a portrait pensive because of how it looks from outside.
- **wistful** — Requires an **object you can name and cannot have** — the childhood house, the version of yourself at twenty. Adds two things pensive lacks: **longing** and **resignation**. The wistful person wants it and has already given up reaching, which is why the ache is half-pleasant rather than raw. Attaches to smiles, sighs, and glances.
- **poignant** — The odd one out grammatically: it labels the **stimulus, not the sufferer**. A film, a detail, a letter is poignant; a person gazing out a window is not. It describes the sharpness of the strike on an observer, and it is the only one that works as **critical praise** — calling art poignant says it earned its ache. Formal register, and it wants one precise detail, not a general mood.

> **On the exam:** The classic trap swaps **poignant** for the other two in a sentence describing a person's mood — remember it modifies what causes the feeling, not the one feeling it; and if a specific lost thing is named in the sentence, the answer is **wistful**, not **pensive**.


<a id="meaning__exalt-to-sacred-status"></a>
### Raising to Sacred Status

All four borrow the vocabulary of religion to describe how a person or thing gets lifted above ordinary judgment. Each implies a holiness the object didn't earn by argument — reverence, godhood, sainthood, consecration — and each can be used straight or sardonically, depending on whether the reader thinks the elevation is deserved. The differences are structural: whether it's a private attitude or a public act, who performs it, whether it ranks the object or merely selects it, and whether it can ever be undone.

- **venerate** — The only one that is purely an attitude — nothing is conferred, no status changes hands, the object is already old and holy and you are simply behaving accordingly. It looks backward at age and tradition (founders, relics, elders), and its failure mode is complacency, not delusion: reverence that stopped being examined.
- **deify** — The maximum — it goes past reverence to actual godhood, and it is the one word here that measures the *worshipper* rather than the object. It's an accusation of lost judgment (the man can now do no wrong), which is why you deify someone else and never yourself.
- **canonize** — An institutional act with a procedure behind it: the Church, the academy, the syllabus. Personal enthusiasm cannot canonize anything, and the effect is permanence — the reputation is filed, closed, put past debate — so the object is typically dead or finished.
- **anoint** — Selection, not ranking: it points forward to a successor and hands over an aura along with the job, so the choice reads as ordained rather than decided. It says nothing about the chosen one's merit, only that someone with standing picked them — hence *self-anointed*, the sneer that nobody else was consulted.

> **On the exam:** The exam separates them by grammar of the act, not by degree of praise: look for who does it (a person's feeling → **venerate**; a body with authority → **canonize**), whether the sentence says "beyond all criticism" (→ **deify**), and whether there's a successor or chosen one in sight (→ **anoint**).


<a id="meaning__real-enough-to-touch"></a>
### Real enough to touch

All four descend from the idea of touch: something is present enough to be registered by the senses rather than merely asserted, imagined, or hoped for. But each stakes out a different arena — proof, atmosphere, embodiment, and the threshold of perception — and only one of them is ever literally about hands. The trap is that they all translate as "you can feel it," which flattens four very different claims into one.

- **tangible** — The **evidence** word: it demands something you can show, count, or put on a table, and it implies the speaker suspects the last offering was talk. Attaches to *results, benefits, assets, proof* — nouns that can be audited.
- **palpable** — The **atmosphere** word: not countable and not proof, but so intense it seems to press on the room. Its natural subject is a collective mood — a courtroom's tension, a crowd's relief — where **tangible** would be absurd because there is nothing to measure.
- **corporeal** — The only one about **having a body**, and it always implies an adversary with none: soul, ghost, patent, idea. Formal and argumentative in a way *physical* is not — you reach for it precisely when embodiment is the contested question.
- **discernible** — Says nothing about substance or intensity — only that the thing sits at the **edge of detection** and had to be looked for. Its native habitat is the negative (*no discernible pattern*), the careful researcher's way of saying we searched properly and found nothing.

> **On the exam:** The GRE swaps **tangible** and **palpable** in sentence completions — pick by what the noun is: measurable proof takes *tangible*, a shared mood takes *palpable*; and **discernible** answers "barely perceptible," never "physically real."


<a id="meaning__reasoning-past-the-evidence"></a>
### Reasoning past the evidence

All of these mark the gap between what you can actually show and what you're willing to say. Each one signals — to the reader, the audience, or yourself — that a claim is running ahead of its support and should be held loosely. The confusion comes from the fact that they flag that gap at different points: the act of leaping, the method of the leap, the evidentiary status of the result, and how tightly you're gripping the conclusion afterward.

- **conjectural** — A **verdict on a claim's evidentiary status**, usually delivered by someone else: it says *this rests on inference, not documentation*. It grades the finished product, not the thinking that produced it, and it makes no comment on whether the claim is confidently held or likely to change — a conjectural reconstruction can be asserted flatly and defended for decades.
- **speculate** — The **act**, and the only one you announce about yourself as a disclaimer — "I won't speculate" is a refusal to be quoted. It needs no data to depart from: you can speculate about a motive, a successor, a cause, from nothing but circumstance. It also uniquely carries the money sense — a speculator bets on price where an investor analyses a business.
- **extrapolate** — The only one that **requires a trend to push**: there must be existing data and a direction to extend it in. That's why accusing someone of extrapolating concedes they had evidence — just too little of it ("from a sample of one"). Neutral bookkeeping in technical prose, a quiet accusation in argument.
- **tentative** — Describes not the evidence but **the grip** — how firmly the thing is being held. A well-supported conclusion can still be tentative because it awaits sign-off or replication, and a date can be tentative with no reasoning involved at all. Alone in the group it also covers physical manner: a tentative knock, a tentative step, where the word reports timidity rather than uncertainty about facts.

> **On the exam:** The classic trap swaps evidentiary status for commitment status — a "tentative conclusion" may be fully evidenced and merely unratified, while a "conjectural" one is unsupported no matter how firmly stated; likewise, extrapolate demands an existing trend where speculate demands nothing.


<a id="meaning__getting-better-after-illness"></a>
### Recovering, Restoring, Reviving

All four sit on the upswing after something has been drained, damaged, or knocked down — the return trip from depletion to full strength. They split on three axes: whether the word names a *state* you're in, a *trait* you have, or an *act* done to something; whether the recovery is slow or fast; and whether what comes back is *health*, *shape*, *quantity*, or *energy*. Confusion comes from the shared upward direction, not from shared grammar — two are adjectives, two are transitive verbs.

- **convalescent** — The only one that describes a person *stuck in the middle of it* — not a capacity, not an action, a status. It is also the only one with genuine sickbed baggage: weeks in an armchair, not a brisk comeback. Where **resilient** praises speed, **convalescent** presumes slowness.
- **resilient** — A standing trait, present before the blow and proven by it — you are resilient in advance, whereas you only become convalescent after the fact. It concedes real damage and emphasizes *speed of return to former shape*; it's the only member that applies to materials (a bent spring, foam).
- **replenish** — Purely quantitative and transitive: the object is a stock, reserve, or supply that was drawn down, and the refilling stops at the old level. Nothing bodily and nothing about vitality — you replenish a larder or an aquifer; you cannot replenish a patient.
- **invigorate** — The energy is *administered from outside* — a cold plunge, a new hire, a cash injection — and the target need not have been depleted at all: a healthy person can be invigorated. That's the sharp break from **replenish**, which requires a prior shortfall and only tops it back up.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable "get better" words: GRE sentences fix the answer by what is being restored — a *level* (replenish), a *pulse* (invigorate), a *shape after a blow* (resilient) — and by whether the slot needs a slow middle state (convalescent) or a fast bounce.


<a id="meaning__refusing-to-give-an-inch"></a>
### Refusing to Give an Inch — and What Fails to Move Them

All four describe something that will not yield to outside pressure, and all four are the losing party's verdict rather than the holder's self-description. The difference is never *how* immovable — it's *what kind of pressure is being applied and failing*. Reason, offered terms, tears, and apology are four different levers, and each of these words names the one that bounces off. Get the lever right and the group stops being interchangeable.

- **obstinate** — The baseline, and the only one that needs no counterparty: **obstinate** is a standing trait, resistance to *argument and reason* generally, with no particular petitioner in the room. It's also the only one in this group that takes inanimate objects — an obstinate stain, lid, cough — because it just means "won't yield to repeated effort."
- **intransigent** — Requires a **negotiation**. Terms have been tabled and refused; without an offer on the table the word doesn't apply. Its home is political and diplomatic — unions, parties, peace talks — and the exasperation comes from the person across the table, not from a bystander. Alone in this group it flips admiring with some ease: an intransigent defender of principle.
- **obdurate** — The pressure that fails here is **pity**, not argument. Someone is begging, the suffering is visible, and you feel nothing — so the fault is in the heart, not the reasoning. Uniquely moral and near-biblical in register: an obdurate sinner, an obdurate creditor. The speaker isn't describing you, they're condemning you.
- **implacable** — Not holding a position — **coming at you**. It points outward at a target, and what fails against it is *appeasement*: apology, concession, surrender. The others could simply sit still forever; **implacable** things keep advancing, which is why it extends to tides, age, and deadlines. Aimed at resolve rather than malice, it reads as formidable rather than petty.

> **On the exam:** The stem hands you the failed lever — an offer refused, a plea ignored, an apology that changed nothing — and the three wrong answers are all correctly \"stubborn\" but wrong about which lever failed.


<a id="meaning__respectful-yielding"></a>
### Respectful yielding: attitude, gesture, temperament, rank

All four describe one party giving way to another. They split on *what* is doing the yielding: an attitude you hold, a gesture your body performs, a character defect others accuse you of, or a slot you occupy on a chart. Two are neutral or even flattering, one is corrosive, and one is pure structure with no feeling in it at all. The GRE lives in the gap between yielding by position and yielding by disposition.

- **deference** — The only one that can flatter you. It's an inner attitude, freely chosen and self-limiting — you concede the point but keep your own judgment intact. The idiom **in deference to** means "out of respect for," not "in submission to," and it is the giveaway.
- **obeisance** — The only one that requires a body. Not what you feel or where you rank — a bow, a curtsy, a kneel, performed where others can see it. Because the staging is the point, modern prose almost always uses it to mock: whoever "pays obeisance" is being watched by an unimpressed narrator.
- **subservient** — The only outright insult, and it's about temperament, not position. The judgment isn't kept in reserve — it's been handed over. Nobody applies it to themselves; it's a verdict passed from outside, and it stains the person being served as much as the one serving.
- **subordinate** — The only structural, morality-free member: it names a rung, not a disposition. A subordinate may be defiant and still be a subordinate. The verb is the exam's favorite — you **subordinate X to Y**, deliberately sacrificing something real so the higher-ranked thing prevails.

> **On the exam:** The trap is **subordinate** vs. **subservient** — rank versus grovelling; and the verb *subordinate ... to*, where the answer hinges on something valuable being deliberately given up.


<a id="meaning__theory-before-facts"></a>
### Rigid by Doctrine: dogmatic, doctrinaire, ideologue, martinet

All four describe someone whose fixed system outranks the situation in front of them: the conclusion was reached before the evidence arrived, and no case is allowed to change it. Each is an accusation — never self-applied — and each names a different site of the rigidity: the way beliefs are asserted, the way theory is applied, the person defined by the system, or the way rules are enforced. The split that matters is whether the rigidity is about ideas at all, or merely about procedure.

- **dogmatic** — **Dogmatic** locates the fault in *delivery* — the flat, unarguable assertion. It's the only one of the four that scales down to a single trivial opinion (dogmatic about coffee, about Kubrick); it needs no political system behind it, just a tone that ends the conversation. It also modifies utterances and manner, not only people: a dogmatic tone, a dogmatic pronouncement.
- **doctrinaire** — **Doctrinaire** locates the fault at the point of *application* — the theory meets a concrete case and refuses to bend to it. It presupposes a named body of thought and collocates with it (*doctrinaire Marxist*, *doctrinaire free-market policy*), and its usual damage is practical: the policy fails while the doctrine stays pristine. You can be dogmatic in a bar; you're doctrinaire in a committee room.
- **ideologue** — **Ideologue** is a noun and a whole identity — not a manner or a habit but a classification of the person by the system they serve. Its home turf is political writing, where it sits directly opposite *pragmatist*: the ideologue turns down the workable deal on principle. Where doctrinaire faults the reasoning, ideologue faults the man.
- **martinet** — **Martinet** involves no doctrine at all — the rigidity is about rules and discipline, not beliefs, so it can be paired with total intellectual emptiness. It requires a chain of command: it takes people with power over subordinates (officer, boss, hall monitor) and fixates them on trivia — the untucked shirt, the wrong-coloured ink — while the rule's purpose goes unserved.

> **On the exam:** The trap is **martinet**: GRE blanks that say only "rigid," "unyielding," "inflexible" will bait you toward it when the sentence is actually about *ideas* (choose dogmatic/doctrinaire/ideologue) — martinet is right only when the context supplies subordinates and rules to enforce.


<a id="meaning__rise-above-the-rest"></a>
### Rise above the rest

All five describe ending up above something else — but they differ in *what* that something else is. One is a moving rival, one is a reputation, one is a whole category, one is a dead-weight obstacle, one is active opposition. Choosing correctly is almost never about strength or degree; it's about identifying the thing being risen above and what happens to it afterward. Get the object right and the word picks itself.

- **outstrip** — The only one here that is **quantitative**: it wants rates, volumes, numbers — demand outstrips supply, costs outstrip revenue. Both parties were moving and are still moving; **outstrip** reports a widening gap, not a defeat, and awards no credit to the winner.
- **eclipse** — The contest is over **attention**, not measurement. What gets eclipsed still exists and may still be excellent — it has simply stopped being looked at, usually because something newer stands in front of it. Almost always involves a predecessor, and almost always shows up passively: *his early work was eclipsed by...*
- **transcend** — The thing risen above is not a rival but a **category or limit** — a genre, a form, the body, death. Where the others leave you on the same scale in a better position, **transcend** takes you off the scale entirely, and it carries open admiration plus a philosophical or spiritual tint the rest lack.
- **surmount** — Its object is an **inert obstacle** — poverty, prejudice, bad odds, a language barrier — never a person you beat. The obstacle doesn't shrink or lose; it stays exactly where it was and you get over it. Formal, unshowy, and most commonly encountered in its negative: **insurmountable**.
- **prevail** — Alone in this group it needs **active opposition and duration** — a war, a lawsuit, a long argument — so it never fits a race or a quick win. It's intransitive (*prevail over/against*, never "prevail someone"), and its second sense is the sleeper: **prevailing** = currently dominant or widespread, as in the prevailing wind or view.

> **On the exam:** The trap is the object, not the meaning: a completion that supplies a number wants **outstrip**, an obstacle wants **surmount**, a genre wants **transcend**, a forgotten predecessor wants **eclipse** — and in reading passages **prevailing** almost always means "widespread," not "victorious."


<a id="meaning__rouse-someone-to-act"></a>
### Rouse someone to act

All five describe one party moving another party into action — none of them involve ordering, and none guarantee the action happens. What separates them is the *mechanism* (moral appeal, irritation, a spark, a jolt, slow heat), the *moral verdict* (who gets blamed — the rouser or the roused), and the *kind of act* produced (worthy, unlawful, ill-judged, or merely hoped for). Get the mechanism and the blame right and the group stops being confusable.

- **exhort** — The only one with no leverage at all — **exhort** is pure moral appeal from someone who cannot compel, which is why exhortation is so often ignored (papers exhort ministers; ministers shrug). It's also the only member that assumes the urged act is *good*.
- **goad** — The mechanism is irritation, not persuasion: **goad** needles until the target acts to make it stop. Uniquely, it takes a single victim rather than a crowd, and the resulting act is characteristically stupid — *goaded into* a fight, a slip, a rash reply. Blame lands on the goader, sympathy on the goaded.
- **incite** — **Incite** is the legal accusation — one spark, a crowd, an unlawful or violent act (*incitement to riot*). It wants a deed as its object, not a mood, and it moves fast: a speech and then the mob. Where *goad* targets a person's temper, **incite** targets a group's readiness.
- **galvanize** — The one that flatters everyone: **galvanize** is a jolt that admires both jolt and jolted, and it presupposes the target was *inert* — you cannot galvanize the already-active. Where **incite** produces a riot, **galvanize** produces a campaign, a turnout, a movement.
- **foment** — **Foment** is the slow, off-stage one — sustained heat over months rather than a single moment, and always deliberate (nobody foments by accident). Its object is a condition of trouble, not a single deed: you foment unrest, discord, resentment; you cannot foment goodwill.

> **On the exam:** The trap is the blame axis: sentences with a positive tail (*a speech that ___ the volunteers*) want **galvanize**, and swapping in **incite** or **foment** — the two the test offers as bait — poisons a neutral sentence with criminal intent.


<a id="meaning__ruin-on-a-huge-scale"></a>
### Ruin on a huge scale

All four describe destruction well past ordinary misfortune — the scale at which recovery is doubtful and the event gets remembered rather than merely regretted. All are formal enough that using them for a bad haircut reads as a joke. They separate on three axes: whether the word blames a cause or just measures the wreckage, whether it stresses total failure or total transformation, and whether it qualifies an event (adjective) or *is* the event (noun).

- **calamitous** — The verdict word: it looks backwards at a **decision** and holds someone responsible — a calamitous policy, appointment, invasion. Where the others describe what happened, **calamitous** implies a chooser who should have known better.
- **catastrophic** — Measures **completeness of failure**, not blame or aftermath — the thing stopped working all at once and cannot be repaired. The engineering sense (*catastrophic failure*: gave way instantly, not gradually) keeps it the most literal and least rhetorical of the three adjectives.
- **cataclysmic** — The only one about **transformation** rather than damage: afterwards the landscape is unrecognisable and a new order stands. That's why *cataclysmic shift* works with no casualties at all — a sentence where nothing was destroyed but everything realigned wants this word and rejects **catastrophic**.
- **conflagration** — A **noun**, and a specific object: fire — or a war spoken of as fire, spreading outward from one local flashpoint until it consumes everything adjacent. It names the burning thing itself; the others are labels you attach to some other event.

> **On the exam:** Part of speech eliminates **conflagration** instantly in adjective slots; among the rest, the trap is treating them as interchangeable intensities — look for whether the sentence stresses a blamed decision (**calamitous**), a total breakdown (**catastrophic**), or a world remade (**cataclysmic**).


<a id="meaning__savage-public-criticism"></a>
### Savage public criticism

All of these describe criticism that is harsh, sustained, and meant to be heard by more people than the target. None of them fits a quiet correction: each assumes an audience, a critic with some standing to attack, and a target who comes off worse for it. What separates them is not how angry the critic is but what the attack *is* — a formal verdict, a methodical demolition, an undignified pounding, a thunderous scolding, or a wound that actually landed. Part of speech splits them too: three verbs, one noun, one adjective.

- **castigate** — The verdict word. **Castigate** names the offence — you castigate someone *for* something specific, from a seat of moral authority, and the sentence usually says what they did wrong. It is the least noisy of the group and the most judicial: an inquiry report castigates; a shouting match does not.
- **excoriate** — The most brutal verb here, and the most itemised. **Excoriate** is castigation carried on point by point until nothing is left standing — sustained flaying rather than a single pronouncement. It also elevates the critic: an excoriation implies the attacker had the standing to make it stick.
- **lambaste** — The one that makes the critic look excessive. **Lambaste** is pounding, not reasoning — it keeps swinging after the argument is over, and it carries the older sense of a physical thrashing. Journalistic in flavour; ministers get lambasted on front pages, and the word never suggests the attack was fair.
- **objurgation** — The only noun, and the only one that is a *scolding* rather than a judgement — volume and duration, not findings. Bookish enough that using it is usually a raised eyebrow: label a father's rant an **objurgation** and you have made him ridiculous. Lives in prose, not in speech.
- **scathing** — The only adjective, and it attaches to the attack, not the attacker: a **scathing** review, dismissal, footnote. It adds two things the verbs don't — wit and scorn on the critic's side, and proof of damage on the target's. Criticism that bounced off was never scathing, however loud.

> **On the exam:** The GRE rarely separates these by intensity — it separates them by grammar and framing: a blank needing a noun takes only *objurgation*, one modifying *review* or *report* takes only *scathing*, and a sentence that names the specific failing points to *castigate* over the vaguer *lambaste*.


<a id="meaning__say-it-again"></a>
### Say it again

All four turn on something happening more than once — content restated, ground covered again, a condition kept running past its natural end. The splits are three: *what* recurs (a sentence, a set of points, a practice), *who is doing it* (a speaker on purpose, or a society by default), and *whether the recurrence is judged useful or wasteful*. Two of these are things a speaker does to their own words; one is what a group does to a bad situation; one is the verdict passed on repetition after the fact.

- **reiterate** — One point, restated in roughly its original form, because the speaker thinks it didn't land — the repetition is deliberate and mildly aggrieved ("let me reiterate" = *you should have caught this*). It takes a single claim or position, never a whole talk and never a practice.
- **recapitulate** — Many points, compressed and put back in order — the detail is deliberately dropped, which is what separates it from restating something as it was. Structurally end-loaded: it belongs to the closing argument or final slide, and it presumes an audience that already sat through the long version.
- **perpetuate** — Nothing is being said at all — a practice, myth, or system simply keeps running, and you are the one keeping it alive. The others are things a speaker chooses to do in a moment; this is usually done passively, over generations, and the word itself is the accusation.
- **redundant** — The only judgment here rather than an act — it labels repetition as needless *because* it duplicates, which is the charge an editor makes about someone else's prose. Note the two senses that flip the valence: British "made redundant" (laid off) and engineering redundancy, where the duplication is the safeguard and the word turns approving.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating **perpetuate** as a fancy synonym for repeating a statement — it takes conditions and practices, not sentences; and **redundant** in a technical passage often means the *intended* backup, not the flaw.


<a id="meaning__saying-it-in-few-words"></a>
### Saying It in Few Words

All of these live in the space where something is short — a reply, a line, a style — and the shortness is the noticeable thing about it. What separates them is the *verdict* attached to the shortness: whether it reads as coolness, coldness, wit, discipline, or nothing at all. Two of them judge the speaker's temperament, one judges the quality of the line, and two are nouns naming the shortness itself, only one of which extends beyond words. Getting them wrong doesn't just flatten meaning — it flips the emotional sign of the sentence.

- **laconic** — **Laconic** describes a *standing habit*, not one reply — it's a temperament word, applied to the person who is always like this. The withholding reads as self-possession: he could have elaborated and didn't need to, and you're meant to find that composed rather than hostile.
- **terse** — **Terse** attaches to a single utterance and reads its temperature as *cold*. It's the word you reach for when the shortness is a message — irritation, reserve, conversation closed. A laconic man is a type; a terse email is an event, and someone got it.
- **pithy** — **Pithy** is the only one grading the *content*: it certifies the line was good. It says nothing about the speaker's manner or mood — a chatty, warm person can produce a pithy sentence — and it cannot be applied to a short answer that was merely short.
- **brevity** — **Brevity** is the flat noun for shortness with no verdict built in — it measures, it doesn't praise the wit or diagnose the chill. It's also the only member with a *time* sense, and there the emotional sign inverts: the brevity of a life or a season is a loss, not a virtue.
- **economy** — **Economy** isn't about being short — it's about nothing being *wasted*, which is why a long novel can have it and a one-word answer can lack it. It's also the only one that leaves language entirely: economy of gesture, of motion, of means. It credits the maker's control.

> **On the exam:** The GRE pairs these by temperature in Sentence Equivalence — a blank praising a speaker's wit takes **pithy**, not **terse**; a blank about a chilly reply takes **terse**, not **laconic** — and it hides **economy** behind the financial sense so you skip the "nothing wasted" reading.


<a id="meaning__saying-little"></a>
### Saying little

All four describe someone who says less than they could — the words are there, and they don't come out. They split on *why* and *what kind of little*: a lasting temperament, a specific subject fenced off, a style of delivery, or a performance meant to be noticed. Note that none of them means shy: shyness is inability, and every word here involves a person who has the material and withholds it. The GRE cares almost entirely about which axis each one lives on.

- **reticent** — **Reticent** is the topic word: it needs an *about*. He talks freely for an hour and goes quiet on his finances — that's reticence, and it says nothing about how chatty he is otherwise. Alone among these it points at self-disclosure specifically, which is why it reads as discretion or as concealment depending on who's asking.
- **taciturn** — **Taciturn** is the temperament word: it describes the person, not a topic or an occasion. There's no subject he's avoiding — he's like this at dinner, at work, and in ten years' time. It's the only one here you could apply to someone who has nothing whatever to hide.
- **laconic** — **Laconic** describes the *style of what does get said*, not the amount of silence. The laconic man answers — in four words, dryly, and the compression is the effect. It's the only one that can be a compliment about delivery: unflappable, deadpan, more force per word.
- **coy** — **Coy** wants you to notice the withholding — the silence is bait, not a fence. It's the only one here that's a performance aimed at an audience, and the only one carrying an eye-roll: the coy speaker is teasing, flirting, or managing you. A reticent CEO won't discuss the numbers; a coy one hints that there's something to discuss.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating **reticent** and **taciturn** as interchangeable — look for an "about X" in the sentence (reticent) versus a description of the person's standing character (taciturn); and don't let **coy** slip past as mere shyness, since it always implies calculation.


<a id="meaning__saying-the-delicate-thing"></a>
### Saying the delicate thing

All four describe handling something that could go wrong if handled clumsily — a feeling, a secret, a risk, a fine distinction. Each praises restraint and fine judgement over bluntness, which is why they blur. They split on **what is being protected**: the listener's feelings, someone else's privacy, your own exposure, or nothing at all — just the fineness of the thing itself.

- **tact** — The only noun here, and the only one that requires a person in front of you with feelings at stake — it lives in the moment of delivery, choosing words so a hard truth lands without wounding. Note the asymmetry: you almost never hear it praised, only missed (*tactless*).
- **discreet** — Not about sparing feelings but about guarding information — there is always a third party being protected, and the measure is what you *withhold*. It also covers not being noticed at all: a **discreet** enquiry is one nobody registers as a question.
- **circumspect** — The caution points at your own exposure, not anyone else's: you survey the consequences before committing. It's the only one that governs *acting* as much as speaking, and the only one that can be a fault — too circumspect means too slow to move. Formal; you write it.
- **subtle** — Describes the thing, not the person's virtue — a shade, a difference, an argument, a hint so fine it's easy to miss. Consequently it's the only member that can turn against you: a **subtle** poison or **subtle** manipulator uses the same fineness to deceive.

> **On the exam:** The classic swap is **discreet** for **circumspect**: check whether the sentence protects someone else's secret (discreet) or the actor's own neck (circumspect). Also watch the homophone *discrete* (= separate) and **subtle**'s sinister sense in negative contexts.


<a id="meaning__scold-someone-sharply"></a>
### Scolding: heat, rank, and hurt

All five verbs cover telling someone off for a fault — disapproval delivered *at* the offender, not merely opinion expressed about them. What separates them is not the offence but the posture behind the voice: how hot it runs, whether the speaker outranks the target, whether the fault gets named, and whether the impulse is to punish, to correct, or simply to show the wound. Register matters too: one of these belongs to shouting matches, the rest to written English.

- **berate** — The only one measured in **duration and decibels** — a tirade, not a sentence, usually with an audience. It's also the one that makes the *speaker* look bad: berating implies lost temper and enjoyed volume, where the other four leave the scolder's composure intact.
- **upbraid** — The fault gets **named, to the face** — you upbraid someone *for* a specific thing, which is exactly what berating (pure noise) never bothers to do. Bookish: it's what a narrator says a character did, not what happens in a real kitchen argument.
- **chastise** — The **rank gap is the point** — parent, bishop, coach, editorial page, correcting a subordinate *for their own good*. Alone in the group it retains a shadow of physical punishment from older and biblical use, which is why it lands heavier than any purely verbal telling-off.
- **admonish** — The **mild** one, and the only one that faces **forward**: it comes with advice or a warning attached (*admonished them to keep silent*). The aim is that you fix it, not that you feel it — which is why a judge admonishes a jury, an act no one would call a scolding.
- **reproach** — Powered by **hurt rather than authority** — "you let me down," not "you broke a rule" — so it can come from a friend, a mother, or your own conscience, and can be delivered by a look with no words at all. Also the group's live **noun**, surviving in *beyond reproach*, where it means the blame itself, not the act of blaming.

> **On the exam:** Sentence-equivalence traps lean on the two odd senses — **admonish** as forward-looking *warn/urge* and **reproach** as a noun meaning disgrace — while completion items key on the posture word in the stem (*gently*, *at length*, *from the bench*), which rules in exactly one of these.


<a id="meaning__settled-hostility"></a>
### Settled hostility vs. settled dislike

All five name a dislike that has hardened — not a flash of temper but something that persists and colors how the holder behaves. The differences aren't strength so much as **what the feeling attaches to and what it's doing in the sentence**: is it a heat between two people, a motive behind an act, a standing relationship, a cold judgment about a person or idea, or a wish to be somewhere else? Two of them cover being enemies; two cover simply not being able to stand something. One is used to accuse.

- **animosity** — The one with **temperature**. It's hostility as an atmosphere — bad blood you can hear in a tone of voice, usually personal and usually with a backstory (a feud, a snub). Where *enmity* is the standing relationship, animosity is the heat that keeps flaring inside it; where *animus* is the motive, animosity is the mood.
- **animus** — The **accusation** word: it names hostility as the *cause* of an act. You don't just feel animus, you act on it, and someone else alleges it — a firing, a prosecution, a rule *motivated by* animus. It always points back at the hostile party's mind, which is why it's the courtroom and op-ed choice; nobody writes that a jury found animosity.
- **enmity** — Names a **relationship, not an emotion** — the state of being enemies. It can lie completely dormant (two clans at enmity for a century, never speaking) where animosity has to be felt to exist. Typically mutual, often inherited, and scaled up: houses, nations, factions. Absurdly grand for a coworker.
- **antipathy** — Cold **dislike without the war**. It wants distance rather than damage, and unlike the hostility words it needs no history and no target who wronged you — it's often unaccountable, felt before it can be justified. It's also the one that takes **abstractions and groups** comfortably: antipathy toward regulation, toward reform, toward a whole class of people.
- **aversion** — The least social and the only **register-neutral** member: it points at a *thing or activity*, not a person, and implies nothing bad about the object — an aversion to paperwork, to cold water, to risk. Clinical enough for a psychologist or an economist to use with a straight face (*risk aversion*, *aversion therapy*). It describes what you avoid, not who you resent. Fixed preposition: aversion **to**.

> **On the exam:** The GRE splits this group by object and role: person-and-history (animosity), motive-for-an-act (animus), mutual standing state (enmity), person-or-idea judged coldly (antipathy), thing-or-activity avoided (aversion) — so read what the blank attaches to before ranking intensity.


<a id="meaning__shameless-nerve"></a>
