### Shameless nerve

All of these describe nerve — boldness that has crossed a line other people were respecting. The line differs: sometimes it's shame, sometimes rank, sometimes caution, sometimes the decent instinct to at least hide what you're doing. Most are the offended onlooker's verdict rather than a neutral description, so the choice usually encodes who is judging whom and on what grounds. One of them can be admiring, and one says the nerve isn't real at all.

- **effrontery** — The charge is **shamelessness itself** — the person should have been embarrassed and wasn't. It lives in a fixed frame (*had the effrontery to*), and what follows is always something the speaker finds indefensible. Rank is irrelevant here: an equal or a superior can show effrontery, because the offence is the missing blush, not the overstepped place.
- **temerity** — The charge is **presumption of standing** — you acted above your station toward someone you owed deference to. It encodes a hierarchy that **effrontery** doesn't need: the private who questions the general has temerity; the general doing the same thing has none. It also carries a whiff of recklessness — nerve that hasn't reckoned with consequences.
- **audacious** — The **only one here that can be a compliment**. It marks the ignored limit without ruling on it, so *an audacious plan* thrills and *an audacious lie* appalls, entirely on the sentence's say-so. Where the others arrive pre-loaded with disapproval, **audacious** waits to be told.
- **brazen** — The scandal is **openness**, not the act. A brazen lie is told to your face by someone who knows you know — sneaking would concede that the rule mattered, and they won't. It's the only one with a verb (*brazen it out*: outlast an accusation by refusing to look ashamed), and it carries contempt for the audience, not just disregard.
- **bravado** — The **only one where the nerve is fake**. It names a performance — swagger, loud talk, defiance staged for watchers — and using the word calls the bluff: the display is covering fear. The others describe boldness someone had; **bravado** describes boldness someone is advertising, hence *empty*, *false*, *a touch of*.

> **On the exam:** The trap is reading all five as negatives: **audacious** is the fence-sitter that can praise, so in a positive-daring context it's the answer the other four can't be.


<a id="meaning__show-a-claim-is-false"></a>
### Show a claim is false

All four sit at the point where a claim meets something that cuts against it. What separates them is *who or what does the cutting* and *whether it works*: a person marshalling proof, a person merely objecting, a public unmasking, or a mute fact that contradicts on its own. They also differ in whether the claim was ever respectable to begin with, and in one case the verb regularly ends up defending the claim rather than destroying it.

- **refute** — **Refute** is the only one that scores the point: it asserts the disproof landed and the matter is settled. It needs an arguer with evidence or logic — you cannot refute by objecting loudly. Using it of yourself is a large claim, which is why careful writers say *dispute* until the work is actually done.
- **gainsay** — **Gainsay** is contradiction by assertion alone — mouth against mouth, no proof implied and no success implied. Its habitat is the negative (*no one can gainsay*, *there is no gainsaying*), so in practice the word most often certifies that a claim is unassailable.
- **debunk** — **Debunk** requires a target with standing — a cherished myth, a celebrated theory, a reputation people bought into. It is public, deflating, and flatters the debunker as the plain-dealer against humbug; you cannot **debunk** a typo or a private hunch, only something that had believers.
- **belie** — **Belie** takes no arguer at all: its subject is a thing — a calm voice, a quarterly figure, a shabby facade — that silently contradicts. Direction is everything, since the subject is the deceiver or the disprover and what follows is the claim being undercut. It also carries the disguise sense the others lack, and it never means *reveal*.

> **On the exam:** The GRE punishes the loose senses: **refute** treated as "deny" (it means "disprove, successfully"), **gainsay** read as defeating a claim when its negative frame usually upholds one, and **belie** flipped so the subject reveals rather than misrepresents.


<a id="meaning__showy-for-the-audience"></a>
### Showy — and whether anyone meant it

All four describe something that draws the eye: display, colour, decoration, standing out. They split on two axes. First, intent — is the showiness deliberate, staged for an audience, or does the thing simply stick out? Second, what gets judged — the person's motive, their flair, or the surface of the object or style itself.

- **conspicuous** — The only one indifferent to intent: it reports visibility, not showmanship. A coffee stain, a lone red coat in a grey crowd, a missing guest — anything that fails to blend into its surroundings qualifies, and a *conspicuous* thing may be desperately trying not to be noticed.
- **ostentatious** — Convicts the motive, not the thing. It says the display exists to be admired — which is why it works on virtue as easily as money: **ostentatious** piety, grief, modesty. Call something this and you have accused someone of performing.
- **flamboyant** — The one you can be complimented with. It reads as flair owned and enjoyed — a conductor, a waistcoat, a signature — and it imputes no insincerity and no vulgarity, only theatre. The showiness entertains rather than solicits.
- **florid** — Attaches to surfaces and styles, not to people's behaviour: prose, music, ornament clotted with flourishes until the sense drowns. Uniquely in this group it also has a purely physical sense — a red, flushed complexion — with no display involved at all.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable "showy" synonyms: **conspicuous** needs no performer, **florid** needs no person, and only **flamboyant** can be praise.


<a id="meaning__shrewd-read-of-people"></a>
### Shrewd Judgment: Reading People, Money, and Motives

All of these praise a fast, accurate read of people and situations — the ability to size up what is really going on and what it's worth. This is worldly intelligence rather than book learning: it is earned by experience and measured by results, not by credentials. They split along three axes: how much self-interest is implied (working an angle vs. simply seeing clearly), how grand the register is (marketplace vs. lectern), and whether the insight looks at the present situation or at where it is heading.

- **astute** — The angle-spotter: sees the opportunity in a situation and moves on it first. It is the polite word for a talent that, described unkindly, would be called cunning — and it attaches naturally to negotiators and politicians, where finding the advantage is the job.
- **shrewd** — The emphasis is defensive and valuational — you can't be fooled and you know what things are actually worth. It's the one that survives dislike: you can call an opponent shrewd through gritted teeth, because it credits effectiveness without crediting character.
- **canny** — Caution, not flair. Its person is hard to cheat and never overpays — the low, steady competence of knowing when to walk away. Note the ceiling: canny is careful, never dazzling, and it leans hardest of the group toward money and bargaining.
- **perspicacious** — The only one with no whiff of self-interest: it sees *through* people rather than profits from them. Formal and cerebral — penetration of motive, the kind of insight you attribute to a critic or a novelist, not to someone closing a deal.
- **sagacious** — Alone in the group, it points forward: judgment vindicated by how things turned out. You apply it retrospectively to a decision that looked unremarkable at the time, and it carries a grand, elder-statesman dignity none of the others have.
- **acumen** — The noun, and the one that must be domain-bound — *business*, *political*, *financial* acumen. It names the capacity as a possession someone has in one arena and may entirely lack in another, which is why a brilliant scholar can have none of it.

> **On the exam:** The GRE separates these by what the blank rewards: **perspicacious**/**sagacious** fit sentences about insight or foresight for its own sake, while **astute**/**shrewd**/**canny** need a payoff — a deal, an angle, an advantage — in the clause; and **acumen**, the lone noun, is usually given away by the modifier before it.


<a id="meaning__shut-in-by-force"></a>
### Shut in by force

All four describe being held inside a boundary you did not draw — an outside hand (a law, a wall, an authority, an iron) fixing where you may go or how far you may reach. They split on what does the confining and what gets confined: an abstract limit on a power, masonry around a body, a precautionary cordon, or a cuff on a wrist. They also split on blame: one indicts the confiner, one merely states the limit, one is protective housekeeping.

- **circumscribe** — The only one that confines no body — it bounds a **scope**: a power, a role, a freedom, a life's options. It is also the only one neutral about justice: a constitution **circumscribes** a president perfectly legitimately, where a manacle always accuses. Formal, near-legal, and the limits are set in advance rather than clapped on mid-struggle.
- **immure** — The masonry word — walls, cells, cloisters, no door being opened. Uniquely in this group it can be **chosen**: you **immure yourself** in a library or a monastery, which no one does with manacles or quarantine. Literary and faintly gothic; it wants stone, not procedure.
- **quarantine** — The only member keyed to **suspicion, not guilt** — you hold the possibly-exposed, not the confirmed sick, and you release them when the doubt clears. Also the only confinement aimed at protecting *others* rather than punishing or limiting the one held, which is why it stays neutral in tone: a **quarantined** file is set aside pending judgement, not condemned.
- **manacle** — The only one that names a body part — **wrists** (fetters take the ankles) — and the only one with an oppressor built in. Dungeons, slave ships, chain gangs. Figuratively it demands real tyranny: **manacled** by debt or by law, never by a crowded calendar.

> **On the exam:** The trap is tone-matching: a sentence blaming no one wants **circumscribe**, one indicting a tyrant wants **manacle** — and if the confined party is only *possibly* contaminated, it is **quarantine**, not the "isolate" the sentence dangles.


<a id="meaning__sign-of-what-s-coming"></a>
### Sign of what's coming

All five say the same basic thing: something visible now stands for something not yet here. None of them assert the future event — they assert a *sign* of it, and the sign is almost always read as bad news. What separates them is grammar and grip: whether the sign is a verb the world performs, a noun you can point at, or an atmosphere you can only feel; and how much dread is welded into the word before you add any context.

- **portend** — The workhorse verb — the one a news anchor uses. It wants a stated outcome as its object (*portends a wave of layoffs*, *portends trouble for the ruling party*), so it commits you to naming what's coming. It's also the least emotionally loaded of the three verbs here: gravity without shudder, and the only one you could steer toward a good outcome without it collapsing into a joke.
- **presage** — **Portend** in a higher register — the same job done by a word that wants a red sky rather than a quarterly report. It's also the only verb in this group with a live noun form: a presage is the omen itself *or* the foreboding it plants in you, so it can name the feeling as well as the sign. Reach for it in prose, not in speech.
- **forebode** — The dread is inside the verb, not in the sentence around it. **Portend** is directionally steerable; nothing ever forebodes good news, so the word needs no adjective to darken it. It is also the only one here that a *person* can do — you forebode disaster, meaning you feel it coming. And the bare verb is nearly extinct: the GRE will hand you **foreboding**, noun or adjective.
- **harbinger** — The only noun, and the only one that can be a human being — a herald, a forerunner, someone or something that arrives *before* and announces. Because it's a separate arriving thing, never the event, it survives happily on good news (*a harbinger of spring*) where the verbs would sound arch. But its habitual company is *doom*, *decline*, *recession*, so it still makes people brace.
- **ominous** — The adjective, and the one that names no outcome at all. The verbs need an object — you portend or presage *something*. **Ominous** just marks the atmosphere: a silence, a pause, a 3am phone call is ominous with no clause following. It also describes a forecast, never an attack; the growling dog is threatening, the hush before the growl is ominous.

> **On the exam:** The trap is part of speech, not meaning — a blank taking a noun rules out portend/presage/forebode instantly, and a blank with no named consequence after it wants ominous, not a verb.


<a id="meaning__slanted-toward-one-side"></a>
### Slanted toward one side

All four say the same basic thing: even-handedness is missing. Something — a person, an essay, a survey question — has already picked a side, and what looks like inquiry is really advocacy. They split on *why* and *how visibly*: whether the tilt is unconscious or engineered, hidden or announced, aimed at a conclusion or at a rival group. The GRE lives in that gap, because in loose English any of them can be glossed "biased."

- **partial** — The mildest, coolest, and the only one that isn't an accusation of bad faith — a soft tilt, often unconscious, often just affection for the favourite. It's the one that attaches to a role sworn to neutrality (judge, referee, examiner) and the only one with a ready-made antonym, **impartial**. Also the only one that can turn warm: *partial to* means fond of.
- **tendentious** — Here the slant is engineered *and* concealed — the piece wears the costume of neutral analysis while steering you. It attaches to artifacts (a history, a footnote, a poll question), never to a temperament, and the charge is dishonest presentation rather than heat. Unlike a polemic, it will not admit what it's doing.
- **polemical** — The one-sidedness is announced, not hidden: this is declared combat, written to demolish an opponent, and everyone in the room knows it. That openness is why it's the only word here that can be neutral description or even praise — in an op-ed or a seminar, swinging is the job. Its failure mode is heat, not deceit.
- **chauvinistic** — The only one about group identity rather than argument: my country / my sex / my team is simply better than yours. It attaches to a person and their swagger, not to a text's reasoning, and it flatters the self — it needs an out-group to look worse. The picture it paints is smug and a bit ridiculous.

> **On the exam:** The trap is concealment vs. display: **tendentious** hides its agenda behind a neutral pose, **polemical** advertises it — and only **partial** is mild enough to fit a judge who merely leans.


<a id="meaning__sleep-inducing"></a>
### Sleep-inducing vs. sleepy vs. shut down

All three sit in the territory of sleep and shut-down energy, and each can describe a lecture hall, a hot afternoon, or a stalled institution. The confusion is grammatical as much as semantic: one names the *cause* of drowsiness, one names the drowsiness *or* its cause, and one names the *state* left behind — a noun for inertia, not for sleep. They also differ in what they blame: a dull thing, a heavy mood, or a body and system gone inert.

- **soporific** — Points at the **cause**, and points accusingly. Clinically it's just a sedative, but in every other context **soporific** is a verdict on something's dullness — the speech, the prose, the meeting made you sleep, and the speaker is being dryly witty about it. It's the only one of the three that works as an insult.
- **somnolent** — The reversible one: **somnolent** describes the drowsy person *and* the thing that made him drowsy, with no blame in either direction. It paints atmosphere — a dozing village, a courtroom after lunch — where *soporific* would be scoring a point. Heavy eyelids, not failure.
- **torpor** — A **noun** for the aftermath, and the only one that need not involve sleep at all — **torpor** is inertia: no energy, no motion, no appetite for either. It's a condition, not a mood or a criticism, and it scales from a hibernating animal to decades of administrative stagnation.

> **On the exam:** Sentence equivalence loves the cause/state split: a blank following "reduced the region to a state of ___" wants **torpor**, not the adjectives — and a blank describing the *speech itself* wants **soporific**, not the audience's **somnolent**.


<a id="meaning__slips-out-of-your-grasp"></a>
### Slips out of your grasp

All four describe something you fail to get hold of — but each locates the failure in a different place. In one, the target keeps moving; in another, a person is deliberately deflecting; in a third, the thing sits perfectly still and is simply too fine to register; in the last, it is fully on display and still gives up nothing. The sorting questions: is there an agent with intent, is there a pursuit, and is the problem that you can't reach it, can't notice it, or can't interpret it?

- **elusive** — **Elusive** requires a pursuit but not an adversary — it describes the *result* of chasing, so a cure, a scent or a concept can be elusive with no intent whatsoever. It's the only one here that attaches naturally to something you *want* (that elusive promotion), and the only one built on motion away from you.
- **evasive** — **Evasive** needs a conscious agent dodging a *specific* incoming thing — a question, a subpoena, a missile. Unlike **elusive**, it's about intent rather than outcome: a witness can be caught out instantly and still be evasive. Of speech it's a soft accusation you can print without a libel suit.
- **subtle** — **Subtle** involves no escaping at all — the thing holds still and you simply lack the resolution to catch it. It's the only one normally used as a compliment about craft, and the only one that applies to *degree*: a shade, a shift in wording, half a note.
- **inscrutable** — **Inscrutable** is the opposite of hidden: the face, the tone, the verdict sit right in front of you and reading them yields nothing. Where **subtle** means you failed to *notice*, inscrutable means you noticed everything and still can't *interpret*. Formal, and almost always aimed at the outside of a mind.

> **On the exam:** The classic trap is swapping **elusive** and **evasive** — take evasive only when someone is deliberately deflecting a specific challenge, elusive when something is merely never caught.


<a id="meaning__slow-something-s-progress"></a>
### Slow it down, don't stop it

All four describe interference that makes an action slower, harder, or clumsier without ever making it impossible — the thing still limps forward. The obstruction is typically impersonal and incidental (weather, paperwork, an injury, missing data) rather than deliberate sabotage. Because they overlap so heavily in meaning, they separate mostly by texture: friction beside you, weight on you, or a body in the path. Three are verbs; one is the noun that names the obstruction itself.

- **hinder** — The plainest and mildest of the set — the everyday Anglo-Saxon default, with no image behind it and no formality to it. It attaches naturally to forward motion (**hinder** progress, growth, recovery) and is the only one that reads comfortably in the negative: *nothing hindered them*. If a sentence wants generic friction with no particular flavor, this is the word.
- **hamper** — Adds **weight and encumbrance**: the subject is loaded down and working at reduced capacity, not blocked. It runs to the passive almost by reflex — *hampered by* fog, budget cuts, a torn hamstring — and what hampers clings to the actor rather than standing in the way. Watch the trap noun: a large lidded basket, which the exam will offer as a decoy definition.
- **impede** — Something is literally **in the path** (Latin: feet shackled). Unlike the others, it takes flow and passage as objects — impeded visibility, blood flow, traffic, drainage — where *hinder* and *hamper* would sound odd. Slightly more formal and more clinical, and it presumes no ill will: you impede by happening to occupy the space.
- **impediment** — The noun, and the only member that names the obstruction rather than the act. It labels a **standing condition** rather than a passing event — a speech impediment, a legal impediment to marriage, an impediment to trade — and it carries the most formal register here. Impediments are *removed* or *overcome*, never smashed through.

> **On the exam:** The distractors are usually true-stop words — thwart, foil, preclude, stymie — so pick from this group only when the action is still happening; among themselves, let the frame decide: "___ by" wants **hamper**, a flow or passage wants **impede**, a noun slot wants **impediment**.


<a id="meaning__slow-hidden-harm"></a>
### Slow, hidden harm

All four describe harm that isn't a single visible blow. The damage accumulates, works on something over time, and is usually reported rather than witnessed — which is why all four sit in formal registers (medicine, policy, research, editorials) and none of them fit a mugging or a car crash. They split on two axes: how much moral heat the speaker brings, and whether the harm actively hides itself.

- **deleterious** — The **biology and medicine** word: it attaches to *effects* on an organism, a body, a system's functioning — a deleterious mutation, deleterious to the soil. Zero moral judgment; a gene can be deleterious and nobody is to blame. It reads as a measurement, not an accusation.
- **detrimental** — The only one that is essentially **relational**: harm reckoned against a specific interest, so it wants a *to* — detrimental to morale, to your case, to the company's standing. Its harm is loss or disadvantage on a ledger, often reversible, and it's the weakest of the four; a policy can be detrimental without anything being destroyed.
- **pernicious** — The one carrying **moral condemnation**. It attaches to ideas and influences rather than substances — a pernicious myth, a pernicious doctrine — and it tells you the speaker is educated and alarmed. Where the others report harm, **pernicious** denounces something corrupting.
- **insidious** — Describes the **manner of advance, not the magnitude**: it looks harmless, or nobody is watching, and you learn of it from the wreckage. This is the one where **concealment is the whole point** — a compounding debt, an addiction, a cancer. Something can be insidious and small; it cannot be insidious and obvious.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable "harmful": pick by what the sentence emphasizes — a clinical/physical effect (deleterious), damage to a named interest (detrimental), moral corruption (pernicious), or the fact that it went unnoticed until too late (insidious).


<a id="meaning__sly-cleverness"></a>
### Sly cleverness

All five describe getting what you want by indirection — trickery, misdirection, a route around the rules — rather than by force, argument, or straight dealing. The cleverness is never in question in any of them; what varies is how much the word forgives it. Each sits somewhere on a slide from grudging admiration to flat accusation, and each attaches to a different thing: the schemer's long experience, the single sly move, the polish of the execution, the cold self-interest behind it, or the crooked path itself. Two of them also carry an innocent literal sense that the sly sense has almost buried.

- **wily** — The one that implies **a long track record and a weaker hand**. **Wily** is evasive rather than constructive — feints, dodges, letting the stronger party overcommit — and it goes to veterans: the wily old fox, the wily negotiator who has seen this move before. A teenager can be crafty; almost nobody is wily at nineteen.
- **crafty** — The most **small-scale and domestic** of the group. **Crafty** fits one contained move — the kid who talks his way out of chores, the real term buried in clause nine — not a career of scheming, and it scales down to the nearly harmless in a way *cunning* and *devious* never do.
- **artful** — The only one whose emphasis falls on **how well it was done**. An **artful** dodge is admired as a performance; the handling is smooth enough that you half-enjoy being handled. It also keeps a fully clean sense — an *artful* arrangement of flowers, meaning tastefully contrived.
- **cunning** — The **coldest and most predatory**, and the only one that is also a noun (*won by sheer cunning*). Where the others name a tactic, **cunning** names a faculty — an almost animal instinct for advantage, indifferent to whom it costs.
- **devious** — The only one aimed at **the route rather than the person's wit** — the loops, the cover story, the third party who "happened" to mention it. It retains a live literal sense of *winding, indirect* (a **devious** mountain track), and it is the group's harshest word when pointed at an institution or a contract.

> **On the exam:** The GRE rarely pits these against each other — it tests the buried senses: **devious** as *winding/indirect* (of a path) and **artful** as *tastefully contrived* (of an arrangement), where a context containing no deception at all rules out every synonym you were braced for.


<a id="meaning__socially-clumsy"></a>
### Socially clumsy

All five cover a failure of grace — someone or something lands badly in front of others, and there's a wince. But they split on *what* failed and *what form the word takes*: two are verdicts on a person (their breeding, their body), one is a verdict on their skill, and two are nouns naming the botched moment itself rather than the botcher. The tone ranges from half-fond to faintly contemptuous, and picking the wrong one misstates who is being judged and how harshly.

- **gauche** — The only one that indicts your **upbringing**. **Gauche** says the blunder came from never having learned the rules — and the speaker, by using it, claims to know them. It judges taste, not ability or coordination, and it's a standing condition rather than a single slip.
- **gawky** — The only one about the **body**. **Gawky** is limbs and coordination — too tall, not yet in control — and implies nothing about tact, skill, or class. It's also the mildest and the most affectionate, because it assumes you'll outgrow it.
- **gaffe** — A **countable public event**, and almost always **spoken**. A **gaffe** happens at a podium or on a hot mic; it's the tactless or inconveniently true thing that escaped, reported with relish. Nobody *is* gaffe — you commit one, and it's over by next week.
- **infelicity** — The **euphemism**, and the one about **wording on the page**. An **infelicity** is a phrase that lands wrong in a manuscript, not a person who lands wrong in a room — and choosing it concedes the writer meant well. It's the only word here that is a courtesy.
- **inept** — The only one about **competence at a task**. **Inept** says you did the thing badly — the negotiation, the repair, the handshake — not that you offended anyone's sense of decorum. It carries the speaker's contempt, but for your ability, not your breeding.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable "awkward": watch whether the sentence needs a noun for the blunder (gaffe, infelicity) or an adjective for the person, and whether the failure is of skill (inept), breeding (gauche), or coordination (gawky).


<a id="meaning__solidly-skilled"></a>
### Solidly skilled

All four say a person can actually do the thing — skill that's been demonstrated, not promise or potential. They differ almost entirely by altitude and by what the speaker is signalling: where on the scale from "met the standard" to "the room was impressed" the praise lands, and how much effort the doing appears to cost. Two are adjectives applied to a person, two are nouns naming the ability itself. Ordered here from floor to ceiling.

- **competent** — The floor. **Competent** certifies the absence of failure, not the presence of quality — which is why reviewers use it as a slur ("a competent thriller"). It's the only one here whose connotation flips with context: in law (*competent to stand trial*, *court of competent jurisdiction*) it means authorised, and the faint praise disappears entirely.
- **proficient** — One rung up, and audibly **earned** — it credits drilling and training rather than gift, and it stops deliberately short of brilliance. It's also the fussiest grammatically: you're proficient *in* or *at* something, never proficient full stop.
- **facility** — Not a level of skill but a **quality of execution**: it looks easy. A noun, and the only word here that comments on visible effort — which is why it can turn barbed (*a facility for excuses*), implying the ease came too cheaply to be worth much.
- **prowess** — The ceiling, and the only one that carries an **audience** — prowess is displayed and someone is impressed. Formal, faintly heroic (it started as courage in battle), so it sounds like boasting in the first person and absurd on small tasks. It arrives bolted to a domain: *military*, *athletic*, *technical prowess*.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating **competent** and **proficient** as praise: sentence-completion items pair them with concessive signals ("*though* the performance was ___, it never thrilled"), where only the low-ceiling words fit and **prowess** or **facility** is the wrong-because-too-flattering distractor.


<a id="meaning__soothe-someone-s-anger"></a>
### Soothing anger: what the peace cost you

All of these are about taking the heat out of someone's anger — a grievance already exists, and someone is acting to bring the temperature down. They differ almost entirely in **what the peace costs and who is above whom**: whether a price was paid, whether the soother was the weaker party, and whether the calmed party ends up satisfied or merely quiet. The gloss "calm someone down" is identical across the set; the sneer, the tribute, and the surrender are not. One of them describes only a manner rather than an act.

- **mollify** — The gentlest and the only one aimed squarely at **feelings rather than demands** — you **mollify** fears, concerns, hurt pride, not a list of terms. It names no price and no power gap, just a softening gesture; note how often it appears negated ("failed to mollify"), which no other word here does as a matter of habit.
- **placate** — Names the tactic — a concession — and quietly rates it **cheap**. "A few tweaks to **placate** the board" tells you the tweaks were token and the board was a nuisance being managed; the cynicism attaches to the person soothed, not to the soother.
- **appease** — The only one that prices the peace as **surrender**: you got quiet by yielding to demands, and the word says the yielder was weak and the demander will be back. It alone also takes appetites as objects — **appease** hunger, curiosity — where calming a person isn't involved at all.
- **pacify** — Condescending: it treats the other side's anger as **noise to be switched off** rather than a claim to be answered, so the **pacified** party ends up quiet, not satisfied. Uniquely, it scales up to territory — armies **pacify** a region — which is why it reads as a euphemism in official prose.
- **propitiate** — Presumes a **hierarchy with you at the bottom**: gods, kings, inspectors, the furious department head. You pay upward — an offering, a sacrifice — and the ritual smell means using it of an ordinary person mocks them as a petty deity collecting tribute.
- **conciliatory** — An adjective describing **manner, not payment** — a **conciliatory** remark concedes literally nothing, it just lowers the temperature and signals willingness to end the fight. The only positive word here: dignified, diplomatic, and criticised at worst as looking soft.

> **On the exam:** The exam plants the clue in the cost or the power gap — "gave in to every demand" (appease), "offered up to an angry superior" (propitiate), "tone that conceded nothing" (conciliatory) — and offers a bland soother like mollify or placate that fits "calmed" but ignores that clue.


<a id="meaning__sparkling-liveliness"></a>
### Sparkling liveliness

All five sit on the bright, high-spirited end of temperament: something is animated, up, giving off energy rather than sitting still. They split on the *channel* that energy takes — social charm, quiet good mood, resistance to being pushed down, sheer noise, or verbal brilliance — and on what noun each can legally attach to. Several also carry a second life outside people entirely: floating objects, rising markets, rough seas, flashes of light.

- **vivacious** — **Vivacious** is charm in company — the energy comes out as talk, laughter, and animation directed at other people, so it needs an audience the way the others don't. It describes a person's manner, never a mood, a market, or a noise level; and it's applied to women far more than men, which gives it a faintly dated edge.
- **jocund** — **Jocund** is the quiet one: bright spirits with no output — no noise, no wit, no charm offensive, just lightness in the air. It's also the only member marked for register, belonging to verse and pastiche; call a meeting jocund and you're joking. It can settle on a morning or a landscape, not just a person.
- **buoyant** — **Buoyant** presupposes downward pressure — it praises what didn't sink, so it implies bad news survived rather than good spirits displayed. It's the only one that describes an economy or demand (rising, healthy) and the only one with a literal physics sense. Quiet resilience, not visible sparkle.
- **boisterous** — **Boisterous** is the only one defined by volume and bodies — loud, physical, spilling over furniture — and the only one that can double as a complaint (a boisterous crowd may need managing). The good humour is what keeps it out of *rowdy* territory. Extends to wind and sea: rough, wild.
- **scintillating** — **Scintillating** rates *output*, not temperament: an essay, a first half, an hour of conversation. It measures cleverness rather than cheer — you can be scintillating while cold — and it hints at flash over depth. It also takes sarcasm better than any other compliment in English; said flat, it means tedious.

> **On the exam:** The GRE tests the noun, not the mood: a buoyant *economy*, a boisterous *crowd*, scintillating *conversation*, a vivacious *hostess* — pick the word whose sense-range covers the subject, and remember scintillating rewards wit while boisterous only rewards volume.


<a id="meaning__reasoning-that-only-looks-sound"></a>
### Specious, Fallacious, Sophistry, Spurious: reasoning that only looks sound

All four are formal, negative verdicts delivered after inspection: something presented as legitimate has been examined and found not to hold up. They differ on two axes. First, **what is broken** — the logical machinery of the argument, or its very right to be taken seriously. Second, **whether anyone meant it** — these words run from an honest mistake in the steps, through a suspiciously well-polished surface, to a flat accusation of knowing deceit. Choosing wrongly either accuses a sincere person of lying or lets a liar off as merely confused.

- **fallacious** — The only one of the four that is neutral about the arguer's motives — **fallacious** locates the defect purely in the inference, so a sincere person can be fallacious all day. It also has technical teeth the others lack: you can usually name the fallacy (affirming the consequent, post hoc). Note the sting is that the conclusion is *unearned*, not necessarily untrue.
- **specious** — Unlike **fallacious**, this word is about *appearance* — it says the thing was built to survive a first glance and fail a second. Attach it to a single argument, excuse or claim, not to a person or a body of work, and only when the surface plausibility is the point. **Specious** implies you did the second look; **fallacious** implies you did the logic.
- **sophistry** — The one noun in the group, and the only outright accusation of bad faith: it says the arguer *knows* and argues anyway, with visible pleasure in his own cleverness. Where **specious** describes a flaw the arguer might not have noticed, **sophistry** names a practice — a whole style of arguing, not one bad step. Reserve it for the tobacco lawyer, not the confused undergraduate.
- **spurious** — The odd one out: it attacks *standing*, not reasoning, so it reaches things that don't argue at all — a forged charter, a fake pedigree, a correlation thrown up by noise. Calling an argument **fallacious** or **specious** engages with it; calling it **spurious** refuses to, saying it never had a legitimate basis to begin with. And it needs no deceiver — data produce spurious results with nobody lying.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable synonyms for "false": look for context clues about *blame* (sincere error → fallacious; deliberate → sophistry) and about *what* is defective (the inference → fallacious/specious; the origin or legitimacy → spurious).


<a id="meaning__spoil-by-mixing-or-staining"></a>
### Spoiled from Within: Adulterate, Debase, Vitiate, Tarnish

All four describe something good being degraded rather than destroyed — the object survives, keeps its name, and still looks roughly like itself, but it is no longer worth what it was. The damage comes from inside or from something added, not from a blow landed from outside. What separates them is *what* gets spoiled: the substance, the value, the validity, or just the gleam.

- **adulterate** — The only one that requires an actual added ingredient — something cheaper was physically mixed in, usually for profit and usually in secret. It names a fraud with a recipe: milk plus water, oil plus oil, heroin plus baking soda. Watch for the negative, **unadulterated**, which the GRE uses far more than the verb.
- **debase** — Targets **worth and dignity**, not substance — the coin still reads *silver*, the office still carries its title. It is the only one in the group that comfortably takes a person as object in the moral sense (*debase yourself*), meaning made to act beneath your station. There is always an implied *before*, a higher value that has been talked down.
- **vitiate** — Attacks **validity**: after this, the thing no longer counts. One false premise, one fraudulent signature, one procedural defect, and the argument, contract, or consent is void — the flaw needn't be large, only fatal. It is the group's legal-philosophical term, and the only one you can apply to reasoning.
- **tarnish** — Purely **surface and gradual** — the shine is gone, nothing was added and nothing was invalidated. It attaches almost exclusively to metal and to reputations, and presupposes there was lustre to lose. Coolest of the four in tone: no moral outrage, no fraud alleged, and unlike the rest it can be polished off.

> **On the exam:** The GRE punishes over-reading strength: a blank about an argument or a contract wants **vitiate** (validity destroyed), not **tarnish** (reputation dulled) — and **adulterate** is wrong unless something was literally mixed in.


<a id="meaning__spoiling-for-a-fight"></a>
### Spoiling for a fight

All five describe hostility as a *habit* rather than a passing temper: the person (or thing) is set up to produce conflict. What separates them is the kind of conflict, its heat, and who's watching. Some mean fists, some mean argument, some mean nothing worse than bickering — and one of them can be aimed at an inanimate clause in a contract.

- **belligerent** — The only one where the fight is **already happening** — the hostility has left the face and reached the voice, the shove, the war. Also the only one with a noun sense: **belligerent** states are nations formally at war, which is why the word straddles the police blotter and the peace treaty.
- **truculent** — Menace held in reserve — the scowl, the folded arms, the flat refusal. **Truculent** almost always points upward at authority (the teenager, the hostile witness, the shop steward), and unlike the others it transfers to prose meaning *savagely wounding*, not merely quarrelsome.
- **pugnacious** — The only word here that can be a compliment. **Pugnacious** carries relish and energy — the combativeness is a talent, usually exercised in words: the columnist, the cross-examiner, the undersized striker. Nobody is pugnacious for an evening; it's a permanent build.
- **contentious** — The only one that attaches to **things** as well as people — a contentious border, clause, or appointment is one that *generates* argument. Of a person it means argument specifically, never violence, and it's the word for a performance review: dry, formal, damning.
- **fractious** — The weakest and most condescending: a nuisance, not a threat. **Fractious** is the observer's word for someone else's bad temper — the fractious toddler, the fractious passenger — and it's the only one that describes a *group* squabbling internally and liable to fly apart (a fractious coalition).

> **On the exam:** The GRE usually tests the odd senses, not the fight: **contentious** attached to an issue rather than a person, **fractious** attached to a coalition rather than a brawler, and **pugnacious** in a sentence where the tone is admiring.


<a id="meaning__spread-widely-outward"></a>
### Spread widely outward

All four take something concentrated in one place and move it outward until it covers a wide area. The tests that separate them are mechanical: does the thing multiply as it travels, does the original mass survive, is there an intended recipient, and does the spreading make it weaker. Some of these verbs care about the message arriving; others care only that the clump broke up.

- **disseminate** — The only one whose object is essentially always **content** — findings, guidelines, propaganda — and the only one with an intended audience it was aimed at. **Disseminate** is a deliberate institutional push from a source that stays intact and keeps sending; ministries and journals disseminate, wind and crowds do not.
- **propagate** — **Propagate** is the self-replicating one: each recipient becomes a new transmitter, so the quantity grows rather than merely travels. That's why it fits cuttings, signals, and software errors — and why, aimed at a belief, it accuses you of knowingly multiplying something false.
- **disperse** — **Disperse** is about the mass, not the message — there is no recipient and nothing is transmitted, only a concentration that stops being one. Uniquely, it can be issued as an order to people (police disperse a crowd), and its success is measured by the gathering ceasing to exist.
- **diffuse** — **Diffuse** ends in evenness and weakness: the thing spreads until it's uniformly present and nowhere strong. It's also the only member with a common adjective sense, and on the GRE that adjective is a criticism of prose — everything present, no centre, so nothing lands.

> **On the exam:** Expect **diffuse** as an adjective in a sentence about writing (paired against concise/trenchant), not as a verb — and expect **propagate** where a careless reader picks **disseminate**, since only propagate implies the thing reproduces itself as it goes.


<a id="meaning__stale-worn-out-sayings"></a>
### Stale sayings: from merely flat to falsely wise

All four are verdicts on language that has lost its force through repetition — the speaker is not describing a remark, but convicting it. The shared accusation is that nothing new was thought before the mouth opened. They split along two lines: two are adjectives that judge a thing's quality, two are nouns that name the offending remark itself; and each adds a different aggravating charge on top of staleness — tedium, laziness, false profundity, or sedation.

- **banal** — The widest net and the only one that reaches past words — a **banal** film score, sofa, or gift can all qualify, so long as the thing was supposed to be interesting. It is also the only one that needs no history: a compliment can be **banal** the first time it is uttered, because the charge is sheer predictability, not a record of overuse.
- **hackneyed** — Requires the track record **banal** does not. **Hackneyed** points at the wear itself — the phrase, metaphor, or plot twist got used to death, usually because it worked. The charge is the writer's laziness in reaching for it, and it lands almost only on language and literary devices; a **hackneyed** chair is nonsense.
- **platitude** — A noun, so it names one specific sentence you can quote back. What makes it a **platitude** rather than merely a stale line is the moral posture: it sounds like wisdom and asks you to nod. "Everything happens for a reason." The accusation is pretension — you had nothing, so you dressed nothing up as insight.
- **bromide** — A **platitude** with a job to do: sedation. The **bromide** is deployed to smooth over grief, conflict, or an awkward question so nobody has to keep thinking — hence the accusation is evasion, not just emptiness. It alone can also name the *person* ('he's a complete bromide'), and it is the bookish one, at home in criticism and political columns rather than speech.

> **On the exam:** The classic trap is **banal** vs **hackneyed** (only **hackneyed** requires prior overuse, and only **banal** applies to non-verbal things) and **platitude** vs **bromide** (look for a "consoling," "soothing," or "reassuring" clue in the sentence — that clue selects **bromide**).


<a id="meaning__standing-between-two-sides"></a>
### Standing Between Two Sides

All four words live in the gap between two parties that are apart — opposed, separated, or simply unable to deal with each other directly. Something or someone occupies that gap: carrying, brokering, substituting, or finally closing it. They diverge on three questions: does the middle figure serve both sides or just one, does it hold any power to compel, and is the word naming the position, the activity, or the result?

- **intermediary** — The only one that names a **seat, not a deed**. An **intermediary** is defined by geography — it sits between — and may add nothing but its own presence and its own fee. Hence the commercial sneer in "cut out the intermediary," which no one says about a mediator.
- **mediate** — **Mediate** is the active labour of the middle position, and its signature is *powerlessness*: the mediator shuttles and coaxes but cannot rule, so "a mediated settlement" quietly certifies that both sides consented. Alone in this group it also has a flat academic sense — *mediated by* = transmitted through — where no dispute exists at all.
- **proxy** — The others stand *between* two sides; a **proxy** stands *for* one of them, carrying its delegated authority and acting in its name. Its second life is scientific: the stand-in measurement for a quantity you cannot reach — the only word here that can substitute for a *thing* rather than a person.
- **reconcile** — Not a middle figure at all but the **outcome** the middle figure is after, and it presupposes a prior break — a quarrel, a discrepancy in the books, a fate you fought. Its reflexive form (*reconcile oneself to*) has no counterpart in the others: a private surrender with no second party involved.

> **On the exam:** The GRE rarely tests the dispute-settling sense — expect **mediate** in its colourless \"transmitted through\" use and **proxy** as a stand-in variable in a science passage, where the negotiation reading is a trap.


<a id="meaning__stingy"></a>
### Stingy: Withholding What Could Be Given

All five describe holding back what could be given — money, praise, detail, effort — and giving less than the situation calls for. The shared frame is *sparing to a fault*: not the admirable economy of **frugal** or **thrifty**, but withholding that invites judgment. What separates them is the source of the tightness (greed, poverty, caution), whether it describes a whole character or a single act, and how bookish the word sounds.

- **miserly** — The only one that paints a picture: the hoarder shivering to save on coal. **Miserly** is greed plus self-denial — the tightness hurts the person doing it, which is why it carries pity as well as contempt. It's also the plainest word here; you can say it out loud in anger.
- **parsimonious** — The audit-room word: cold, formal, judgmental without any pity. Where **miserly** imagines a personality, **parsimonious** reads like a finding about someone's habits. Uniquely, it flips positive off money — a *parsimonious explanation* is lean and elegant, and that reversal is prime GRE bait.
- **penurious** — The only one that can mean *actually broke*. **Penurious** describes living as though there is nothing — and the insult version says you look destitute by choice. Bookish, essay-and-novel register; the ambiguity between poverty and meanness is deliberate, and context alone resolves it.
- **stinting** — Attaches to an act, not a character: you **stint** on portions, on effort, on praise, in this instance. It implies something was owed and got rationed. Watch its habitat — it lives mostly in the negative (*unstinting*, *without stinting*), so a bare positive on the exam means grudging short-changing.
- **chary** — Motive is caution, not greed. The **chary** person holds back because handing it over feels risky — and it takes *of* or *about* (**chary of praise**, **chary of lending**), which no other word here requires. Mildest and least damning: it can even read as prudent, only faintly tight-fisted.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating all five as interchangeable insults: **parsimonious** turns into praise when it modifies a theory or explanation, **penurious** may simply mean poor, and **chary** signals wariness rather than greed — pick the wrong one and the sentence's motive clause stops making sense.


<a id="meaning__stop-resisting"></a>
### Stop resisting

All four describe the moment resistance stops and the other side gets its way. They split on the backstory each one assumes: whether a fight ever occurred, how long it lasted, and which party was doing the pressing. They also split on who looks bad afterward — some paint the giver-in as weak, one paints them as having been the harsh one, and one paints nobody badly at all.

- **acquiesce** — The only one where no fight ever happened — the objection stayed inside your head. It measures consent by silence, so it needs a power gap to make sense (a boss, a regime) and it faintly indicts you for not speaking up. Grammar matters: you acquiesce **in** or **to** something.
- **capitulate** — Demands a prior siege: a standoff, a campaign, months of holding out, then the break. Uniquely, it implies you accept *the other side's terms*, not a compromise — the winner sets the conditions. Applied to a person or institution, it is close to an accusation of cowardice.
- **yield** — The neutral, physical one: the thing **gives** rather than breaks. It can happen instantly, without any prior refusal, and can be a courtesy or a tactic rather than a defeat ("I yield to my colleague"). It also carries a sense none of the others has — to *produce* a return, as a crop or a bond does.
- **relent** — Casts you as the one who was being hard — refusing, punishing, pressing — so the giving way reads as mercy rather than defeat. It is also the only one that takes impersonal subjects: rain, heat, and pain relent. Its negative, relentless, is the far commoner word.

> **On the exam:** The GRE picks between these on backstory, not on strength: sentences signal "held out for months" (relent/capitulate) versus "never objected aloud" (acquiesce) — and it loves testing yield and relent through their adjectives, unyielding and relentless.


<a id="meaning__stopping-and-starting"></a>
### Stopping and starting

These all describe something that fails to run steadily — it comes and goes, flares and stops, or veers off with no rhythm you could predict. The shared complaint is unreliability rather than badness: the thing exists, it just won't hold. They split on *what* is irregular (gaps in one process, scattered separate events, or quality itself) and on how much blame lands on whoever is responsible.

- **intermittent** — **Intermittent** is the group's neutral instrument reading: one thing that keeps cutting out and coming back. It describes the gaps in a continuing phenomenon — power, rain, a signal — and passes no judgment on anyone's character or effort. If a scientist or engineer would write it in a report, this is the word.
- **sporadic** — **Sporadic** counts scattered instances rather than interruptions: separate occurrences popping up here and there with no pattern. It's the only one at home with events spread across space as well as time — sporadic gunfire, sporadic outbreaks, sporadic protests — and the only one whose connotation genuinely swings (sporadic resistance may impress; sporadic attendance won't).
- **fitful** — **Fitful** adds restlessness: short bursts that flare and die, so the thing never settles into itself. Where *intermittent* rain simply resumes, **fitful** sleep is unsatisfying by definition — the word tells you the process failed to take hold, which is why it lives with sleep, breezes, and recoveries that don't stick.
- **erratic** — **Erratic** is the only one about deviation rather than timing — not "it stops and starts" but "you can't predict what it will do or how well." It measures against a norm that ought to hold, and applied to a person it hints at instability: erratic driving, erratic form, erratic behaviour reported by witnesses.
- **desultory** — **Desultory** indicts the doer, not the schedule: aimless *and* unenthused, drifting from thing to thing because nobody cared enough to finish. It attaches to human effort — conversation, reading, revision, an investigation — never to rain or a signal, and it's the formal, quietly withering one.

> **On the exam:** The GRE decides between these by what the blank attaches to: machinery and weather take **intermittent**, scattered incidents take **sporadic**, a person's uneven performance takes **erratic**, and only half-hearted human effort takes **desultory** — so a context that supplies "aimless" but no droop of enthusiasm is a trap for it.


<a id="meaning__straining-to-impress"></a>
### Straining to impress

Every word here marks a gap between the show and the substance: someone is working to seem grander, deeper, or more formidable than they are, and an observer has noticed. All five are verdicts delivered from outside — nobody applies them to themselves — and the charge is never that the person is wicked, only that the performance is unearned. What separates them is *what* is being inflated (culture, importance, resolve, territory) and how big the fake is: one tic, one manner, or one whole claim to greatness.

- **pretentious** — The only one whose target is specifically **cultural** credit — taste, learning, depth. It also attaches to objects as readily as to people: a menu, a film, a baby's name can be **pretentious**, where nothing else here can.
- **affectation** — The countable one: an **affectation** is a single item you can point at and list — a borrowed accent, a cigarette holder, a British spelling. The others describe a whole manner; this one is small enough to be faintly ridiculous rather than damning.
- **posturing** — The only charge about **intent** rather than taste or manner. The pose is a stance or a threat, and the accusation is that no action will follow it — which is why it lives in political and negotiating contexts, where the posturer wants leverage, not admiration.
- **pomposity** — Inflates **importance**, and does it entirely through delivery — cadence, ceremony, Latinate weight. Crucially the pompous man believes his own grandeur; he is hiding nothing, which makes him puncturable and comic rather than sly.
- **aggrandize** — The only verb, and the only word that takes an **object** — you aggrandize *yourself*, a rival, an empire. It can also name a real gain in power rather than merely an air of one, and it implies the gain came at someone's expense. Learn it as **self-aggrandizing**.

> **On the exam:** The trap is matching the pose to the wrong target: hollow threats want *posturing*, not *pretentious*; a grand speaking voice wants *pomposity*; and *aggrandize* is the only option that can govern an object.


<a id="meaning__strict-and-demanding"></a>
### Strict and demanding

All five words describe demands that press hard on someone — bars set high, obligations that weigh, penalties that bite. They cluster because English uses "strict" and "severe" loosely for all of them, while each actually names a different part of the machinery: how tight the standard is, how much skill it costs to meet it, how unbending the method must be, how heavy the duty sits, and whether the penalty fits the crime. Three of them (the first three) can be praise in the right context; the last two never are. Getting them right means asking what the severity is *made of*, not how unpleasant it feels.

- **stringent** — **Stringent** measures the *narrowness of the gap you must fit through* — the specification, threshold or condition, before anyone has tried to meet it. It says nothing about how much work meeting it takes or what happens if you fail; tighten a limit from 10ppm to 1ppm and it became more stringent without becoming more painful or more unjust.
- **exacting** — **Exacting** is the only one that measures the *cost to the person performing* — care, skill, stamina drawn out of you. It also uniquely applies to a human demander (an exacting supervisor), where stringent cannot; and it credits that demander with legitimacy, so it exhausts you without insulting them.
- **rigor** — **Rigor** is the noun, and it names *unbendingness of procedure* — no step skipped, no gap papered over, whether in a proof or in a regime's enforcement. It is the group's swing word: praise for a method, condemnation for a person, and in the plural (*the rigors of*) simply hardship endured, with no rule-maker in the picture at all.
- **onerous** — **Onerous** measures *weight of obligation*, and is indifferent to difficulty or skill — the task can be trivially easy and still onerous if you are bound to do it repeatedly and cannot set it down. Where exacting flatters the demand as necessary, onerous mutters that the load is more than your share.
- **draconian** — **Draconian** is the only one that judges a *ratio*: the response versus the offence. It requires a punishment to be in view — a rule with no penalty attached cannot be draconian, however tight — and it is a public accusation aimed at whoever wrote the policy, which is why it appears in headlines and never in self-description.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as one intensity scale: sentences reward the word that matches what the severity attaches to — a *standard* is stringent, a *task or boss* is exacting, a *method* has rigor, a *duty* is onerous, a *penalty* is draconian — and a positive-context blank ("praised for its ___") rules out onerous and draconian outright.


<a id="meaning__swamped-by-too-much"></a>
### Swamped by Too Much

All four describe a quantity that exceeds what the receiver can absorb — the problem is amount, not difficulty. Each frames that excess differently: as water rising, as fire aimed at a target, as blows landing over and over, or as a meal that has gone past enjoyable. Three of them make you a victim under something; one of them makes you merely too full. The GRE keeps them close because "a lot of X" is the shared floor — the answer always turns on *how* the too-much arrives and *what it does to you*.

- **inundate** — **Inundate** has no attacker — the stuff simply arrives, impersonal and plural (*inundated with applications, complaints, submissions*). Nobody aimed it at you; you were just standing where it fell. It is the only one of the four that can be entirely neutral in intent and still crush you by count alone.
- **barrage** — **Barrage** adds a shooter and a target. It is aimed, continuous, and timed to deny you a gap — the receiver is pinned down and cannot answer back. Choose it when the source is a person or press corps deliberately firing *questions, criticism, abuse* at someone specific.
- **assail** — **Assail** is the verb of repeated blows, and uniquely it works from the inside: *assailed by doubts, by nausea, by guilt*. Where a barrage needs an external gunner, **assail** lets your own mind be the mob. It is also the most formal-combative — a newspaper verb (*critics assailed the ruling*) — and gives you **unassailable**.
- **surfeit** — **Surfeit** is the odd one out: no attack, no victim, just an amount that has passed the point of pleasure into queasiness. It is chiefly a noun for the excess itself, and it implies the recipient is sated and slightly sickened — the tenth pastry, not the tenth punch. If nothing hostile is happening and the excess merely cloys, this is the word.

> **On the exam:** Watch the direction of the excess: outside-in and unaimed → *inundate*; outside-in and aimed → *barrage*; inside-out (doubts, memories) → *assail*; no aggression at all, just too much to stomach → *surfeit*.


<a id="meaning__sweet-past-bearing"></a>
### Sweet past bearing

All three describe tender feeling supplied in larger doses than the occasion can absorb — sweetness, nostalgia, pity, affection — and the reader's queasy recoil from it. The shared image is sugar: pleasant in small amounts, nauseating past a point. What separates them is where the excess sits (in the person feeling, in the work manufacturing the feeling, or in the substance itself) and whether the label leaves any room for affection.

- **sentimental** — The only one of the three that can be said kindly — and the only one that names a *disposition*, being governed by tender feeling rather than by judgment. A **sentimental** man keeps the chipped teacup; a **sentimental** novel is being scolded. Neutral until context turns it, and it covers only the soft backward-looking emotions: nobody is sentimental with rage.
- **mawkish** — The critic's verdict, and always hostile. **Mawkish** charges the emotion with being *manufactured* — a eulogy, a ballad, a death scene engineered to extract tears it hasn't earned. It attaches to made things and to the maker's bad faith, and it advertises the speaker's own cool refusal to be moved.
- **cloying** — The only one that works on literal sweetness — icing, liqueur, gardenia perfume in a small lift — as readily as on feeling. **Cloying** locates the fault in the substance and in the *duration*: it was fine, then it kept going and left an aftertaste. Says nothing about sincerity; a perfectly sincere love song can cloy.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable insults: **sentimental** alone can be warm, **cloying** alone can describe a dessert or a scent, and only **mawkish** carries the charge of faked, calculated emotion.


<a id="meaning__take-the-place-of"></a>
### Take the Place Of: supplant, supersede, eclipse

All three describe something new arriving where something older stood. The difference is what actually happens to the old thing: it can be pushed out of its position, stripped of its validity, or left standing but no longer looked at. One is about possession, one is about authority, one is about attention. Choosing among them means asking what the sentence says the predecessor lost.

- **supplant** — The only one of the three with a **loser**: the old thing held the spot and was dispossessed, usually by a rival with something to gain. **Supplant** implies pressure or maneuvering — a courtier, a cheaper technology, an ambitious protégé — where the others imply none.
- **supersede** — Bureaucratic, not competitive: **supersede** cancels the old thing's *standing*, so it no longer counts even if nobody objected. It attaches to things that can be authoritative — editions, regulations, treaties, model numbers — and never to a person elbowed out of a job.
- **eclipse** — The predecessor keeps its position entirely; it just stops being noticed. **Eclipse** is a claim about renown and attention, not possession or validity, which is why it takes comparisons of brilliance — a record, a reputation, an older sibling — and usually appears passively, with a trace of pity for what's in the shade.

> **On the exam:** The sentence, not the verb, carries the giveaway: a rival or motive points to supplant, a rule/edition/version points to supersede, and a comparison of fame or brilliance points to eclipse.


<a id="meaning__talking-too-much"></a>
### Talking Too Much: Where the Complaint Lands

All four cover the same raw fact: a person producing far more speech than the occasion requires. What separates them is not the word count but the angle of attack — whether the speaker is admiring the ease of the flow, dryly noting the excess, or complaining about being trapped. Three are adjectives labelling the talker; one is a verb naming the drift itself. The exam almost never tests "does this mean talkative"; it tests which shade of judgement the sentence has already set up.

- **garrulous** — The only one that is unambiguously a complaint, and the complaint is specifically about **triviality plus digression** — not just too much, but too much about nothing. Choose it when the sentence supplies a captive, suffering listener, or the classic subject (the old man, the seatmate, the barber).
- **loquacious** — Names quantity while withholding the verdict — the diction is arch enough to signal the speaker is being polite about it. Reach for **loquacious** when the sentence is amused or ironic rather than annoyed (*a loquacious witness*, *loquacious after two glasses*); the excess is noted, not indicted.
- **voluble** — Measures **ease, not quantity** — the words arrive fluently, rapidly, with no groping or stalling. It is the only one of the four that can be straight praise (*a voluble advocate*), and the only one that fits a short, fast, perfectly on-point outpouring.
- **ramble** — The verb for the *structural* failure: drifting off point, burying the thesis. It says nothing about volume or fluency, and it is never an accusation of error — a **rambling** answer is tiring, not wrong. Note the benign walking sense (a Sunday **ramble**), which the other three have no equivalent of.

> **On the exam:** Sentence Equivalence loves pairing these as near-synonyms, then hinging the answer on a single clue word: "effortlessly"/"never hesitated" forces **voluble**, "tedious"/"about nothing at all" forces **garrulous**, "wandered from"/"never reached the point" forces **rambling** — and **loquacious** is the safe filler that only works when the sentence stays neutral.


<a id="meaning__small-persistent-annoyance"></a>
### The Drip, Not the Fire: Small Persistent Annoyance

All four sit at the low end of the anger scale: irritation that comes from repetition and pettiness rather than from any single outrage. Nothing here is a fire — it's a drip, and the sufferer's characteristic gesture is a sigh, not a shout. The real dividing lines are grammatical and directional: some name the *thing* that grates, one names the *feeling*, one describes the *person* the grating has worn down. Register splits too, from plain complaint to the vocabulary of judges and editorialists.

- **irksome** — **Irksome** describes the annoying thing, and the annoyance is *tedium* — a pointless step, a duty you must repeat, a chore with no interest in it. It is the mildest and most trivial word here: an irksome task is boring and wearing, not hard. Its faint bookishness signals a speaker registering complaint while making clear they're too civilised to make a scene.
- **nettlesome** — **Nettlesome** also describes the thing, but the thing is a *problem that resists solution* — it stings, it keeps coming back, it won't be settled cleanly. Where irksome means dull, nettlesome means thorny and genuinely difficult, which is why it attaches to questions, issues, and details rather than to chores. This is the register of the editorial page and the bench.
- **vexation** — **Vexation** is the only noun, and the only word that names the *emotion itself* (or, by extension, its source). It adds helplessness: the teeth-grinding of someone stuck with an obstacle they have no power to remove. You can feel vexation; you cannot feel irksome. Legal usage keeps a sharper edge alive in *vexatious litigation* — suits filed to harass.
- **exasperated** — **Exasperated** points at the *person*, not the irritant, and marks the endpoint: patience already spent. It requires a history — the fifth explanation, the third failed attempt — so it cannot describe a first offense the way the others can describe a first chore. Powerless and deflated, it collocates with *sigh*, *groan*, *eye-roll*, never with a raised fist.

> **On the exam:** The exam swaps these across grammatical roles — a blank describing a worn-out *person* takes exasperated, a blank describing the *task* takes irksome, the *feeling* takes vexation — and separates irksome from nettlesome by whether the annoyance is merely tedious or actually unsolvable.


<a id="meaning__the-high-point"></a>
### The high point

All three mark the top of something's rise — the moment or stretch when a career, empire, athlete, or reputation is running at maximum. The confusion is that each borrows its picture from somewhere different: an orbit, the sky, and a lifespan. That picture decides what the word can attach to, how grand it sounds, and whether it hints that the fall has already started.

- **apogee** — The geometry word: **apogee** is the far end of an *arc*, so it drags the whole trajectory in with it — the climb before, the descent after. It is the coolest and most analytical of the three, at home describing a style, a movement, or a genre rather than a person's glory.
- **zenith** — The flattering one: **zenith** looks straight up, and its subject is power, fame, or fortune — someone is *at the zenith of his influence*, never at the zenith of a design trend. Where apogee is neutral geometry, zenith is grandeur, which is exactly why writers deploy it right before narrating the collapse.
- **prime** — Not a point but a *span*, and a bodily one — **prime** is the years of full vigor (*past his prime*), so it fits athletes, wine, and timber, not empires. It is also plain English rather than formal, and its GRE-relevant sense is the unrelated verb: to prepare in advance, as in priming a pump or a witness.

> **On the exam:** Two traps: **apogee** and **zenith** are close enough to be the matched pair in Sentence Equivalence (pick both), while **prime** is rarely tested as a high point at all — it shows up as the verb meaning *to prep beforehand*.


<a id="meaning__the-model-others-copy"></a>
### The model others copy

All four name the thing other things get referred back to — the case that sets the terms of comparison. They split on *what kind* of standard is meant: a moral summit worth admiring, a first template that later versions repeat, the defining specimen of a category, or a bare measuring line. Two of them praise, two of them merely classify, and the ones that classify work perfectly well on failures, frauds, and disasters.

- **paragon** — The only one that is pure praise, and it attaches to a **virtue**, not a category — *a paragon of patience/integrity/restraint*. Because the compliment is absolute, it is the only member of the group that can be turned into a weapon by sarcasm.
- **archetype** — Claims **priority and depth**: the original template that later versions keep re-enacting (the Hero, the Trickster). Says the thing reached the bottom of the pattern rather than merely scoring high on it — which is why it dignifies without praising a specific quality.
- **paradigmatic** — The **classifier's** word, and an adjective, not a noun — it says *this is the standard instance of the type* and stops there. Where **archetype** implies the type came from this case, **paradigmatic** only says this case displays it most cleanly; a paradigmatic bureaucratic failure is still a failure.
- **benchmark** — Cold, quantitative, and possibly **mediocre** — it's a line you measure against, not an ideal you look up to, and things routinely beat it. Alone in the group it demands **comparability** (same test, same way, on everything) and alone it works as a verb: *benchmark it against last year's*.

> **On the exam:** The trap is assuming all four commend: **paradigmatic** and **benchmark** sit comfortably in sentences about failures, scandals, and low bars, while **paragon** cannot — check whether the blank praises or merely categorizes.


<a id="meaning__a-crafted-general-truth"></a>
### The One-Line Truth: Earned, Issued, or Counterfeit

All four name the same object: a short, freestanding sentence that asserts a general truth about life and is offered as wisdom. Form doesn't separate them — length, shape and subject matter can be identical. What separates them is the verdict baked into the label: whether the compression earned something, whether the speaker's standing is doing the work, or whether the line is counterfeit depth. Choosing the word is passing judgment on the saying, not describing it.

- **aphorism** — The compliment of the group: it credits **craft** — balance, economy, a twist of wit that makes the line worth remembering. It states what *is*, not what to do, and needs no famous speaker; the sentence itself does the earning.
- **dictum** — **Borrowed authority**, not wit. A dictum weighs because of who issued it — a judge, a critic, a founder — so it can be flat and unquotable and still qualify. It also carries an official, ex cathedra tint (cf. legal *obiter dicta*) that the others lack entirely.
- **platitude** — A pure accusation, and the charge is **counterfeit profundity**: a moralizing line that wears the face of insight and asks you to nod. It indicts the speaker for having nothing to say — the standard verdict on condolence speeches and mission statements.
- **bromide** — A platitude with a **sedative purpose** — trotted out to soothe grief or close down a hard question so nobody has to think. It accuses the speaker of *dodging*, not merely of being unoriginal, and uniquely can name the person as well as the remark: a bromide is also a crashing bore.

> **On the exam:** The GRE plays the polarity: a blank flanked by "merely," "hardly," or a concessive "though widely quoted" wants platitude/bromide, while praise words ("polished," "trenchant") want aphorism — and in Sentence Equivalence, platitude/bromide is the near-certain synonym pair, with dictum planted as a trap because it fits the definition but carries no contempt.


<a id="meaning__thrown-off-composure"></a>
### Thrown off composure

All four involve poise giving way — someone's balance, thread, or calm is disturbed by something outside them. They split along three axes: who occupies the subject slot (the disturbing thing, the person doing the disturbing, or the person disturbed), how visible the damage is, and how long it lasts. Two are momentary and social; one is a small defeat inflicted by an opponent; one is sustained churn that need not involve poise at all.

- **disconcerting** — Describes the **stimulus**, never the victim — a stare, a pause, a mismatched smile *is* disconcerting; a person is disconcert**ed**. The speaker stays fully articulate while saying it, which is the point: it's the cool, faintly clinical word chosen precisely to signal that no panic is involved, only wrong-footedness.
- **discomfit** — The only one that implies an **adversary**: someone does it to you, and what collapses is your argument, your poise under cross-examination, your plan. Its old sense of routing an army still colours it — being discomfited is a small defeat with a winner, not just a bad moment. Formal, bookish, and nearly always passive.
- **flustered** — The **visible symptom**, and the mildest and briefest: you go pink, lose your thread, start the sentence again. Uniquely, the cause can be pleasant — a compliment flusters you — so it carries no hostility and often a touch of affection, where discomfiting is something done at your expense.
- **agitate** — The outlier: it means sustained stirring, not a single moment of lost face, and it reaches beyond people to liquids and to politics. **Agitate** *for* or *against* something — campaign persistently — is the GRE's favourite sense and has nothing to do with anyone's composure.

> **On the exam:** The trap is usually **agitate**'s political sense ("agitate for reform"), planted where the sentence's emotional context baits you toward the "rattle someone" reading; secondarily, watch the direction of **disconcerting** vs **discomfit** — one names the cause, the other takes a human object.


<a id="meaning__to-the-point"></a>
### To the Point

Every word here says a thing fits the matter at hand — but they split into two jobs that the exam keeps confusing. The first job is **admissibility**: does this belong in the discussion at all? That's a gatekeeper's ruling, and it says nothing about whether the remark was any good. The second job is **craft**: granting that it belongs, how well was it chosen — for precision, for timing, for pleasure? A dull, clumsy remark can pass the first test; a dazzling one can fail it.

- **germane** — The structural test: does this actually attach to *this* question? **Germane** is nearly binary and nearly always contested — you meet it negated, in the mouth of whoever is trying to shut a line of argument down. It grants nothing about quality or importance; a germane point can be trivial and badly made, it just isn't out of order.
- **pertinent** — Adds worth to attachment. Where *germane* asks "does it connect," **pertinent** rules that it connects hard enough to deserve the room's time — a verdict from someone with standing to make it (chair, judge, examiner). "Not pertinent" is dismissal by weight; "not germane" is dismissal by scope.
- **apposite** — Drops admissibility entirely and praises **aim**. It attaches to things *said* — a quotation, an analogy, an example — and means the remark landed on the precise nerve of the matter, not merely near it. The bookish verdict of a critic; you cannot call a policy or a person apposite.
- **apropos** — Praises the **moment**, not the content. An apposite remark stays apposite whenever you make it; an **apropos** one owes its force to arriving exactly then. It is also the only member with a prepositional life — *apropos of your last point* — and it keeps an urbane French air that reads as cultivated aloud, mannered on the page.
- **apt** — The plain-clothes member: neutral register, no ceremony, and the only one carrying senses that have nothing to do with relevance — *apt to overreact* (inclined), *an apt pupil* (quick to learn).
