Even in its fit sense it merely certifies accuracy; it neither delights like *felicitous* nor claims the surgical strike of *apposite*.
- **felicitous** — Fit **plus pleasure** — the listener feels a small click of rightness, which none of the others promises. Reserved for phrasing, titles, metaphors, and timing, and it is the only one whose negative is in live circulation: *infelicitous* is how a reviewer calls a line clumsy without saying so.

> **On the exam:** Two traps: **apt** usually appears in its *tendency* sense (a near-synonym of *prone*, minus the disapproval), and blanks demanding relevance-as-admissibility (germane, pertinent) will offer craft words (apposite, felicitous) that praise the wrong thing.


<a id="meaning__too-many-words-on-the-page"></a>
### Too many words on the page

All of these describe words outrunning their content: text or talk that occupies more space than the point inside it justifies. The complaint is never that the ideas are wrong — it's that they arrive padded, stretched, or spread so thin that nothing lands. Three are verdicts on the finished prose; one is the act of producing it. And one of them isn't really about length at all, which is where the group turns slippery.

- **verbose** — The plain, everyday count-the-words charge, and the only one here with a neutral technical use (**verbose** mode in software, where you asked for the extra output). It's the workaday editor's markup on a bloated contract or slide deck — it says "cut this," not "I suffered."
- **prolix** — Adds *tedium* to sheer length — the reader's endurance is now part of the complaint, not just the word count. It's markedly bookish where **verbose** is ordinary, and it never softens: no neutral sense, no technical use, always a critic looking down at four pages that should have been one.
- **diffuse** — The odd one out: it indicts **structure, not volume**. A short paragraph can be diffuse if its material pools everywhere and concentrates nowhere; its opposites are *cogent* and *trenchant*, not *brief*. It also carries a whole non-critical life the others lack — heat, light, and power **diffuse** through a medium with no insult implied.
- **expatiate** — The only **verb**, and the only one describing the speaker's act rather than judging the finished text — you **expatiate** *on* or *upon* a subject. Its disapproval is the mildest and driest here: it concedes you genuinely had material, then raises an eyebrow at how much of it you delivered unasked.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating **diffuse** as a synonym for long-winded — GRE sentences use it for writing that is unfocused rather than lengthy, and reserve **prolix**/**verbose** for the antonym slot opposite *concise*, *succinct*, *pithy*, *laconic*.


<a id="meaning__too-nervous-to-act"></a>
### Too nervous to act

All four describe nerve failing — fear or self-doubt standing between a person and the action they could take. What separates them is *where the fear comes from and how the speaker judges it*: a settled trembling temperament, a low estimate of one's own worth, a duty abandoned to save one's skin, or a hair trigger that fires at nothing. Two of them describe a person's steady character, one describes a moment of reactivity, and one is less a description than a charge laid against someone. Get the source wrong and you get the word wrong.

- **timorous** — The fear is of *deciding* — of the moment where you'd have to commit. It's a chronic condition, not an episode, and the register is bookish enough that it works on abstractions: timorous prose, a timorous policy, a board that hedges every quarter. Faintly withering, but it accuses no one of anything worse than shrinking.
- **diffident** — The only one where the fear points inward: not at danger but at yourself. A diffident person may be perfectly brave — they simply won't press their own claim, speak first, or believe they've earned the room. And the speaker is usually on their side, implying the low self-estimate is mistaken.
- **craven** — Not a temperament but a verdict. It requires a duty that was owed and dropped — a capitulation, a silence, a surrender — and it says the motive was self-preservation. Nobody applies it to themselves; it's an accusation, at home in an editorial, and it condemns the choice rather than describing a feeling.
- **skittish** — Reactivity, not character: fine one second, bolting the next, over a plastic bag. It carries the built-in judgment that the reaction outran the threat, so it quietly calls the subject *unreasonable* rather than weak — which is why it attaches so easily to horses, investors, and markets. Always a little belittling; never tragic.

> **On the exam:** The trap is over-reading: sentences that merely establish hesitancy will bait you toward **craven**, which requires a betrayed duty; and **diffident** is regularly confused with *indifferent*, which it has nothing to do with.


<a id="meaning__too-sacred-to-touch"></a>
### Too sacred to touch

All three sit at the point where something is set apart from ordinary handling. Two of them describe protection — a thing walled off from being touched, changed, or breached — and the third describes what that kind of thing *feels* like from the outside. The trap is that they split along different axes: status conferred vs. condition preserved vs. sensation inflicted, and sincere reverence vs. raised eyebrow.

- **sacrosanct** — The only one that points at the **defenders** rather than the thing. Someone has ruled a budget line, a meeting slot, a founder's vision beyond argument — and the writer usually thinks that's a bit much. Watch for the sardonic edge; it is the standard modern use, and neither of the others has it.
- **inviolate** — Describes the **achieved state**, not the rule: still whole, never breached. Where *sacrosanct* names a prohibition, **inviolate** reports that the prohibition held. Fully sincere — the speaker is glad — and ceremonial enough that it lives in treaties, constitutions, and elegies rather than in office talk.
- **numinous** — Nothing to do with being protected. This is the **shiver**: awe laced with dread, the sense that something vastly larger is present and possibly attentive. It's a sensation a place inflicts on you, not a status anyone grants it — so a shrine can be sacrosanct and feel like nothing at all.

> **On the exam:** The exam plants **numinous** among protection words so you match it on "sacred" alone — check whether the sentence describes a rule being enforced (sacrosanct/inviolate) or a feeling being experienced (numinous); and if the tone is dry or critical, the answer is sacrosanct, never inviolate.


<a id="meaning__trace-to-a-source"></a>
### Tracing something back to its source

All three connect a thing to where it came from — a cause, an author, an origin. The split is who is doing the connecting. Two of them are acts of judgement performed by a person who names the source and could be wrong; the third is a statement about the world in which the effect itself does the pointing and no claimant appears at all. Watch the syntax, because it encodes exactly that difference.

- **ascribe** — The bookish one, and the one that most readily takes **qualities and motives** rather than just causes — you ascribe cunning, malice, or divine mercy to someone, which is a hair's breadth from *impute*. It flags the claim as inference on evidence (style, precedent, reasoning), so it lives in scholarship, criticism, and law where the assignment is arguable by design.
- **attribute** — The plain, everyday member of the trio — the default verb for **causes and authorship** (*attributed the delay to weather*, *attributed to Caravaggio*) where **ascribe** would sound self-consciously literary. It is also the only one with a noun life: an *attribute* is an essential quality of a thing, not an assignment made about it.
- **stem from** — No one assigns anything — the **effect is the subject** and the origin is the object (*the dispute stems from a misunderstanding*), so the sentence has no claimant to be wrong. It attaches to abstractions only, never to authorship or physical objects, and it drifts toward diagnosing trouble: failures stem from things far more often than triumphs do.

> **On the exam:** The trap is direction and subject: sentence completions supply a cause-first frame (*X resulted in Y*) or put the effect in subject position, which kills **ascribe**/**attribute** and leaves only **stem from** — and vice versa when a named person is doing the assigning.


<a id="meaning__treat-as-unimportant"></a>
### Treat as unimportant

All five reduce something's standing without ever refuting it — no argument is made, no case is answered; the value is simply lowered by treatment. The reduction can land on three different kinds of target, and that is the real fault line: a claim's evidential weight, an object's overall merit, or a person's dignity. Notice too that some require an agent doing it deliberately while others describe a flaw quietly doing it on its own, and that they range from a defensible analytical move to open contempt.

- **belittle** — **Belittle** always has a human victim and a live relationship — boss, parent, rival — and works by narrating someone's achievement as smaller than it is ("she got lucky"). It's the sustained one: repeated, conversational, usually polite, and the harm accumulates rather than lands in a single blow.
- **detract** — **Detract** is the one with no villain — a cracked frame, a weak third act, a shrill ending does the detracting; nobody has to intend anything. It also takes a *thing's* merit rather than a person's dignity, and it is grammatically marked: always *detract from*, never detract something.
- **discount** — **Discount** is epistemic, not social — it operates on claims, testimony, rumours, and data, adjusting how much *weight* they get, not how good they are. Alone in this group it can be entirely correct behaviour (a historian discounts a partisan chronicle), which is why the GRE uses it in neutral academic contexts; the only shadow on it is haste — "he discounted her warning" rarely ends well.
- **slight** — **Slight** is an act, singular and datable — the omitted name, the unshaken hand, the greeting that skipped one person. It's the offence of *omission* rather than statement: nothing was said at all, and that's the wound. It's also the only one that nominalizes into the injury itself (*he never forgot the slight*), which quietly indicts the person still counting.
- **deride** — **Deride** is the loud, public end of the range and the only one that uses *laughter* as the instrument. It's formal and one-sided — the derider has already closed the question and is performing contempt for an audience, so it attaches to proposals, theories, and films in reviews and columns. Where the others lower an estimate, this one declares the thing unworthy of estimating.

> **On the exam:** Sentence completions hinge on the target: evidence gets discounted, a work's merit is detracted from (with obligatory *from*), a person is belittled or slighted — and none of these means *refute*, so a blank following contrary proof usually wants a stronger word.


<a id="meaning__ease-pain-or-severity"></a>
### Turning it down, not off: alleviate, assuage, mitigate, ameliorate, temper

All five reduce intensity without removing the thing. Every one of them is honest about being partial: the pain, the risk, the harm, the fervor is still there, just dialed down. What separates them is not strength but **what they take as an object** — a felt suffering, an emotion, a harm or risk, a whole situation, or a force running too hot — and how warm or institutional the speaker sounds. Choose by object type, not by degree.

- **alleviate** — The object is **suffering as it is felt** — pain, hunger, grief, a burden, boredom. It is the warm, humane one: someone is worse off and you make their experience lighter, while the cause goes untouched.
- **assuage** — Narrower than **alleviate**: the object is an *emotion*, and usually someone else's — you assuage fears, guilt, doubts, anger. The move is consoling and rhetorical, a speaker calming a mind rather than changing any facts; assuaged guilt is quieter guilt, still intact.
- **mitigate** — Cool and institutional, and the object is a **harm, risk, penalty, or damage** — never a feeling. Typically preemptive engineering rather than comfort: the seawall, the hedge, the emissions cut. In law, mitigating circumstances make the offence *look less bad*, not excused.
- **ameliorate** — The object is a **whole condition or state of affairs** — working conditions, overcrowding, depleted soil — not a sensation or a risk. It alone points *upward* toward better rather than downward from bad, and it presupposes the thing was already in poor shape.
- **temper** — The odd one out: what it moderates need not be bad at all — justice, zeal, ambition, optimism. Nothing is subtracted; a **counterweight is added** until the thing sits in proportion. Its objects run hot rather than hurt.

> **On the exam:** The GRE decides these by object, so let the noun pick the verb: fears→**assuage**, risk/damages→**mitigate**, conditions→**ameliorate**, pain→**alleviate**, enthusiasm→**temper** — and remember **temper** is the only one whose object can be something good.


<a id="meaning__twisted-past-following"></a>
### Twisted Past Following

All of these describe intricacy that has crossed the line into unfollowability — and all of them are complaints, not compliments. Each carries a hint that the tangle is not innocent: someone made it this way, and the confusion may be doing work for them. They split on *what* is tangled (a sentence, an institution, a route) and on whether the word names the resulting mess or the act of creating it.

- **convoluted** — The general-purpose charge, and the one that scales down: a single sentence, one clause, one excuse can be **convoluted**. The image is a knot folded back on itself — not a long journey, not an institution, just needless twisting the maker could have avoided.
- **byzantine** — Needs an institution to attach to — a tax code, a permit process, a royal court, a company's politics. **Byzantine** adds what the others lack: factions and insiders. The intricacy isn't merely excessive, it's a moat, and someone on the inside is navigating it comfortably while you can't.
- **tortuous** — The only one with a live literal sense — roads, coastlines, rivers are **tortuous**. The complaint is about the *route*: it arrives, eventually, having detoured through everywhere. Convoluted reasoning is knotted; tortuous reasoning is merely serpentine and far too long.
- **obfuscate** — The verb, and the only word that puts a person in the sentence with intent. The others describe the wreckage; **obfuscate** names the deliberate act of producing it — by piling jargon, caveats and footnotes *on top of* a fact rather than concealing it. Nothing obfuscates by accident.

> **On the exam:** Watch two traps: *tortuous* (winding) vs *torturous* (agonizing) are different words, and in sentence equivalence only **obfuscate** fits a slot needing an action with an agent — the other three describe a state.


<a id="meaning__underhanded-trickery"></a>
### Underhanded trickery

All four cover getting an advantage by deceiving someone rather than overpowering them — the win comes from misdirection, concealment or clever manoeuvring. They split on three axes: **scale** (a whole practice of cheating vs. one move), **legitimacy** (flatly dishonest vs. fair play), and **register** (indictment vs. newspaper column). Two of them name a kind of dishonesty; two name a single tactic, only one of which is even wrong.

- **chicanery** — The only one where the **rules themselves are the weapon** — loopholes, quibbles, fine print, procedural sleight-of-hand. **Chicanery** stays technically legal, which is the whole point of the contempt; it's the professional's word (lawyers, accountants, election officials) for someone who won disgracefully but can't be charged.
- **skullduggery** — Not technically legal at all — **skullduggery** is plainly shady, done out of sight: backroom deals, quiet double-crosses, a rigged committee. What marks it is tone, not method: it's informal and half-amused where *fraud* is prosecutorial, and it's the word for wrongdoing you suspect but cannot prove.
- **ploy** — A unit, not a practice — **one small move** with a hidden motive, not a pattern of dishonesty. It's the cheapest and most trivial of the group (a marketing ploy, a ploy to keep you on the call), and calling something a ploy already announces you've seen through it.
- **feint** — The only honest one. A **feint** is deception the opponent is *meant to notice* — it fails if nobody takes the bait — so boxers, fencers and generals do it inside the rules and nobody calls it cheating. It's also the most physical: a committed-looking movement in the wrong direction so the real strike lands.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating all four as pejorative — sentences about sport, negotiation or war want the sanctioned *feint*, while a sentence whose deception is legal-but-slimy wants *chicanery*, not *skullduggery*.


<a id="meaning__understood-without-being-said"></a>
### Understood without being said

All four cover meaning that travels without being stated outright — the content arrives, but nobody puts it on the record. The split runs two ways. Two are adjectives describing a *state* of shared-but-unspoken understanding; two are verbs describing an *act* of gesturing at something you decline to name. Within each pair, the difference is whether the unspoken thing lives in the logic of what was said or in the silence between two parties, and whether the indirection is about delicacy or about avoiding a name.

- **tacit** — **Tacit** requires two parties and a silence that functions as consent — you said nothing, and that counted as yes. Because it makes the silent party complicit, it attaches to things people want deniability about: tacit approval, a tacit admission, a tacit understanding between rivals.
- **implicit** — **Implicit** needs no audience and no silence — the meaning is logically contained in what was said, and a hostile reader can extract it. It is the word for the premise an argument depends on but never defends. Its second sense flips register entirely: *implicit* trust or obedience is **total**, not unspoken.
- **intimate** — **Intimate** (verb) is the delicate, deliberate hint dropped by someone in a position to say more — the chairman intimated he might step down. Unlike *insinuate* it isn't malicious, and unlike *hint* it isn't casual; it is genteel groundwork laid so the speaker can later deny having said it.
- **allude** — **Allude** is specifically about *not naming* a known referent: the thing exists, both parties can identify it, you gesture at it instead — "recent difficulties," "a certain bestseller." It's the verb of literary reference as much as tact, and it's the only one here that is intransitive: you allude **to** something.

> **On the exam:** The trap is *implicit* meaning **absolute** (implicit faith, implicit obedience) where the sentence rewards "unquestioning," not "unstated"; secondarily, *allude* is wrong wherever the thing is actually named, and *intimate* is wrong wherever the hint is sly or hostile.


<a id="meaning__uneasy-about-what-s-coming"></a>
### Uneasy about what's coming

All four sit *before* the event — the unease of something bad that hasn't arrived yet, not the shock of something that has. They split on what the dread attaches to: a named upcoming event, an ominous sign, a person's permanent character, or your own conscience about an act you're about to commit. Three are feelings; one is what a sign *does*.

- **apprehension** — The neutral-register noun for the feeling, and the only one that needs a specific coming event to attach to — the verdict, the biopsy, the merger. Civil enough to say in a board meeting, and unlike **timorous** it implies nothing about your character: you still show up.
- **forebode** — The only member that can take a non-human subject — a silence, a red sky, a dropped omen *forebodes*, doing the signaling rather than feeling it. When a person forebodes, the dread is objectless premonition, not **apprehension**'s knot about a scheduled event.
- **timorous** — Not a feeling but a verdict on a person: a settled, bookish put-down for someone whose fear has hardened into inability to act. **Apprehension** describes your Tuesday; **timorous** describes your whole disposition, and the speaker is looking down at you when they say it.
- **qualm** — The dread is moral and aimed at your *own* conduct — a flicker of conscience about whether you should do this, not fear of what will happen to you. Smallest of the four, and usually met negated: "no qualms about" firing them.

> **On the exam:** The trap is **apprehension** meaning *arrest* or *comprehension*, and **forebode** being irreversibly bad where *portend* and *presage* are neutral.


<a id="meaning__unexcitable-by-nature"></a>
### Unexcitable by nature

All four describe a person who doesn't visibly react — no flinching, no fuss, no outburst. The distinctions live in *why* the reaction is missing and *who is judging*. In three of them the feeling itself is faint or absent (a matter of constitution or surface); in one the feeling is fully present and deliberately held down. The words also split on approval: some are neutral description, some quiet praise, one is a slur wearing a lab coat.

- **placid** — The most neutral and the most *visual* — it describes a surface nothing ruffles, so it works on lakes and afternoons as readily as on people. It makes no claim about inner life at all, which is exactly why it can slide into faint insult: unruffled shades into incurious, and it is the standard adjective for cows.
- **phlegmatic** — Diagnoses the person's underlying constitution — the alarm never rings because the wiring is slow, not because the surface is smooth. It's the only one of the four rooted in old humoral medicine, so it reads as a claim about someone's fixed type rather than their mood or moment. Praise or complaint depends entirely on whether the crisis deserved a response.
- **stolid** — The one that is openly unflattering: it implies nothing is going on behind the face. Where **placid** leaves inner life unaddressed, **stolid** asserts there isn't much — heavy, dull-blooded, thick. It attaches to faces, expressions, and (in older novels) whole classes of people, and no one calls themselves it.
- **stoic** — The outlier — the feeling is fully present and being held. It requires something to endure (pain, loss, hardship), so it can't describe a lake, a temperament in the abstract, or a pleasant afternoon. It credits the person with self-command rather than describing their thermostat, which is why it's the only reliably admiring word in the group.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable synonyms for \"calm\": look at what the sentence supplies — if there's a hardship being borne, it's **stoic**; if the blank is a criticism of dullness, it's **stolid**; if it's scenery or a surface, only **placid** fits.


<a id="meaning__unimpeachable-honesty"></a>
### Unimpeachable honesty

All three certify that someone or something can be trusted, but they certify different objects. One vouches for a person's incorruptibility in a position of trust; one vouches for whether a statement is actually true; one vouches for the care a conscience takes while doing a job. Confusion comes from the shared halo of "honest" — the work is remembering that a claim can have truth, a person can have character, and an action can have care, and these words don't swap.

- **probity** — **Probity** attaches to a person holding something that isn't theirs — funds, an office, a public trust — and it is the verdict of an institution, not a friend. It is retrospective and ceremonial: you get praised for probity in an obituary or cleared of doubt by an audit, never complimented on it over dinner.
- **veracity** — **Veracity** is the only one that attaches to a *statement* — a document, a testimony, an account can have it, and a person has it only as the reliability behind their claims. It appears mostly under attack (*questioned, disputed, doubts about*), so it signals an investigation in progress rather than a settled tribute.
- **scrupulous** — **Scrupulous** is the only adjective, and it describes conduct in the moment rather than reputation after the fact: refusing the shortcut nobody would have caught. It alone extends to sheer exactness — *scrupulous notes*, *scrupulous attention* — where the honesty becomes care owed to the task.

> **On the exam:** The trap is swapping the object: sentence-completion stems put **veracity** where money and office demand **probity**, and lean on *unscrupulous* in a purely procedural context to make you read the moral sense as mere sloppiness.


<a id="meaning__easily-taken-in"></a>
### Unseasoned and Easily Taken In

All four describe a missing layer of worldly armor — the guard that makes an experienced person pause before believing, or before speaking with confidence about what they haven't lived. The judgment is almost always delivered from outside and from above: someone more seasoned is doing the labeling. They split on two axes — whether the failure is a **standing trait** or a **single episode**, and whether an actual deceiver had to be involved at all.

- **gullible** — The permanent condition, stated bluntly and without mercy: not that someone was fooled but that they are always available to be fooled again. It is the only one of the four that offers the person no excuse — no youth, no inexperience, just a defective filter.
- **naive** — The only one that can be said fondly. It indicts judgment while clearing motive — unspoiled rather than dishonest — so the same word swings from "sweetly naive" to "don't be naive" depending on the speaker's tone. It also alone has a fully neutral technical use (naive subjects, naive art) with no fault implied.
- **dupe** — The only member that is an event, not a character trait, and the only one that requires a deceiver: someone must have actually done the tricking. As a noun it converts that one episode into a label — the mark, the sucker — which is why "I was duped" concedes something about yourself while it complains about someone else.
- **callow** — Not about belief at all — nothing needs to have been swallowed and no con artist need exist. It faults unripeness of character, typically in someone holding forth on experiences he hasn't had, and it is the formal, condescending one, welded to its noun in **a callow youth**.

> **On the exam:** The trap is **callow**, which the exam slots into "easily fooled" contexts where it doesn't belong — it needs an unformed, untested person, not a deceived one; watch also for **naive**'s neutral technical sense (naive subjects, naive art) in science passages.


<a id="meaning__unspoiled-and-pure"></a>
### Unspoiled and pure

All four say a thing is free of some contaminant — nothing has diluted it, dirtied it, worn it, or breached it. The whole group is positive, and each word is a compliment about an absence. What separates them is *what kind of contamination is missing*: an admixture, a history of use, a mark or error, or a violation of something protected. Get the contaminant right and the words stop overlapping.

- **unalloyed** — The contaminant is **dilution** — a lesser element stirred in. Alone in this group it attaches to **abstractions, and almost only pleasant ones**: unalloyed joy, unalloyed admiration, an unalloyed success. You cannot have unalloyed dirt or an unalloyed vow. Watch for it negated — *"not an unalloyed good"* is a polite way of announcing the catch.
- **pristine** — The contaminant is **history**. It says nothing has ever happened to the thing — unused, unwalked-on, still in the box — so it belongs to wilderness, snowfall, coastlines, and second-hand goods whose value is precisely that no one got there first. Unlike **immaculate**, no effort is implied; unlike **inviolate**, nothing was forbidden, it just never came up.
- **immaculate** — The contaminant is **a mark**: a spot, a stain, an error. It describes a state someone *achieved and maintains*, so it fits kitchens, uniforms, restorations, records, and timing — and one crumb cancels it. That's the crisp split from **pristine**: a scrubbed jacket is immaculate, a jacket never worn is pristine.
- **inviolate** — The contaminant is **breach** — and the thing was under protection. It attaches to vows, sanctuaries, borders, rights, secrets: whole because touching them was *forbidden*, not merely because no one bothered. It's the only word here with reverence and the only one that implies a prohibition; high-register, at home in constitutions and treaties rather than speech.

> **On the exam:** The trap is swapping **pristine** and **immaculate** (never used vs. carefully cleaned) and pairing **unalloyed** with a concrete noun or an unpleasant one — it only takes positive abstractions, and the sentence usually negates it to hint at a flaw.


<a id="meaning__very-small"></a>
### Very small — size vs. shortfall

All four say "small," but they split on *what kind of small*. Two measure physical size — how little space a thing occupies, whether under a magnifier or standing next to you. The other two measure an amount against a benchmark: there is some, it just falls short of what the job, the promise, or common decency required. Confusion comes from the fact that all four can precede a quantity noun, but only the second pair carries a verdict.

- **minute** — **Minute** is smallness at the threshold of detection — cracks, traces, discrepancies, things you need equipment or strain to see. It's the only one that flips into a second sense about *attention* ("a minute inspection" = missed nothing), and the only one that would be silly applied to a person's build.
- **diminutive** — **Diminutive** is smallness of **stature**, and it gravitates to bodies — a diminutive boxer, a diminutive aunt. Unlike *minute*, the thing is perfectly visible; the point is that it's smaller than you'd expect, which lets the word tip either fond or faintly patronising depending on the speaker.
- **scant** — **Scant** is the first word here that judges: some exists, but not enough to meet the standard. It sits glued to abstract nouns — scant evidence, scant regard, scant attention — and the reproach lands on whoever supplied too little, not on the world's supply.
- **paltry** — **Paltry** is *scant* with a sneer added. It attaches to sums, wages, offers, turnout — things a giver chose — and says the giver should be ashamed. Where *scant* notes a shortfall, **paltry** calls it insulting; where *diminutive* can be affectionate, **paltry** never is.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable size words: sentence-completion items hinge on whether the blank needs neutral physical smallness (minute/diminutive) or a shortfall with blame attached (scant/paltry), and on whether the surrounding clause supplies the contempt that paltry already contains.


<a id="meaning__voluntarily-let-go"></a>
### Voluntarily let go

Every word here describes a letting-go that is chosen rather than suffered — no theft, no accident, no defeat. What separates them is the shape of the release: whether the thing was ever in your hands, whether anyone receives it, what pressure forced the decision, and whether the act reflects badly on you. Two are cool and procedural, one is judgmental, one happens under duress.

- **relinquish** — The only one that is a **handover**: the thing had a rightful holder and now passes to someone else — the crown, the wheel, the deed, the claim. Formal and transactional, it presumes your title was legitimate; nothing about the act is blameworthy, only reluctant.
- **forgo** — The only one where the thing was **never yours to begin with** — you decline the take rather than release a hold. Forward-looking and undramatic: the dessert, the bonus, the raise you didn't ask for. It costs you an option, not a possession, and it makes you sound sensible rather than wounded.
- **forsake** — The only one that **passes judgment on you**. It needs a bond — a person, a faith, a promise — and the thing left behind is capable of feeling the loss. Literary and reproachful where the others are procedural; the tone turns noble only when what you forsake is a vice.
- **jettison** — The only one done **under load**, to survive: you dump the plan, the policy, the running mate because the vehicle won't stay up carrying it. Nobody receives what you drop — it's destroyed, not transferred — and the point is that you're still moving afterwards.

> **On the exam:** Watch the sentence's pressure cue: a rightful claim handed over → relinquish; something merely available → forgo; survival or lightening the load → jettison; loyalty language (vows, faith, those who trusted you) → forsake.


<a id="meaning__wasteful-with-money"></a>
### Wasteful with money — and the flavour of the blame

All of these hover around spending or using up more than you should, and all of them (in their money sense) disapprove. What separates them is *what the disapproval is aimed at*: the proportion of a single act, the habit of a person, the moral character behind it, or the loss of the thing itself. They also differ in scale — a household eyebrow-raise versus a national treasury — and in grammar, since one is the verb the others describe.

- **prodigal** — The image is *pouring out until the vessel is empty* — money gone, not merely misspent. It's also the only word here with a genuinely complimentary use (**prodigal of praise**, prodigal of detail = lavishly generous), and the only one carrying a famous false friend: it never means "returning" or "repentant."
- **profligate** — The institutional word — it scales up to treasuries, budgets, and policy in a way *spendthrift* never does, and it's the standard partisan accusation (**profligate spending**). Alone in this group it also indicts character directly: a profligate man may be dissolute rather than broke.
- **spendthrift** — The only one that names a **person as a type** — a settled habit, not one bad night. Its natural subject is someone draining a finite, unreplenishable pot (an heir, a lottery winner), and its tone is the mildest here: exasperated head-shaking, not moral condemnation.
- **squander** — The verb of the group, and the only member whose object is routinely **not money** — a lead, a chance, a talent, a decade. It stresses the loss rather than the spending: what's gone was valuable and is not coming back, and a single careless act is enough.
- **extravagant** — Judges **proportion, not depletion** — the thing overshot its occasion, so a rich man can be extravagant forever without wasting anything. It's the only one that can be affectionate or admiring, and the only one that readily leaves money behind entirely: extravagant claims, extravagant praise, extravagant theories.

> **On the exam:** The GRE mostly tests the non-money uses: **extravagant** attached to claims or praise, and the fake "returning home" sense of **prodigal**.


<a id="meaning__weak-and-liable-to-break"></a>
### Weak and liable to break

All four sit on the idea of insufficient strength — something that cannot hold, cannot function, or cannot bear the weight put on it. What separates them is what the weakness attaches to (a body, a character, a link, a capacity), whether the word names the weak thing or the force that weakened it, and above all the speaker's stance: pity, forgiveness, polite doubt, or clinical fact. Choosing wrongly here doesn't produce a slightly-off sentence; it produces the wrong attitude toward the person described.

- **feeble** — The only one that can sneer. **Feeble** is aimed at an *attempt* — an excuse, a joke, a protest — and the verdict is that the effort was made and it was pathetic. Aimed at a body it softens to pity, but it never goes neutral the way *debilitating* does.
- **frailty** — A noun, so it names the condition rather than describing a thing, and it is the forgiving member of the group. **Frailty** treats the flaw as built into the material — hence "human frailty," and the plural **frailties**, the small vices we pardon. Alone here it reaches moral character without condemning it.
- **tenuous** — Attaches to *connections and reasoning*, never to a body: links, evidence, claims, a grasp on power. **Tenuous** says the thing rests on almost nothing and could snap — a thread, not a lie. It's the courteous academic register, which is why reviewers and judges prefer it to blunter *flimsy*.
- **debilitating** — The only one that points at the *cause*, not the sufferer: illness, pain, anxiety, sanctions are debilitating; the patient is not. It marks a threshold — capacity removed, usually for a stretch of time — rather than a degree of misery, and its tone is the flat clinical register of doctors and insurers.

> **On the exam:** The trap is direction and register: the blank wants **debilitating** when it names the agent that stripped capacity, **tenuous** when it modifies evidence or a link, and **feeble** only where the writer is passing scornful judgement on an effort — with **frailty** reserved for when the slot needs a noun and a forgiving tone.


<a id="meaning__weaken-from-underneath"></a>
### Weaken from underneath

All four describe damage done to the support of a thing rather than to its face. Nothing is confronted, knocked over, or destroyed outright: the structure is left standing while whatever held it up is quietly removed, so it fails from below or from within. What separates them is *how long it takes*, *whether anyone meant it*, and *what exactly is lost* — support, control, or validity.

- **undermine** — The slow one. **Undermine** is cumulative erosion over weeks or months — a drip of doubts, leaks, and small slights — and its great feature is deniability: the underminer stays pleasant to your face. It needs a target that rests on accumulated support: authority, trust, morale, a reputation.
- **undercut** — The instant one, and the only one here that is routinely accidental. **Undercut** is a single stroke that pulls the prop away — one exception kills the rule, one nervous laugh kills the speech — so the commonest subject is the speaker's own behavior, not an enemy's scheme. It alone carries the price sense: to undersell a rival.
- **subvert** — The only one aiming at *overturn*, not mere weakening — and it works from inside, which is why it belongs to moles, insurgents, and fifth columns rather than armies. It is also the only word here that can be praise: a novel that **subverts** its genre is being complimented.
- **vitiate** — Not about power or loyalty at all — about **soundness**. One bad premise, one fraudulent signature, one contaminant, and the whole thing no longer counts; in law it renders a contract void outright. Its objects are arguments, evidence, and agreements, never a person's standing, and it is markedly bookish where the others are everyday.

> **On the exam:** Sentence Equivalence loves the undermine/undercut pair as an easy match — check whether the sentence signals slow erosion or a single stroke before pairing; and when the blank concerns validity rather than power (evidence, a claim, a contract), vitiate is the answer none of the others can take.


<a id="meaning__drain-of-strength"></a>
### Weakening Without Destroying

All four describe force being taken out of something that survives the process — strength, capacity, intensity, or effectiveness reduced rather than abolished. None of them means "destroy," and none means "one sharp blow"; each implies something left standing in a lesser state. They split on what gets weakened (a person's vigor, a faculty, a signal, a capability), whether the weakening crosses a functional threshold, and whether the speaker is diagnosing, moralizing, or just measuring.

- **enervate** — The only one aimed at a living being's vigor and *will*, and the only one with a moral tinge — its typical agents are conditions rather than events (heat, luxury, idleness, bureaucracy), and the victim ends up limp and spiritless, faintly deserving of it. You can impair a signal or attenuate a virus; you cannot enervate one.
- **debilitating** — The only one that names a **threshold** rather than a direction: function stops. It says nothing about mechanism or degree of pain, only about outcome — and it is an adjective attached to the cause (a debilitating illness, strike, anxiety), spoken in the flat clinical voice of doctors and insurers.
- **impair** — The one that insists on **partial** damage to a specific named faculty or asset — hearing, judgment, mobility, a credit rating — which keeps working, just worse. Where *debilitating* reports that capacity is gone, **impair** reports it is degraded; and where *enervate* drains a whole person, **impair** always takes one capacity as its object.
- **attenuate** — The only **neutral** member, and usually the only deliberate one: a controlled, gradual reduction along a measurable scale, with no victim and no harm implied. Engineers attenuate signals and virologists attenuate viruses on purpose; lawyers say a fact attenuates a claim. It never touches a person's energy.

> **On the exam:** The GRE baits **enervate** as if it meant "energize" (it means the reverse), and baits **attenuate** as if it were harmful — in context it is often the answer precisely because the sentence signals deliberate, measured reduction with no blame.


<a id="meaning__what-follows-after"></a>
### What Follows After

All three name the aftermath of an act — the thing that happens *because* something else happened. Each insists on a causal link rather than mere sequence, and each carries a formal, written-up register: reports, policy papers, court filings. The splits are direction and stance. Two are nouns for consequences that are anticipated and dreaded; one is a verb for consequences already unfolding on the page, and it takes no object at all.

- **ramification** — The branching one — it flags **multiplicity**, not severity. You weigh the *ramifications* before acting, and the implied worry is that the web is wider than you've mapped, not that someone will come after you. It takes a domain adjective (legal, tax, constitutional, ethical) far more readily than an emotional one.
- **repercussion** — The one that **travels and lands on someone**. It stresses delay and distance — the harm surfaces later, often to a party who had nothing to do with the decision. And it alone can be a threat: *"there will be repercussions"* is a promise of punishment, a sense **ramification** never carries.
- **ensue** — Not a consequence at all but the **verb of it happening**, and only intransitively — chaos *ensues*, but you cannot *ensue* anything. It is retrospective and deadpan where the nouns are anticipatory and alarmed: a reporter's word for what came next ("a brawl ensued"), neutral enough to be used for good outcomes and dry enough to be funny.

> **On the exam:** Sentence Equivalence loves to dangle **ramifications**/**repercussions** as an easy pair — check whether the sentence is about a tangle of effects to trace or a delayed blow to absorb; and if the blank takes a direct object, **ensue** is dead on arrival.


<a id="meaning__put-up-with-it"></a>
### What You Will Not Put Up With

All four mean *to tolerate* — to let something stand without objecting. All four are, in practice, negative-only verbs: the natural sentence is "I cannot ___," "would not ___," "will ___ no." That shared negativity is the trap, because it hides four different refusals: a refusal of taste, a refusal by authority, a refusal to sanction, and a refusal to be morally implicated. What separates them is who is refusing, and what kind of thing they refuse.

- **abide** — The only one that's a matter of **temperament**. **Abide** takes people and their habits — whining, small talk, a certain kind of man — and "can't abide" reports a settled personal allergy, not a moral or official position. It also owns two senses none of the others have: *abide by* a rule, and *abide* meaning to last.
- **brook** — The refusal of **power, announced in advance**. **Brook** appears as *brook no* plus an abstract noun for resistance — dissent, delay, interference — and the speaker is the one who can enforce it. Where the others judge something that exists, *brook no* forecloses something before it starts.
- **countenance** — The refusal to **lend sanction**. To **countenance** is to let a proposed course of action proceed under your name — so the refuser is someone whose approval would have mattered: a board, a bishop, a government. The thing need not be wicked, only unacceptable to authorize. Watch the noun: it also means *face*.
- **condone** — The only one that **presupposes wrongdoing**. You can **condone** a fraud, never a favour — the offence has already happened, and the speaker is looking back at it and declining to be implicated. "I do not condone this" is a moral disavowal; the classic way to actually condone is to say nothing.

> **On the exam:** Sentence Equivalence loves the condone/countenance pair — plug both in and check whether the blank's object is an established wrong (condone) or a proposal awaiting approval (countenance); *brook* is unusable unless the sentence supplies "no."


<a id="meaning__changing-without-warning"></a>
### Whim over reason

All of these describe behaviour that answers to impulse rather than to reason, rule, or principle — so you cannot predict it, and you cannot argue with it. The differences are about *whose* whim it is, *what* it costs you, and *how* it lands on the person described. Some are mild social complaints, one is almost a compliment, one is a warning to get clear, and one is a charge levelled at authority. A single sentence context — a lover, a stock, a king, a fine — usually decides which is right.

- **fickle** — The only one about **loyalty and affection** — it tracks who someone likes this week, not how they behave in general. It's the mildest and most social of the group, a grumble about shallowness rather than a warning, and the blame runs toward you: calling a fan, a lover, or an electorate **fickle** announces that you were the one dropped.
- **mercurial** — The only member that can flatter. **Mercurial** describes temperament — quick, brilliant, swinging between highs — and the speaker is usually half-admiring, which is why it lands on artists, strikers, and star founders rather than on rules or fines. Use it of a market or a statute and the glamour makes it sound wrong.
- **volatile** — The change here **threatens harm**, not just disappointment. It attaches as readily to situations, crowds, markets, and substances as to people, and the implied response is to back away rather than to complain. Keep the literal chemical sense live — evaporating at low temperature — because the GRE will test **volatile** with no human in the sentence at all.
- **capricious** — Whim **exercised over other people**. It presumes a power gap: the capricious one is the king, examiner, employer, or fate, and you are the one who must live under the shifts with no way to predict or appeal them. Colder and grander than fickleness, and it strips the charm out of whimsy — same root, opposite feeling.
- **arbitrary** — The odd one out: it need not involve **change at all**. A rule applied identically every single time is still **arbitrary** if nobody can name the principle behind it — the defect is missing justification, not instability. At full strength it turns political (*arbitrary arrest*), where the charge is unchecked authority; in maths it goes fully neutral (*an arbitrary integer* = any one you like).

> **On the exam:** The trap is filing **arbitrary** under "random/changeable" — GRE sentences use it for a fixed rule with no rationale, and reward **mercurial** where the tone is admiring rather than accusing.


<a id="meaning__willing-to-go-along"></a>
### Willing to go along

All four describe an absence of resistance — someone or something that yields instead of pushing back. They differ in *where the yielding comes from*: openness before the fact, steerability by a handler, a swallowed objection after the fact, or simply never acting at all. Ordered here from most agency retained to least. Two of them also swing away from people entirely and describe **problems** that yield to a method, which is where the GRE most often plants them.

- **amenable** — The only one that is faintly complimentary — it credits the subject with being *open* rather than merely beaten. **Amenable** is forward-looking: you haven't been persuaded yet, you're persuadable, and the door is still yours to close. Nearly always bolted to **to** (amenable to a compromise, to analysis).
- **tractable** — Judged from the hand on the reins. **Tractable** is not openness but steerability — the subject goes where it is led, which is why it's mildly patronizing about people (fine for horses, employees, and undergraduates). Watch for **intractable**, which the GRE uses far more: the stubborn person, the unsolvable equation, the pain that won't respond.
- **acquiesce** — The verb of the group, and the only one that presupposes a prior objection. To **acquiesce** is to have disagreed and then stopped fighting — consent registered by silence, usually across a power gap. Amenable people never minded; someone who acquiesces minded and folded. Grammar tested: acquiesce **in** or **to** a decision.
- **passive** — Not yielding to something so much as doing nothing at all. **Passive** requires no request, no handler, no objection — it just marks the gap between what you could have done and what you did, which is why it reads as reproach. Neutral only in fixed technical pairings (*passive income*, *passive voice*, *passive smoking*), where it means merely "without active effort."

> **On the exam:** The trap is animacy: sentences apply **amenable** and **tractable** to equations, data, and diseases, so a test-taker primed on the people-sense reads "compliant" into a purely technical blank — and **intractable** appears far more often than its positive twin.


<a id="meaning__without-clear-shape"></a>
### Without Clear Shape

All four describe something you can't get a firm outline around — no edges, no fixed limit, no centre of gravity. The confusion is that each locates the shapelessness somewhere different: in the object itself, in how early it is, in a limit nobody set, or in how thinly the material is spread. Only one of them implies the thing is too *new* to have form; only one implies there's plenty of substance, just no focus. Get the source of the formlessness right and the four stop overlapping.

- **amorphous** — The purely spatial one: **amorphous** says the thing has no outline, full stop — no claim about when it started, who blurred it, or whether it will ever firm up. It's the only member with a real technical sense (glass, non-crystalline solids), which is why even its critical use sounds like a diagnosis rather than a complaint.
- **inchoate** — The only one that timestamps the shapelessness: **inchoate** things are formless *because they have barely begun*. It attaches naturally to feelings and movements too new to be named — inchoate rage, an inchoate movement — where amorphous would suggest the thing has simply always been a blob.
- **indefinite** — The only one about a limit that was never *set*, usually by somebody who could have set it. **Indefinite** covers duration as readily as outline — indefinite leave, detained indefinitely — and its chill comes from a withheld commitment, not from any lack of form in the thing itself.
- **diffuse** — The only one where the substance is all present and merely spread too thin to land: a **diffuse** essay has plenty of content, just no centre. It's also the only verb here (heat, light, power diffuse outward), and as a criticism it opposes *concise* and *trenchant*, not *defined*.

> **On the exam:** Traps swap **inchoate** for "incomplete" (it means barely begun, not half-finished) and **diffuse** for "vague" or "empty" (the material is there — it just never concentrates).


<a id="meaning__wilfully-unsteerable"></a>
### Won't Be Steered

All four describe a failure of control — someone or something that will not be directed by the person who is supposed to be doing the directing. Crucially, none of them means simply *immovable*: unlike *stubborn* or *obstinate*, which dig in and refuse to go, these words all involve motion that has escaped its handler. The differences are in who has slipped the leash, whether the escape is defiance or drift, and how much blame the speaker is assigning by choosing the word.

- **headstrong** — **Headstrong** is forward motion on one's own judgement — the person is going somewhere, just not where you said. It's the only one of the four with a warm edge: reserved for the young and spirited, it concedes force of character even while it complains, so a *headstrong* daughter is a problem you half admire.
- **willful** — **Willful** is an accusation, not a description — the speaker is laying blame, and the word can be sworn to in a courtroom. It's also the only one that extends past temperament to single acts done knowingly (*willful blindness*, *willful negligence*), where the sting is that you chose rather than slipped.
- **wayward** — **Wayward** is drift rather than defiance — nobody is being fought, the subject has just floated off the proper course, usually the moral one. Its tone is the preacher's or the disappointed parent's, softened by the hope of return, and it alone attaches freely to inanimate things with a mind of their own: a wayward strand of hair, a wayward pass.
- **restive** — **Restive** requires an authority in the frame and a grip that is starting to slip — troops, a crowd, a province, a horse under a rider. It is the one word here that describes a *collective mood under restraint* rather than an individual character, and it names the state just short of open revolt, which is why the press loves it.

> **On the exam:** The exam's favourite trap is **restive** ≠ *restless* — a restive crowd is on the edge of mutiny, not on the edge of sleep; the second-favourite is a **willful** answer where only the "deliberate act" sense fits the sentence, not the "headstrong person" one.


<a id="meaning__won-t-do-the-work"></a>
### Won't do the work

All five point at work that isn't getting done, and all carry blame. What differs is *where* the fault is located: in a person's settled character, in their competence, in a specific duty they slid out of, in the tempo of an action, or in mere aimless drift. Some brand a whole life; others complain about one afternoon. Some imply the work fell to somebody else; others imply nothing more than that you're late.

- **indolent** — Names a **temperament**, not an incident or an outcome — the indolent man may owe nobody anything, and he is comfortable, not failing. Alone in this group it can be used with a hint of pleasure (an indolent afternoon, indolent heat); none of the others can describe luxury.
- **feckless** — The charge isn't laziness but **ineffectuality** — this one can be busy, well-meaning, full of plans, and still produce nothing. It's a verdict on an entire character and its track record, delivered with dismissal rather than anger: the idle heir, the absentee father.
- **shirk** — The only verb here that requires a **specific obligation** as its object, and the only one implying the work has now landed on someone else. It attaches to duty, responsibility, a hard job — and the implied motive is cowardice or self-sparing, not slowness.
- **dilatory** — Concerns **timing, not effort** — the dilatory party may be working hard, just not yet, and the delay may be deliberate strategy (dilatory tactics, dilatory motions). Its home is the formal complaint: memos, court filings, solicitors' letters, where you're documenting a pattern.
- **dawdle** — The mildest and the most physical — it describes someone **already en route**, drifting, with no duty invoked and no motive at all. "Stop dawdling" is what you say to a child on the walk home; it would be absurd applied to a contractor in breach or a father who abandoned his family.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating **indolent** and **dilatory** as synonyms for "slow" — indolent is unwillingness to exert oneself at all, dilatory is delay in acting; and **shirk** is the only one that needs a duty as its object.


<a id="meaning__work-out-a-hidden-meaning"></a>
### Working out a meaning that won't come easily

All four concern meaning that doesn't arrive on its own — something stands between a reader and what a text, act, or person actually means, and work has to be done to close the gap. What separates them is *where the obstacle sits*: at the surface (you can't even make out the message), in the ambiguity (you can read it two ways and must pick one), in the depth (you've read it and still can't get to the bottom of it), or in the method (a whole disciplined apparatus brought to bear line by line). One is also a noun naming an activity rather than a verb naming a mental act.

- **construe** — The words are perfectly legible — the trouble is they'll bear two readings, and **construe** is the act of making one of them official. Uniquely consequential and adversarial here: someone can construe your silence, your email, your shrug *against* you, which is why the word lives in defensive formulas (*shall not be construed as*). The others describe effort; this one describes a choice someone may be blamed for.
- **decipher** — The obstacle is at the surface, before interpretation even begins: a cipher, a dead script, a prescription pad. You **decipher** to find out what it *says*, not what it means — success is bare legibility, not understanding. It's the only one here that works on physical marks, and the only one whose difficulty vanishes the moment you can read the thing.
- **fathom** — Nothing is illegible or ambiguous — you have all the facts and still can't get to the bottom of it. **Fathom** measures depth in the understander, not obscurity in the object, and it attaches to motives, griefs, and inexplicable decisions rather than to texts. It also reports failure: the idiomatic form is *can't fathom*, spoken by someone who has already tried and given up.
- **exegesis** — The only noun — a body of work, not a moment of insight, so it can't slot in where the verbs go. **Exegesis** is institutional and tooled: original languages, historical context, a method you were trained in, applied line by line to scripture, statute, or canon. It assumes the meaning is already in the text waiting to be drawn out, and it goes sardonic when the apparatus outweighs the object.

> **On the exam:** The exam picks the word by which obstacle the sentence names — illegible marks (decipher), two possible readings (construe), or an unreachable motive (fathom) — and baits you with *exegesis*, which is a noun and cannot fill a verb slot.


---

## Lookalikes and false friends

*Words confused by sight or sound, not by meaning. Mixing these up is the cheapest way to lose a mark.*


<a id="lookalike__acrimonious-parsimonious"></a>
### acrimonious / parsimonious / penurious / sanctimonious

Four long, formal, Latinate adjectives that hiss to the same ending and all sound like character flaws — which is exactly the problem, because only two of them mean anything close to each other. Three describe a defect in a person's dealings (money, money, righteousness); one describes the poisoned air between two parties. The shared register is the trap: each is bookish, disapproving, and the kind of word that appears in an obituary or a court report, so they feel interchangeable in a sentence where only one fits.

- **acrimonious** — **Acrimonious** is the odd one out — nothing to do with money or virtue. It describes *bitterness between two sides*, and almost never a person: divorces, splits, negotiations, board disputes. It presumes a prior relationship, so it carries the sting of allies turned enemies. If the sentence has two parties and a breakdown, this is your word.
- **parsimonious** — **Parsimonious** is stinginess as *policy* — a deliberate refusal to release resources, and it extends past cash to praise, detail, sympathy. Crucially, it says nothing about whether the person has money; a billionaire can be parsimonious. And it is the only word here that can turn positive: applied to a theory or model, it means economical in assumptions, and it is praise.
- **penurious** — **Penurious** is the money word that is *also about poverty*. Its second sense — destitute, dirt-poor — has no counterpart in **parsimonious**, and its stinginess sense implies a meanness that looks like poverty whether or not the poverty is real. Where **parsimonious** describes a choice, **penurious** describes a condition (or a meanness so bleak it resembles one).
- **sanctimonious** — **Sanctimonious** is about morality on display, never money. It attacks the *performance* of virtue, not virtue itself, and it is always an accusation — no one applies it to themselves, and the target usually thinks they're being admirable. It hints at hypocrisy the other three never touch: the lecture and the private sin.

> **On the exam:** The GRE rarely tests these against their synonyms — it drops one into a blank where another is expected (a *penurious* tip vs. a *parsimonious* theory vs. an *acrimonious* split), so read what the adjective attaches to: a relationship, a wallet, a life, or a sermon.


<a id="lookalike__adept-adroit"></a>
### adept / adroit / apt / inept

All four descend from Latin *aptus*, "fitted, suited," and the family resemblance is real: each asks whether a person and a task are well matched. Three of them turn that fit into a judgement of skill — high, high-and-quick, or embarrassingly low — while one keeps the older, plainer meaning of suitedness. The near-identical shells (*-ept*, *-pt*, *ad-*, *in-*) make them easy to swap on sight, and the prefixes do not pair up the way they look like they should.

- **adept** — **Adept** is skill that was *built* — hours logged, technique now automatic — and it's the only one here that can be a noun, naming someone initiated into a difficult art. It attaches to a domain (*adept at cross-examination*), not to a single moment.
- **adroit** — **Adroit** rates a *manoeuvre*, not a résumé: the quick, well-judged move made under pressure, usually social or verbal. The praise is cool and slightly wary — you admire the footwork while noting how easily it could become slick.
- **apt** — **Apt** is the odd one out: its main GRE sense isn't skill at all but *fit* — the phrase that lands exactly right, or the neutral tendency in *apt to*. Where *liable to* and *prone to* forecast trouble, **apt to** predicts without disapproving.
- **inept** — **Inept** is the speaker's verdict, not a fact about training: the thing was botched *visibly*, with a wince attached. Note the prefix trap — it negates *apt*, but it means the opposite of *adept*, and it accuses of clumsiness rather than unfitness (*incompetent*).

> **On the exam:** Two traps: sentence-equivalence pairs *apt to* with *liable/prone to* and counts on you missing that only *apt* is verdict-free; and antonym logic tempts you to read *inept* as the negation of *apt* when its live opposite is *adept*.


<a id="lookalike__allusive-elusive"></a>
### allusive / elusive / evasive / illusory

Four near-twins built on overlapping Latin roots (*ludere*, "to play," plus *vadere*, "to go"), and all four describe something you can't get at directly. In each case the straight line between you and the thing is broken — by hinting instead of stating, by slipping away, by dodging, or by not being there at all. The differences lie in where the failure sits: in the style, in the quarry, in the dodger's intent, or in reality itself.

- **allusive** — The only one that isn't about escape. **Allusive** means *referring* — the thing being pointed at is solidly real and the writer knows exactly what it is; the burden is on you to recognize it. It attaches to prose, poems, and remarks — never to a person ducking a question.
- **elusive** — The quarry is real and usually wanted, and the failure is the pursuer's, not a deception: **elusive** describes what keeps slipping the grasp of whoever is chasing it — a suspect, a scent, a definition. No intent to mislead is implied, and applied to a person it can be outright praise for slipperiness.
- **evasive** — Intent, aimed at a specific incoming thing — a question, a subpoena, a punch. **Evasive** is the only one that indicts: call an answer evasive and you've implied concealment without alleging a lie. (Its movement sense — *evasive action* — carries no blame at all.)
- **illusory** — Answers a different question entirely — not *can I catch it?* but *was it ever there?* **Illusory** says the appearance was genuine and the substance never existed, and it's formal, cool, and reserved for things people badly wanted to be true: security, progress, a recovery.

> **On the exam:** Sentence completions love the elusive/illusory swap: hopes that were never achievable are **illusory**, hopes that stayed just out of reach are **elusive** — only one of them says the thing existed.


<a id="lookalike__amenable-amicable"></a>
### amenable / amicable / inimical

Three formal adjectives that look like relatives and mostly take **to**, each describing how one party or condition stands toward another: cooperatively, peaceably, or destructively. The resemblance is largely an accident of spelling — two come from *amicus* (friend), one does not, and one is its outright negation. What actually separates them is what they attach to: a person's willingness, the tone of a dealing, or the effect of an environment.

- **amenable** — **Amenable** is about tractability, not friendliness — it measures resistance, not goodwill, and a chilly colleague can be entirely amenable. It's also the only one here that takes inanimate subjects: a *problem* can be amenable to modelling, but no problem is ever amicable.
- **amicable** — **Amicable** attaches to the dealing, not the participant — settlements, divorces, partings — and it presupposes a fight that was expected and didn't happen. Where *amenable* says someone went along with a proposal, **amicable** says the whole negotiation stayed free of rancour.
- **inimical** — **Inimical** is the negation of the family and the only negative one: harm without a hater, coming from conditions, policies, or climates rather than from anyone's ill will. It shares *amenable*'s grammar (*inimical to growth* / *amenable to treatment*) but reverses the direction — the thing is set against you rather than yielding to you.

> **On the exam:** The classic trap is treating **inimical** as friendly on the strength of *ami-*, and swapping **amenable** for **amicable** in a blank like "was ___ to the proposal" — only *amenable* can follow a person plus a method or suggestion.


<a id="lookalike__ardent-arduous"></a>
### ardent / arduous / onerous

Three formal adjectives that look and sound like siblings and all signal something *intense* — but the intensity lives in three different places: in the feeling, in the effort, or in the obligation. Two of them are complaints about work; one is a compliment about devotion. The spelling similarity does most of the damage here, since the meanings barely overlap once you see them side by side.

- **ardent** — The only one of the three that praises, and the only one about *feeling* rather than work. **Ardent** attaches to people and their devotion — an ardent supporter, an ardent admirer — never to a task. If the blank is filled by a job, a climb, or a contract clause, ardent is wrong on contact.
- **arduous** — The weight is *exertion over time*. **Arduous** grades the labour a thing costs — long, tiring, physically or mentally taxing — and it can be freely chosen: an arduous ascent nobody forced you to make. It attaches to journeys, training, negotiations, processes; never to people, and never to a duty that is merely tedious.
- **onerous** — The weight is *obligation*, and someone else usually put it there. **Onerous** describes what you're bound to and can't set down — paperwork, upkeep, a lease term — regardless of whether it's hard; a child could do the filing and it would still be onerous. It also smuggles in a grievance: call terms onerous and you're halfway to calling them unjust.

> **On the exam:** The exam pits **arduous** against **onerous** on a task blank and settles it with context: exhausting effort → arduous; imposed, resented duty → onerous. **Ardent** is pure spelling bait — it fails any sentence whose subject isn't a person's enthusiasm.


<a id="lookalike__belie-belittle"></a>
### belie / belittle / betray

Three verbs that start with *be-* and blur together on the page, though only two of them actually compete for meaning. Those two sit at opposite ends of one axis: whether a surface hides an inner truth or leaks it. The third has nothing to do with concealment at all — it's about assigning worth — and gets chosen on shape alone by test-takers who register the prefix and stop reading.

- **belie** — **Belie**'s subject is the cover story — the composed face, the tidy façade, the reassuring number — and what follows is the truth being masked or knocked down. It is the only one of the three that runs concealment-ward; it never means "reveal," no matter how clearly the sentence lets you infer the hidden truth.
- **belittle** — **Belittle** is the outlier: no hidden truth, no leak, just a speaker sizing something down. It requires a human agent talking *about* something from a position of assumed height, and its tone is calm dismissal — "anyone could have done that" — not the involuntary self-exposure the other two describe.
- **betray** — **Betray** runs the opposite direction from *belie*: its subject is the traitorous detail — a tremor, a flush, a half-second pause — and what follows is the secret getting out. The leak is always unintentional, which is why the word carries a faint taste of defection even when nobody has done anything wrong.

> **On the exam:** Watch the subject of the verb: *her steady voice* belies panic, *her shaking hands* betray it — swap them and the sentence still parses but points the wrong way, which is exactly the trap.


<a id="lookalike__beneficent-benevolent"></a>
### bene- / mal-: beneficent, benevolent, benign, magnanimous, malevolent, malign, munificent

All of these are built from Latin *bene* ("well") or *male* ("ill") welded to a root meaning wishing (*volens*), doing (*facere*), or being born/natured (*natus*) — so they all sit on the same axis of goodwill and ill will and look almost interchangeable on the page. The real fault lines are three: **wish vs. deed** (does the word describe what someone feels or what they actually did?), **presence vs. absence** (active good versus merely nothing harmful), and **cost** (does the generosity require money, or a swallowed grudge?). Nearly all of them also imply the subject holds the power in the exchange, which is why several turn sardonic so easily. Only one is primarily a verb.

- **beneficent** — The **deed** half of the pair: the good has already been conferred, so the sentence should contain an actual benefit — funds released, a ward endowed, a pardon issued. If the context only reports a feeling or an intention, this word is wrong; if the subject is a thing rather than an agent (exercise, rainfall), you want *beneficial*.
- **benevolent** — The **wish** half: goodwill as a settled disposition, with no claim that anything was done about it. It is the exact positive twin of *malevolent* and the natural fossil in institution names — *benevolent fund*, *benevolent society*, *benevolent dictator* — where the word survives precisely because it promises kindliness without committing to a payout.
- **benign** — The only member defined by what is **absent**: no threat, no malignancy, no harm. It grades nothing as actively good — a benign tumour is merely not lethal, benign neglect is merely not interference — and it is the only one here that takes tumours, weather, climates, and policies as easily as people. Also the plainest in register; the others are all formal.
- **magnanimous** — Requires a **prior injury or a defeated opponent**. Its whole content is a resentment you were entitled to keep and didn't: the victor praising the loser, the wronged party dropping the charge. The others cost money or cost nothing; this one costs a grudge, and it is void where there was no occasion for spite.
- **malevolent** — Ill will as a **standing nature**, not an episode — heavier and colder than *mean* or *spiteful*, and it may never surface in an act at all. It attaches happily to handless things (a malevolent presence, a malevolent silence). Note the split with *malicious*, which labels a particular deed: malicious gossip, malevolent character.
- **malign** — The group's **verb**, and the harm is done specifically with speech, about an absent person, to third parties — cumulative ill-speaking rather than one wound. It also carries a built-in verdict of injustice: someone *maligned* is usually being told to be undeserving of it. Its adjectival use (*a malign influence*) is the direct opposite of *benign*, not of *benevolent*.
- **munificent** — Measures **scale of gift, not quality of heart** — the size of the sum and the standing of the giver. A patron endowing a library wing is munificent; a friend quietly covering rent is generous but not. It is admiring, public praise, and it says nothing about whether the giver wishes anyone well.

> **On the exam:** The GRE plays the roots against the sentence: *-volent* is wishing, *-ficent* is doing, and *benign* is only the absence of harm — so a blank that specifies "endowed the hospital" rejects **benevolent**, "meant well but never acted" rejects **beneficent**, and "the amendment looked drastic but proved ___" wants **benign**, never **benevolent**.


<a id="lookalike__boisterous-obdurate"></a>
### boisterous / obdurate / obsequious / obstinate / obstreperous

These are confusable by shape, not by sense: four near-identical *ob-* words plus one that sounds like it belongs with them. What little meaning they do share is a person who is hard to deal with — either because they will not yield, or because they yield far too much, or because they are too loud to manage. The trap is that the look-alikes sit on opposite axes: two are about immovability, two are about noise, and one is about total capitulation. Recognising the word is never the problem; sorting which axis it lives on is.

- **boisterous** — The only one in the group you could say fondly, and the only one that isn't formal. It's noise without defiance — nobody is being disobeyed, just enjoyed too loudly. It's also the only member that works on weather: a boisterous sea or wind.
- **obdurate** — Hardness of **heart**, not of opinion. The distinguishing setup is someone pleading and getting nothing: the creditor, the sinner, the judge who will not show mercy. It condemns the person morally, where its near-twin merely calls them unreasonable.
- **obsequious** — The group's inversion — the one word here describing someone with no resistance at all. Where the others refuse, this one agrees with everything, and the agreeing is a tactic: there is something the flatterer wants. Judged entirely from outside, by the onlooker cringing, not the boss being flattered.
- **obstinate** — Immovability on a **position**, held silently and without any moral charge about cruelty — you're just blocking, past the point of sense, maybe against your own interests. It's the only one that transfers to objects: an obstinate stain, an obstinate lid.
- **obstreperous** — Loud **plus** defiant — both parts required, which is exactly what separates it from the merely cheerful noise-word. It's spoken downward by whoever has custody: teachers of pupils, judges of witnesses, cabin crew of passengers, always with a dry composure that avoids saying "screaming brat."

> **On the exam:** The exam pairs the look-alikes as distractors — obdurate vs. obstinate (heart vs. opinion) and obstreperous vs. boisterous (defiance vs. good humour) — and slips obsequious in as a fifth "stubborn" option when it means the exact opposite.


<a id="lookalike__callous-callow"></a>
### callous / callow / fallow

Three near-twins separated by two letters, and each names an absence — of feeling, of experience, of activity. But they land on completely different subjects: one on a hardened adult, one on an untested young person, one on ground or time. Nothing but the spelling connects them, which is exactly why they get swapped. Fix each to its own root and the confusion dies.

- **callous** — The only one carrying a **moral charge** — it accuses. Root is *callus*: skin thickened by repeated friction, so it implies someone who once could feel and got worn down. Uniquely here it attaches to acts and remarks as well as people ('a callous joke'); there is no callow joke or fallow one.
- **callow** — Blames **inexperience, not hardness** — the fault of having lived too little rather than too much. From the unfledged, featherless bird: soft where *callous* is thick. It fits only young people, and it comes down from an older speaker — a condescension, never a charge of cruelty.
- **fallow** — The only **non-person** word and the only one that isn't a criticism. It describes land or a stretch of time, and it is quietly optimistic: the field was ploughed and rested on purpose, and the harvest is expected back. Call a decade fallow and you are being kind.

> **On the exam:** Two traps: **callow** slotted into a sentence about indifference to suffering (that's *callous*), and **fallow** read as a synonym for barren or wasted — fallow promises recovery, barren denies it.


<a id="lookalike__chary-wary"></a>
### chary / wary / weary

Three words separated by a single letter, and only two of them are even about caution. *Chary* and *wary* both describe a guarded stance toward something — each takes *of*, and both mark the speaker as unwilling to proceed at face value. *Weary* has no caution in it at all; it belongs to exhaustion. The whole group turns on the fact that all three fit the same frame, "___ of his promises," and each produces a different sentence.

- **chary** — The only one about **rationing**. **Chary** measures how little you hand over — praise, money, detail, trust — so what follows *of* is the thing being withheld, not the thing being feared. It makes the speaker look sparing, even tight-fisted, rather than suspicious: a chary editor gives few compliments, not fewer risks.
- **wary** — Eyes open, aimed at a target. **Wary** carries active distrust of a specific person, offer, or claim — what follows *of* is the suspected danger, not a resource. It withholds nothing and doesn't retreat: you can be wary of a man and still take his deal, watching him the whole time.
- **weary** — The odd one out — no caution, only depletion.
