- **liability** — The only one running the other way: the legal sense is primary, and the everyday insult is borrowed from it. Calling someone a **liability** isn't name-calling, it's bookkeeping — it puts them in the debit column and implies exposure you'll eventually have to pay for, not mere annoyance. That's what makes it colder than *burden* or *nuisance*.
- **sanction** — The only auto-antonym in the group: the two senses don't merely differ, they contradict — bless or punish. Both require an institution with standing (a state, a board, a church), so **sanction** is never a friend's approval or a personal grudge. As a plural noun it's almost always the penalty; as a verb, almost always the approval.
- **entitled** — The only one where a preposition decides the meaning. **Entitled *to*** something is statutory and judgement-free — refunds, leave, a hearing. **Entitled** bare, in front of a person, is a moral verdict saying the claim is imaginary and the claimant insufferable. Sense 1 is granted by law; sense 2 is granted by the self.

> **On the exam:** The GRE nearly always wants the sense you didn't reach for first, and the tell is grammatical, not semantic — check the article, the plural, and the preposition before you check the meaning.


<a id="second-meaning__legal-words-whose-tested-sense-is-figurative"></a>
### Courtroom Words Off Duty

All four come from the courtroom and the police station — seizing a suspect, charging a crime, showing sufficient grounds — and all four are tested on the sense that has walked out of that building and into ordinary prose. The legal weight never fully drops off: each keeps the force of a formal proceeding while pointing at a face, a report, a system, or a response. The confusion is directional. In some of these the figurative use has taken over and the legal one is nearly dead; in others the literal legal sense is exactly the buried meaning the exam is fishing for.

- **arresting** — The only one that is praise, and the only one where the figurative sense has fully displaced the legal one — nobody reads **arresting** as "performing an arrest." What gets seized here is the *viewer's attention*, not a suspect, and the compliment is cool and critical rather than warm: an **arresting** face may be severe or odd, never merely pretty.
- **apprehension** — Runs the trick backwards — the everyday sense (dread) is the decoy and the courtroom sense (the **arrest** of a suspect) is what's usually being tested. It is also the only word here with a third, non-legal shell: *grasp of the mind*, comprehension, as in a truth beyond human **apprehension**. If the sentence rewards neither dread nor arrest, take the intellectual sense.
- **indictment** — Doesn't shed the courtroom, it borrows it whole: the figurative **indictment** casts a fact or a report as prosecutor and names a defendant — a policy, an industry, an entire system. That's the line against ordinary criticism, which is an opinion someone holds; an **indictment** is presented as the evidence itself pressing charges. Still only a charge, never a verdict.
- **warranted** — The only one that judges *fit* rather than performing an action: it asks whether the grounds were sufficient for the response, so it attaches to intrusions, assumptions, force, optimism. It concedes nothing about whether the act was wise or kind — only that the evidence licensed it — and the GRE overwhelmingly tests the negative, where **unwarranted** always charges disproportion.

> **On the exam:** The trap is context priming: a passage about crime pushes you to read "apprehension" as dread and "arresting" as police work, when the answer usually needs the sense the surrounding subject matter did *not* prime.


<a id="second-meaning__fencing-and-card-table-tactics"></a>
### Fencing and card-table tactics

All three are borrowed from the duel and the game table, and all three name a *move* inside a contest rather than a state of affairs: something one player does to another while the other is still playing. That shared arena is what blurs them — each involves an opponent, an advantage, and a moment. What separates them is direction and stance: one misleads, one gets a move stopped, one gets a move judged. Each also carries a second sense the exam prefers to the obvious one.

- **feint** — The only one that **must be seen to work** — it aims at the opponent's *attention*, a committed-looking movement one way so the real blow lands another. Hence it stays morally clean: fencers, boxers and generals feint and no one calls it dishonest, whereas the other two invite a verdict.
- **foil** — The only **reactive** one — it needs an attempt already in motion (a plot, an escape, a heist) and describes what happens *to* someone else's move; you can't foil an intention. It also casts roles: the foiler is the hero, the foiled faintly absurd. The noun sense abandons combat entirely — a foil doesn't oppose, it *flatters by contrast*, throwing another's qualities into relief.
- **ploy** — The only one that is a **verdict rather than a description**: calling something a ploy convicts it of small, cheap self-interest and says the speaker has already seen through it. Scale is built in — one move, not a campaign — and nobody applies it to their own manoeuvre.

> **On the exam:** GRE prefers the off-sense: **foil** almost always means the Watson-to-Holmes contrast, not "thwart" — and it will offer **feint** and **ploy** as interchangeable when only *ploy* carries contempt.


<a id="second-meaning__stable-and-field-words-for-the-mind"></a>
### From Stable and Field: Farm Words That Went Mental

Every word here started in a barn, a pasture, or a nest, and every one now earns its keep describing minds, careers, institutions, and tempers. The literal sense is still technically alive — you can bridle a horse, leave an acre fallow — but the GRE almost never wants it. The confusion is that a reader who knows the farm sense guesses at the human sense, and a reader who knows the human sense forgets the image that governs it. The image is the key: what the animal or field is doing tells you exactly what the abstraction does.

- **ruminate** — The only word here with **no outside agent** — the cow chews its own cud, and the thinker chews his own grievance. Where the others are done *to* something (a horse, a field, a bureaucracy), **ruminating** is entirely self-administered and, uniquely in this group, produces nothing by design: it loops rather than arrives.
- **bridle** — The restraint word — **bridle** points inward at force you already have and want steered (*bridle your temper*), which is the exact opposite vector from *goad*. It's also the only entry with a second human sense hiding inside it: *bridle at* an insult, where the head snaps back like a checked horse's. That reflex reading, not the restraint reading, is the one people miss.
- **goad** — The spiked stick, so **goad** supplies motion from outside and does it by pain — not persuasion, not encouragement. Unlike *bridle*, which credits the restrainer with discipline, **goad** puts the blame on whoever wields it: the goaded person's bad behaviour is understood as extracted from him.
- **fallow** — Unproductive on purpose, with a return expected — the only word in the group that describes an absence of output while insisting nothing is wrong. Set against *hidebound*: **fallow** is a pause in a healthy thing, not a defect in a stuck one, so a fallow decade is forgiven and a hidebound one is not.
- **hidebound** — From skin shrunk tight to the animal's frame, so the rigidity is **structural and permanent** — no recovery implied, which is precisely what separates it from *fallow*. Always an insult, always aimed at rules and the bodies that keep them; it says the thing cannot flex, not merely that it won't right now.
- **fledgling** — The one bird among the livestock, and the one hopeful word: it marks a **beginning with lift**, where *hidebound* marks an ending with none. Note the sympathy — it grants that the venture is fragile without predicting failure — and note that it lands on institutions and companies far more than on individual beginners.

> **On the exam:** Sentence-equivalence sets exploit the pairs: *bridle*/*goad* both concern shaping behaviour but in opposite directions, and *fallow*/*hidebound* both mean "producing nothing" while disagreeing entirely about whether it's fixable — read the sentence for direction and blame, not just for idleness or control.


<a id="second-meaning__geography-as-narrow-mindedness"></a>
### Geography as narrow-mindedness

All three start as literal map words — a province, a parish, an island — and all three are used on the GRE in their figurative sense: a mind whose reach stops at some boundary. The charge in every case is limited *range*, never limited intelligence; each can be leveled at someone perfectly capable inside their own patch. What separates them is which feature of the map does the metaphorical work: distance from the centre, size of the patch, or the water around it.

- **provincial** — The only one that also indicts **taste** — the target is behind the times and unpolished, not merely limited. It carries a built-in hierarchy, so it can only be spoken downward from an assumed centre, which is why it makes the speaker sound snobbish in a way the others don't. Also the only one of the three that works as a noun for a person: *a provincial*.
- **parochial** — Measures the **size of what you care about**, not your polish or your isolation. It attaches most naturally to disputes, concerns and interests — a parochial quarrel is one whose stakes evaporate a mile outside the village. No suggestion of backwardness: a parochial committee can be sophisticated and well-informed, just aimed at a trivially small target.
- **insular** — Points at the **barrier** rather than the smallness — sealed against outside influence, and comfortable that way; complacency is baked in. It's the standard diagnosis for a self-sufficient group that has stopped importing (a discipline, a nation, an elite institution), so unlike the other two it can describe the powerful centre rather than the periphery. Coolest and most clinical of the three.

> **On the exam:** The exam usually keys on the literal sense you've forgotten (parish, island, non-capital) or forces a choice between them via context: "sealed off, incurious" → insular; "small-stakes, only matters locally" → parochial; "unsophisticated, behind the metropolis" → provincial.


<a id="second-meaning__homographs-a-wholly-different-word"></a>
### Homographs: A Wholly Different Word

Each of these is a word you've read a thousand times in its ordinary sense — a month, a unit of time, what's inside a box, an everyday enthusiasm. The GRE ignores that sense entirely and tests a second one that arrives from a different direction: a different stress pattern, a different part of speech, sometimes a different root word that just happens to share the spelling. The danger isn't that the tested meaning is hard; it's that the familiar meaning fires first and you never look again. Treat a spelling you recognize instantly as a signal to slow down, not speed up.

- **august** — The only one in this group whose decoy is a proper noun: **august** the adjective (aw-GUST) is a different stress pattern from August the month (AW-gust), and it means reverence-commanding dignity. Its distinguishing risk is tonal — because the word is so lofty, examiners like to plant it where the surrounding sentence is deflating it, and the correct reading is sarcasm.
- **minute** — **Minute** (my-NEWT) shifts stress and vowel away from the time unit (MIN-it) and lands on smallness — and specifically smallness at the edge of detection, which is why it extends to an inspection that overlooks nothing. Unlike the others here, its two tested senses are related to each other; the break is only from the everyday meaning.
- **content** — The split in **content** (con-TENT) is grammatical: the familiar meaning is a noun (CON-tents of a package, web content), while the tested meaning is an adjective or verb about wanting nothing further. Watch for it in a slot no noun can fill — *content to*, *content with*, *contented himself* — and note it's the only word here whose tested sense carries a whiff of settling for less.
- **keen** — **Keen** is the outlier with no pronunciation clue at all: the verb *to keen* — to wail loudly over the dead — is a separate Irish-derived word wearing the same four letters, and nothing in the sound tells you which you've got. Only the grammar does: if *keen* takes a subject and a mourner, it isn't the eager or sharp adjective, and note the emotional flip — that verb is the one bleak entry in a word otherwise about honed edges.

> **On the exam:** The sentence will make the common sense grammatically or logically impossible — a noun-only word sitting in an adjective slot, an "eager" reading in a funeral sentence — so let the syntax, not your first recognition, pick the meaning.


<a id="second-meaning__humours-and-planets-as-temperament"></a>
### Humours and planets as temperament

Ancient physiology held that a person's fixed disposition came from bodily fluids and the planets that ruled them — blood, phlegm, and quicksilver each producing a recognizable type. The literal substances have dropped away, and what survives in modern English is the temperament: a settled, constitutional way of being, not a mood someone happens to be in today. All three are formal, all three describe what a person *is* rather than how they are reacting, and all three can be praise or diagnosis depending on whether the writer thinks the situation warranted a reaction. The trap is that they are not synonyms of each other — each one preserves a different piece of the old theory.

- **sanguine** — The only one with *content* — it names what the person believes, not just how much they react. It's directional and takes an object: you are **sanguine** *about* the deficit, the tumour, the quarter. That pointing-at-a-threat is the whole word; strip the bad news away and it has nothing to describe.
- **phlegmatic** — Not a belief but an absence of amplitude. The **phlegmatic** person has no view on how things will turn out — they simply didn't spike. Where sanguine is cheerful, this is flat, and the flatness extends to everything, not just to trouble: slow to anger, slow to enthusiasm, slow to move.
- **mercurial** — The only one describing *change* rather than a steady level — the other two name a setting the person is stuck at, this names the swinging. It's also the only one that flatters: quicksilver implies quickness of mind, so it attaches to the gifted and the difficult together — the star striker, the temperamental director.

> **On the exam:** Sentence-equivalence pairs "sanguine" with "phlegmatic" as though both just meant calm — but only sanguine asserts a good outcome, and only phlegmatic can mean torpid; watch also for the literal senses (sanguine = blood-red, mercurial = quicksilver-like) surfacing in older passages.


<a id="second-meaning__in-name-only-not-in-fact"></a>
### In name only, not in fact

Something real happened, or really exists — the fee was charged, the apology was given, the title was conferred — and none of it carries the weight the form promises. The gap is between the outward record and the actual substance behind it, and each of these words locates that gap somewhere different: in the size of what was given, in the label attached to it, or in the attention paid while doing it. All three let a speaker grant the fact and withhold the credit, which is why they read as understated criticism rather than open accusation.

- **token** — **Token** attacks the *amount*: deliberately just enough to be pointed at, calibrated to buy credit at the lowest possible price. It implies a calculating actor who knew what would have been adequate and paid less — a token raise, a token seat on the board — which is why it's the only one of the three that shades into charges of bad faith (tokenism).
- **nominal** — **Nominal** attacks the *label*, not the actor. The title, the price, the designation is perfectly genuine — it just isn't backed by power, money, or effect, and the speaker states this flatly, usually as an insider's clarification rather than a complaint. It alone has an innocent technical sense (as-specified, unadjusted: nominal thrust, nominal wages) with no hollowness in it at all.
- **perfunctory** — **Perfunctory** attacks the *manner of doing*. The act may be full-sized and fully authorized; what's absent is attention — it was executed mechanically, as a duty discharged. It's the only one here that describes a person going through motions, and the charge is indifference, not stinginess or emptiness of title.

> **On the exam:** Sort by what the emptiness attaches to: **perfunctory** modifies how an act was performed, **token** how much was given, **nominal** what something is called — and watch for nominal's on-spec technical sense in finance/engineering contexts, where it means the opposite of hollow.


<a id="second-meaning__homely-words-that-mean-to-tolerate"></a>
### Innocent-Looking Words That Mean "To Tolerate"

All five verbs cover the ground between *permit* and *endure*: letting something objectionable stand instead of moving against it. None means *enjoy* or *approve* — each is a form of non-objection, which is why they cluster so tightly in the negative ("will not ___"). What makes the group treacherous is that most of them wear an innocent disguise; as nouns they are a stream, a face, and an ancestor. The exam's interest is almost entirely in the buried verb.

- **brook** — **Brook** comes from power and shuts the door: a general, a deadline, a constitution *brooks no* delay. It is nearly frozen in that negated formula, takes an abstract object (dissent, interference, argument) rather than a person, and announces a rule rather than reporting a feeling.
- **abide** — **Abide** is the temperamental one — *can't abide* is personal, visceral distaste for a person, habit, or noise, closer to "my skin crawls" than to any policy. It is also the only member with a compliance sense (*abide by* a ruling), where the object is a rule you follow rather than a nuisance you endure.
- **countenance** — **Countenance** is official sanction: to countenance something is to let it proceed under your public gaze, which lends it legitimacy whether you like it or not. That is why refusing to countenance is a stance a board, a court, or a government takes — the noun sense (*face*) explains it, since to countenance is to give something your face.
- **forbear** — **Forbear** is the outlier: it restrains *your own* action, not someone else's conduct. You could sue, correct, retaliate — and you hold back, so the provocation is built in and the word is warmly approving rather than coolly neutral. It also takes *to* plus a verb (*forbore to comment*), never a noun object.
- **condone** — **Condone** is the only one that presupposes a wrong — you cannot condone a kindness. It is the morally loaded member, which is why *"I don't condone this"* is a speaker distancing himself from an offence, and why condoning is usually done by silence from someone who had the standing to punish.

> **On the exam:** Expect *brook* and *countenance* offered as a Sentence Equivalence pair inside a negated clause, with *forbear* dangled as the trap — it points at the speaker's own restraint, not at permitting another's behavior.


<a id="second-meaning__kitchen-words-for-people-and-prose"></a>
### Kitchen words for people and prose

All five started at the table and ended up in criticism: flavour, sweetness, sharpness, temperature and appetite, borrowed to judge prose, performances, remarks and people. The palate metaphor does real work in each — the critic is positioned as someone tasting, and the verdict is about how much sensation arrived and whether it was welcome. What separates them is where on the plate the fault lies: too little, too much, just right — or not in the dish at all, but in the diner.

- **insipid** — The charge is **nothing there at all** — flavour that was promised and never arrived. It indicts the *thing*: an insipid novel is the novel's fault, and the word implies the critic tasted attentively and came back empty-handed. Of the two deficiency words here, this is the literary sneer.
- **tepid** — Also a deficiency, but of *heat*, not flavour, and it lands on the **audience, not the object** — tepid applause and a tepid endorsement describe people who couldn't be bothered, not a bland performance. Its sting is indifference rather than contempt: nobody is attacking you, which is worse.
- **cloying** — The only excess word here: flavour was present and **kept coming until it turned**. It has a time signature the others lack — briefly pleasant, then curdled — and its home turf is sweetness and sentimentality specifically, not intensity in general.
- **piquant** — The lone **compliment** in the group, and it insists the sharpness is small, deliberate and enjoyable — a well-judged tang, not a mouthful of chilli. Where the others convict, this acquits, and it flatters the speaker's palate as much as the thing described.
- **relish** — The only **verb**, and it describes the eater rather than the dish — appetite visible on the face. It attaches most tellingly to things one shouldn't enjoy (a fight, an enemy's discomfort), and its negative is pure understatement: *I don't relish the prospect* means dread.

> **On the exam:** The classic swap is **insipid** for **tepid** — one says the work had no flavour, the other says the crowd had no warmth; check whether the blank sits on the object or on the reaction.


<a id="second-meaning__leaning-and-liking-not-incompleteness"></a>
### Leaning and liking, not incompleteness

Each of these has a famous everyday sense that has nothing to do with the tested one — incomplete, fitting, sloping — and behind it a second sense meaning *disposed toward*. In that second sense all three describe a leaning rather than a commitment: something short of a decision, a settled habit, or an outright preference that a person has not necessarily acted on. They differ in who is doing the leaning, whether it counts as a flaw, and whether the object is a course of action or a thing you simply enjoy.

- **partial** — The only one of the three that can be an **accusation**: a *partial* judge has quietly taken a side, and the leaning is a failure of fairness — this is what *impartial* denies. It is also the only one that can express liking rather than tendency, but strictly in the frozen phrase *partial to* + a noun (*partial to sherry*), a mild, almost self-deprecating admission of taste.
- **apt** — Reports an observed pattern in someone else that follows from their character — *he's apt to interrupt* is prediction, not confession, and unlike *prone* or *liable* it passes no judgment on whether the outcome is bad. It attaches to behaviour (*apt to* + verb) and can never mean fondness; an **apt** person is skilled or well-suited, not fond of anything.
- **inclined** — The first-person **hedge**: *I'm inclined to agree* announces a lean while keeping the exit open, so the object is a decision still pending rather than a habit already established. It is voluntary and revisable — no flaw implied, no track record cited, which is exactly why committees and diplomats reach for it.

> **On the exam:** Sentence-equivalence stems bury these in contexts that bait the famous sense — a "partial" observer isn't half an observer, an "apt" student in a tendency sentence isn't a clever one; check whether the blank wants bias, prediction, or a hedge.


<a id="second-meaning__nautical-words-on-dry-land"></a>
### Nautical words on dry land

Each of these began at sea — cargo going over the side, a line dropped to measure depth, ships running side by side, a hull that won't sink — and each now does most of its work on land, in offices, markets and arguments. The trap is that the figurative sense isn't free-floating: the original physical image still constrains what the word can attach to and what it implies. Knowing the literal sense is what tells you the figurative one is narrower than its dictionary synonym. Test yourself on which nautical picture is still doing the work.

- **jettison** — The only one here that is an act with a victim: something gets given up, and the ship keeps going. Its nautical logic survives as a precondition — there must be *load* and *distress*, which is why **jettison** can't replace a casual *discard*; you jettison the thing you wanted to keep.
- **fathom** — The only one whose two senses split cleanly by part of speech: the noun stayed at sea (six feet of depth), the verb went entirely mental. And unlike the others, **fathom** normally reports a failure — *can't fathom* — so the sounding line comes up short rather than touching bottom.
- **abreast** — The only one about relative position between two things both in motion, and the only one that demands a preposition to go figurative (*abreast of*). It doesn't describe you alone; it describes the gap between you and a subject that keeps moving, so it always implies effort you have to keep spending.
- **buoyant** — The only adjective, and the only positive one — a standing property, not an act or a position. Its physics is passive: **buoyant** things don't climb, they refuse to sink, which is why it fits both a person absorbing bad news and a market absorbing a bad quarter.

> **On the exam:** The GRE plants the nautical word in a landlocked sentence (a budget, a memo, a motive) and offers a literal-sea distractor plus a too-broad synonym — *discard* for **jettison**, *know* for **fathom**, *informed* for **abreast**, *joyful* for **buoyant**; the right answer is the one that keeps the original image's constraint.


<a id="second-meaning__not-what-the-look-alike-suggests"></a>
### Not what the look-alike suggests

Each of these sits one letter, one prefix, or one root away from a much commoner word — and that commoner word is the one your brain supplies. The real definitions aren't obscure; the problem is that the wrong reading arrives first and feels fluent, so nothing signals an error. In several cases the true sense is not merely different from the decoy but close to its opposite. Learning them means learning the decoy alongside them, because on the exam the decoy is what's being tested.

- **apologist** — The decoy is *apology*: readers expect regret, and there is none. An **apologist** concedes nothing — they argue the thing was defensible all along — so the word marks an accuser's contempt, not a defender's remorse. It's also the only one here that's a label pinned on someone by opponents rather than a description they'd accept.
- **disinterested** — The decoy is *uninterested*, which is a shrug. **Disinterested** is about stake, not attention — the person may be gripped by the case and still qualify, as long as no outcome pays them. It's the only word in this group that functions as praise, and the praise is specifically about fitness to judge.
- **nonplussed** — The decoy is built into the spelling: *non-* reads as "not fazed," so people use it to mean unruffled. It means the exact reverse — so fazed that the reaction machinery jams. Note it describes a momentary state, where the others here describe a standing trait or position.
- **ingenuous** — The decoy is *ingenious*, one letter away and about cleverness. **Ingenuous** is nearly its opposite: no calculation at all, frankness that comes from never having learned to guard oneself. Alone in this group it carries affection — the speaker is charmed even while noting the person is unprotected.
- **officious** — The decoy is *official*, and the whole insult turns on that gap: an **officious** person acts out an authority they don't have. It's the one word here that pictures a specific behaviour — inserting yourself, unasked, into someone else's business — rather than an inner state or a structural position.

> **On the exam:** Sentence-equivalence and text-completion items are built so the decoy sense *also* fits the blank loosely — check whether the sentence rewards impartiality or boredom, bewilderment or composure, cleverness or innocence, before choosing.


<a id="second-meaning__ordinary-verbs-that-mean-to-restrain"></a>
### Ordinary words that mean "to restrain"

Every word here holds something back without destroying it — the force is still there, still moving, just slowed, capped, steered, or weighed down. That shared meaning is easy; the distinctions live elsewhere. Ask who is applying the restraint (an agent choosing to, or circumstance imposing it), whether it's wanted or resented, and whether the thing restrained is a moving body, a rising quantity, a hot impulse, or an effort in progress. Most of these also hide their GRE sense behind a common everyday one.

- **check** — **Check** is the arrest of forward motion at a moment — an advance checked at the river, anger checked before it lands. Alone in this group it works as a countable noun for the restraining thing itself (*a check on executive power*), which is why it dominates constitutional and political prose.
- **curb** — **Curb** applies to a quantity or rate you want lower but not zero — inflation, emissions, spending, drinking. It's a dial being turned down over time rather than a body being stopped, and it's the house verb of policy writing: an authority acting deliberately on something with its own upward momentum.
- **bridle** — **Bridle** implies steering something powerful you own or command — your tongue, his ambition — so it moralizes in a way the others don't, carrying self-discipline and formal register. It's also the only word here with a second intransitive life: *bridle at* an insult, offence taken for one's dignity and visible in the body.
- **temper** — **Temper** doesn't push against the thing — it adds the opposite ingredient until the result sits in proportion (justice with mercy, zeal with caution). Uniquely in this group the outcome is an improvement, not a diminishment, and the objects are always something running hot.
- **hamper** — **Hamper** is the only one where nobody chose the restraint: circumstance imposes it, it's unwanted, and it drags rather than caps. Watch the passive collocation — efforts are *hampered by* rain, budget cuts, missing data — and note the object is an activity in progress, not an impulse or a quantity.
- **inhibit** — **Inhibit** locates the brake inside the system — a psychological block or a chemical/biological damping, not a hand applied from outside. Cold inhibits growth; the inhibited speaker isn't forbidden, they simply can't get it out, which is why *inhibitions* means shyness rather than rules.

> **On the exam:** Two traps at once: the everyday noun senses (a tick mark, a pavement edge, a picnic basket, losing your temper) are decoys, and once you're in the right sense the answer hinges on whether the restraint is deliberate and desired (check/curb/bridle), improving by admixture (temper), or an unwelcome drag (hamper/inhibit).


<a id="second-meaning__touchable-sounding-words-that-mean-obvious"></a>
### Patent, Manifest, Palpable: Obvious Wearing Another Coat

All three mean *obvious* — not needing proof, argument, or a second look — and all three arrive at that meaning through a more concrete sense the reader is likelier to know first: a legal grant, a cargo list, a thing you can touch. That extra baggage is exactly what separates them. One is used to call out a falsehood, one is the institutional word for something coming plainly into view, and one measures how hard a thing presses on you rather than how easily it is seen.

- **patent** — Keeps bad company: **patent** overwhelmingly attaches to falsehood and absurdity — a patent lie, patent nonsense, patently unfair. It carries an accusation, that someone tried to pass off the indefensible and the speaker is not having it. Nobody calls a kindness patent.
- **manifest** — The institutional, unaccusing one — the word a judge, doctor, or diplomat uses (*manifest error*, *manifest injustice*). Alone in the group it has a live verb, and that verb sets its direction: something latent — a disease, a talent, a grudge — surfaces into view. It reports what has become visible; it doesn't charge anyone with lying about it.
- **palpable** — Grades intensity, not visibility. It attaches to atmospheres and collective moods — palpable tension, palpable relief in a courtroom or a crowd — things that press on a room rather than facts that can be established. Its literal sense is still alive in medicine (*a palpable mass*), which the others have no equivalent of.

> **On the exam:** The exam hides the adjective behind the famous noun — a sentence about inventions or ship cargo where **patent**/**manifest** must mean "obvious" instead — and offers **palpable** for a plain fact, where it needs a felt atmosphere.


<a id="second-meaning__physical-sharpness-verbal-sharpness"></a>
### Physical sharpness → verbal sharpness

Every word here starts as a physical property — burning, biting, scraping, puckering, honing, piercing — and gets lent to speech, mind, or manner. The literal sense is never dead; it tells you exactly *how* the figurative sharpness works, and therefore what it implies. The real fault line is not intensity but attitude: some of these condemn the speaker as bitter, some half-admire them as clever, and some are straight compliments about the quality of a mind. Getting the group right means asking what the sharpness does to its target and what it reveals about whoever wielded it.

- **caustic** — **Caustic** is the one with bitterness behind it — chemical burn, aimed at a person, meant to leave a mark. Where *trenchant* wins an argument and *mordant* gets a laugh, caustic just corrodes; it indicts the speaker's state of mind as much as it damages the target.
- **mordant** — **Mordant** is the only member that is *funny*. The bite is intellectual and dry, and the word half-compliments the wit even while the target bleeds — satirists and obituarists are mordant, which is precisely why a merely nasty remark (caustic) never earns the label.
- **abrasive** — **Abrasive** describes a *manner*, not a remark — the only word here that needs no wit, no aim, and no sentence. It's texture: friction, no social cushioning, wearing rather than wounding, usually chronic and often unintentional. The classic use is the HR euphemism for someone effective and exhausting.
- **astringent** — **Astringent** is cold where caustic is hot — puckering, drying, faintly medicinal, the sting that's supposedly good for you. It carries no bitterness and no joke, and applied to a prose style or a critic's discipline it usually reads as praise for severity, not an accusation of cruelty.
- **trenchant** — **Trenchant** is about *accuracy*, not damage — the only word here that hurts purely by being right. No hostility is implied at all; you can be trenchant in perfect good temper. It praises the mind that produced the analysis, which is why it lives in reviews, essays and legal argument.
- **penetrating** — **Penetrating** describes what the sharpness *reaches* rather than what it destroys — it gets past the barrier, to the thing being hidden. Uniquely in this group it also runs on gaze, cold, smell and sound. Flattering to the observer, uncomfortable for the observed; nothing is criticized, only exposed.
- **keen** — **Keen** is sharpness as *capacity*, not as an act — a blade, a wind, an eye, a mind, honed rather than blunt, with no target and no victim. It's also the only word here that swings positive-eager (*keen to help*), and the only one hiding a wholly unrelated verb: to keen is to wail over the dead.

> **On the exam:** The trap is assuming the whole group is hostile: **trenchant** and **keen** are compliments and **astringent** often is, so the answer usually turns on whether the sentence rewards accuracy, wit, or bitterness — and on the buried second senses (keen = eager/to wail, mordant = dye fixative, astringent = skin toner).


<a id="second-meaning__plain-nouns-that-turn-into-verbs-of-promotion"></a>
### Plain Nouns That Turn Into Verbs of Promotion

Each of these started as something concrete — a prizewinner, a courtroom pleader, a ticket hustler, a lion, a rubbed piece of metal — and each has a second life as a verb meaning *to raise something's public standing*. That's the shared job: making a cause, a person, or a reputation look better in front of an audience. They split on three axes: **what** gets promoted (an idea, a policy, a human being, an existing reputation), **who** is doing it (a lone partisan, a paid mouth, a whole crowd), and **whether the word is sneering at the promoter**. Two of these are clean; three come with a built-in raised eyebrow.

- **champion** — The only one where the promoter **pays a cost**: you attach your name to a cause and absorb the incoming fire, usually over years. Its object is a cause or an underdog, never your own image — and unlike *advocate*, it implies combat rather than argument.
- **advocate** — The **argumentative** one: you make the case, recommend the course of action, plead on the record. Its lawyerly root shows in the object — you advocate *a policy*, a specific thing to do, where a champion fights for a whole cause. Neutral about cost and about who benefits; the word itself passes no judgement on you.
- **tout** — The one that **implicates the promoter**. Touting is loud, repetitive, and interested — you're talking it up because you stand to gain, and the claim is inflated. Note that its object is typically a product, candidate, or result being sold, and its favourite construction is passive: *touted as* is a setup for the disappointment.
- **lionize** — Its object is always a **person**, and its subject is always a **crowd** — critics, salons, the press. Unlike *tout*, nobody in particular is profiting; the fuss is genuine but faddish, and the writer using the word usually thinks the adulation outran the achievement.
- **burnish** — Its object is an **abstraction you already have**: a reputation, credentials, a legacy. This is the only one that cannot start from zero — you buff an existing surface, you don't build it — and the only one whose usual target is the promoter's *own* standing, which is why it reads as PR.

> **On the exam:** The literal noun sense is the decoy; past that, the split is connotation — **tout**, **lionize**, and **burnish** all carry a whiff of the undeserved, so any sentence hinting at self-interest, faddishness, or cosmetic fixes rules out **champion** and **advocate**.


<a id="second-meaning__plain-verbs-doing-abstract-work"></a>
### Plain verbs doing abstract work

These are short, ordinary verbs you have known since childhood — which is exactly the problem. Each carries a second, more abstract sense that the everyday meaning crowds out, and the GRE writes its sentence around the abstract one. You don't misread them because they're hard; you misread them because you're sure you already know them and stop reading. The tell is usually the grammar: an inanimate subject, an adjective hanging off the end, an object that couldn't possibly take the literal sense.

- **inform** — **Inform** is the only one here whose tested sense reverses direction: nothing is handed over, something soaks in. The subject is an abstraction (a conviction, an exile, a training in law) and the object is a whole body of work it silently shapes — no speaker, no listener, no fact transferred. If you can ask *who told whom*, you're on the wrong sense.
- **render** — **Render** is the one you disambiguate by sentence shape, not by meaning: an adjective trailing behind it (*rendered moot, rendered inert*) locks in "cause to become" every time. It is also the formal-register member of the group — you render what is owed or due (aid, a verdict), which is why it sounds legal where *inform* and *reflect* sound merely thoughtful.
- **coin** — **Coin** is the narrowest here — its abstract sense takes only language as its object, never a device, method, or plan. It also smuggles in two claims the others don't: authorship (someone specific minted it) and uptake (other people picked it up). A word nobody repeats was never coined.
- **prime** — **Prime** is the trap of quality vs. sequence: the familiar adjective means *best*, but the tested verb means only *beforehand* — a primed surface, pump, or witness is readied, not improved. Alone in this group it turns sinister with human objects, where preparing someone shades into coaching or setting them up.
- **reflect** — **Reflect** carries two abstract senses, and the second is the sneaky one: in *the delay reflects poorly on management*, the grammatical subject is the evidence and the person judged never gets named — blame by ricochet. Its thinking sense is backward-facing and unhurried, reviewing what's already done, unlike deliberating (toward a decision) or pondering (at a puzzle).

> **On the exam:** Sentence equivalence blanks pick these because both everyday and abstract senses are grammatical — only the inanimate subject or the trailing adjective reveals which one is in play.


<a id="second-meaning__praise-shaped-words-that-damn-faintly"></a>
### Praise-shaped words that damn faintly

Each of these looks like a compliment and functions as a limit. The praise is real but bounded, and the bound is the message: something cleared a bar, or was small, or was well-intentioned — and the reader is meant to notice what went unsaid. All four also carry a second, non-evaluative sense (legal fitness, physical crossability, literal smallness, plain approval) that the GRE prefers to test, because students only know the flattering surface.

- **competent** — **Competent** grades the *person's* qualification, not the output: it certifies that nothing went wrong and stops there. It's the only word here with a hard technical sense that carries no shading at all — *competent to stand trial*, *court of competent jurisdiction* means authorised, full stop.
- **passable** — The faintest of the four — **passable** names the threshold explicitly: it scraped over and halted. Where *competent* implies a trained person, *passable* is a verdict on a thing that survived inspection (a meal, an accent, an imitation), delivered by whoever was doing the inspecting. It alone has a physical sense: a road, not a performance.
- **modest** — **Modest** deflates *scale*, not quality — a modest raise is a genuinely good raise that happens to be small. That makes it the one word here that never questions whether the thing was done well. It's also the only one that can describe character as a virtue: declining to boast about something you actually have.
- **laudable** — **Laudable** is the only unambiguously positive word here — the damning is by omission. It fastens onto aims, attempts and restraint, so praising the goal quietly concedes the result is unmentionable. Its formal, editorial register makes the praise institutional and distant rather than personal.

> **On the exam:** The GRE rarely tests the warm reading: it builds a sentence whose contrast signal ("merely," "though," "at best") forces the deflating sense, or drops **competent** and **passable** into legal/geographic contexts where the faint-praise reading is the trap.


<a id="second-meaning__proper-nouns-carrying-a-fixed-character"></a>
### Proper Nouns That Became Verdicts

Every word here started as a name — an empire, a city, a lawgiver, a tribe, a knight, a soldier — and hardened into a permanent judgment about one trait. The origin is dead weight on the exam: you are never asked about Byzantium or Don Quixote, only about the single quality the name now stands for. The trap is that several of them describe rules, several describe bareness, and several describe a person's whole outlook, so they cluster into near-neighbours that are in fact answering completely different questions: is it *tangled*, or *harsh*? Is the *room* bare, or the *sentence*? Is the fool *lovable*, or *smug*?

- **byzantine** — **Byzantine** attacks a structure's *navigability*, not its cruelty. The complaint is that you cannot find your way through — layered clauses, hidden channels, procedures no one will explain — and that the maze conveniently protects whoever built it. A byzantine rule can be entirely lenient; it just takes six months and an insider to work out what it says.
- **draconian** — **Draconian** attacks *proportion*, and nothing else. The rule may be one sentence long and perfectly clear — that's the point; the penalty is simply wild against the offence. It targets policies and the people who write them, so it lands on a curfew, a sentencing law, an attendance code, never on a personality.
- **spartan** — **Spartan** describes *physical conditions* stripped by choice — the bunk, the cell, the unheated room, the plate with nothing on it. What separates it from poverty is discipline: someone could have added comfort and didn't. It's the only word here that can be sincere self-description, since austerity is something people boast about.
- **laconic** — **Laconic** applies the same stripping to *speech*, with an added charge spartan lacks: withheld words. The speaker had more to say and declined, so the shortness carries attitude — cool, dry, faintly withering. Judge it by what's implied, not by word count: a laconic reply is short *at* you.
- **philistine** — **Philistine** is a verdict on *taste*, and it is the only word here that indicts the speaker too — you can't use it without claiming a higher perch. The charge isn't ignorance of art but comfortable, unbothered contempt for it: the man who thinks a poem's uselessness settles the matter and is pleased with himself for saying so.
- **quixotic** — **Quixotic** is the group's one *warm* condemnation. It grants the person good motives and even gallantry, and faults only their grip on reality — the goal is worth wanting and cannot possibly be had. Nothing here is smug or self-serving; the quixotic figure is typically sacrificing something for a cause that will not repay him.
- **chauvinistic** — **Chauvinistic** is a verdict on *loyalty turned comparative*. Devotion alone isn't enough — the chauvinist requires outsiders to be inferior, which is why it slots so readily into "male chauvinist." It paints the holder as boastful and faintly absurd rather than menacing, and it is never self-applied.

> **On the exam:** The classic swap is byzantine↔draconian (tangled vs. brutally harsh) and spartan↔laconic (a bare room vs. bare speech); expect the sentence's object — code, cell, reply, crusade — to be the only clue.


<a id="second-meaning__saying-it-without-saying-it"></a>
### Saying it without saying it

All three move information without a plain statement carrying it. Something is conveyed — a suggestion, a reference, a hidden feeling — while the words that would name it outright are never spoken, so the sender can be understood without being on record. The group splits on control: two of these are the sender's deliberate choice of indirectness, and one is a leak that happens against the sender's will. The GRE tests all three in their quiet senses, not their famous ones.

- **intimate** — **Intimate** plants *new* information delicately — the listener didn't already know the thing, and now does, but you never said it. The value is deniability: a chairman who *intimates* he may step down has told the board and committed to nothing. Only this word's whole point is the escape hatch.
- **allude** — **Allude** points at something *already known to both parties* — a scandal, a poem, an unread inbox — and simply declines to name it. No new information is transferred; the listener supplies the referent. It also has a grammar tell the others lack: it needs **to**, and its object is a thing that exists independently of the speaker.
- **betray** — **Betray** is the only involuntary one — nobody chooses to betray a feeling. The subject is typically not a person but the traitorous detail (a flush, a tremor, a pause) that escapes and exposes what its owner was working to hide, which is why the word keeps a residue of treachery even in this sense.

> **On the exam:** Classic second-meaning trap: each word's loud sense (private/close, refer-vs-elude, disloyalty) is the decoy — check whether the sentence wants deliberate hinting, indirect reference, or an unintended leak.


<a id="second-meaning__metal-and-coinage-words-for-reputation"></a>
### Shine, Alloy, and Worth: Forge Words Gone Abstract

Every word here starts at the forge or the mint — polishing metal, letting it dull, cutting a coin with cheaper stuff, mixing an alloy, quenching steel — and the GRE only ever wants the abstract sense. They split along one fault line: some work on the **surface** (how bright a reputation looks) and some work on the **composition** (whether something inferior got stirred into the substance itself). Within the composition group they split again, on whether the mixing is fraud or craft. Get the axis right and the answer choices sort themselves.

- **burnish** — The only improvement in the group, and it works purely on the outside: **burnish** adds shine to something that already has standing — a legacy, credentials, an image. Because it can't create substance, it carries a PR smell the others don't; the word implies someone is managing appearances.
- **tarnish** — The exact inverse of *burnish*, and equally superficial: **tarnish** takes the gleam off, slowly, and leaves the thing intact — a tarnished career is still a career. It also presupposes admiration (nothing dull can be tarnished), and unlike *sully* or *besmirch* it is cool and reportorial rather than morally indignant.
- **debase** — Where *tarnish* stops at the finish, **debase** attacks worth itself: the coin still reads *silver*, the office still carries its title, but the value inside has dropped. It's the only one here that can drag a *person* down morally — made to act beneath themselves — and it names the fall in value, not the act that caused it.
- **adulterate** — **Adulterate** names the act *debase* leaves implicit — the specific pouring of something cheap into something pure, sold as if nothing happened. That makes it an accusation of fraud with a profit motive behind it, and it stays comfortable with physical goods (milk, oil, a drug supply) where *debase* has drifted toward the abstract. You'll meet **unadulterated** more often than the verb.
- **unalloyed** — The group's only adjective, only positive, and the only one describing a resulting state rather than an act of change. **Unalloyed** attaches almost exclusively to good abstractions — *joy, delight, success* — never to misery, and it most often shows up negated ("not an unalloyed good"), which is the polite way to announce a catch.
- **temper** — Here the mixing is skill, not sabotage: **temper** adds a counterweight — mercy into justice, caution into ambition — so the result is proportioned rather than cheapened, and nothing is removed. Its objects are always something running hot (zeal, expectations, criticism), which is the tell that separates it from *adulterate*'s passive, unsuspecting victim.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating "mix something in" as automatically bad — adulterate and debase condemn, temper compliments; and burnish/tarnish sound like value change when they only touch the shine.


<a id="second-meaning__siege-engineering-inside-an-argument"></a>
### Siege engineering inside an argument

Every word here is borrowed from fortification and siege — walls propped from outside, tunnels dug beneath foundations, artillery aimed at a target, troops dug into trenches — and on the GRE all of them arrive figuratively, applied to claims, reputations, policies and positions. The shared picture is a structure that either stands or falls depending on what is under it and what is fired at it. They become confusable because they all describe a *move* in that siege; they differ in direction (adding support vs. removing it vs. battering), in timescale (one stroke vs. a campaign), and in whether the damage is done in the open or out of sight.

- **buttress** — The only one that names the *material* of the support: you **buttress** a claim **with** evidence, data, a precedent. The support is external, engineered, and deliberately added — and it attaches to positions, cases and regimes, never to a mood or a person.
- **bolster** — Where *buttress* tells you what the support is made of, **bolster** tells you about the object's condition: it was sagging. It is also the one that takes feelings and aggregates — morale, confidence, a currency, a defence — which *buttress* will not.
- **undermine** — The exact inverse of *buttress*: support removed from below rather than added from outside, and removed slowly. **Undermine** implies a campaign with an agent behind it, conducted deniably — the damage is visible long before the hand that did it is.
- **undercut** — Same downward direction as *undermine*, but a single stroke rather than a campaign — and the only word in this group that is routinely **accidental or self-inflicted**: one hedged sentence **undercuts** your own thesis. What's left is still standing, just hollow.
- **assail** — No engineering at all — this is frontal, in the open, and on the record, the opposite posture to *undermine*'s tunnelling. Its force is in repetition (blow after blow), and it is uniquely the verb for attack **from within**: assailed by doubts, by nausea. Hence **unassailable**.
- **barrage** — Primarily the noun for what *assailing* feels like from the receiving end. A **barrage** is aimed and sustained enough to pin the target down with no chance to answer — which is why it collocates with questions, criticism, abuse directed at someone who cannot fire back.
- **entrenched** — The only static word here: it describes the *state of the target*, not a move made against it or for it. It is silent on merit — an **entrenched** attitude may be wrong and still immovable — and usually arrives as a complaint about an obstacle, explaining why the siege was needed at all.

> **On the exam:** The GRE pairs buttress/bolster and undermine/undercut as if interchangeable — decide by the object (evidence for a claim vs. a sagging morale) and the timescale (one stroke vs. a patient campaign), not by direction.


<a id="second-meaning__stress-shifts-meaning-shifts"></a>
### Stress shifts, meaning shifts

Every word here is a familiar adjective or noun that hides a less familiar verb — and the verb is the one the GRE tests. Say them aloud and the shift is audible: the final syllable goes from a swallowed schwa (*-uht*) in the adjective/noun to a full *-ATE* in the verb, and with `attribute` the stress itself jumps (ATT-ribute the noun, a-TRIB-ute the verb). The trap is that the everyday sense is so loud in your ear that you read the verb as if it were the adjective, and the sentence collapses into nonsense. Learn each one as two separate entries that happen to share a spelling.

- **appropriate** — The only verb here that is **acquisitive** — it moves a thing into your possession. And it is the only one whose morality is set entirely by who does it: a committee **appropriates** funds (pure accounting), a novelist **appropriates** a plot (quiet theft dressed in a respectable word).
- **deliberate** — The one where the *adjective* is the damning sense and the verb is the calm one. **Deliberate** cruelty accuses; a jury that **deliberates** is merely taking its time. Note it's the group's only verb that needs no object — you deliberate *over* a thing, you don't deliberate it.
- **intimate** — The widest gap in the group: nothing on the surface connects "deeply private" to "hint at." The verb is a communication move and a defensive one — you **intimate** something precisely so you can later deny having said it. Compare *insinuate*, which is nasty; **intimate** is drawing-room polite.
- **articulate** — The one word whose two senses are actually the same idea — jointedness — rather than two strangers sharing a spelling. Where **intimate** blurs a thought to make it deniable, **articulate** does the reverse: it takes something shapeless and gives it edges and joints you can point at.
- **attribute** — The only one that points *backward*, to origin: it names where a thing came from, and quietly concedes you can't prove it (a canvas is **attributed** to Caravaggio only when the signature is missing). Note the stress jump — the noun is ATT-ribute, the verb a-TRIB-ute — which none of the others do.
- **subordinate** — The only verb in the group that is inherently comparative and demands **to**: you **subordinate** X *to* Y. It doesn't take, name, or clarify anything — it ranks two things and sacrifices the loser. Watch the adjective too: it's structural (a rung on the org chart), never *subservient*, which is a character judgment.

> **On the exam:** The GRE plants these in verb slots where your ear automatically supplies the adjective — if a sentence goes strange, re-read the word as a verb before you re-read the sentence.


<a id="second-meaning__swollen-and-flushed-overwritten"></a>
### Swollen, flushed, heavy → overwritten

Each of these begins as a description of a body or an object — distended with fluid, red in the face, too massive to move gracefully — and then gets aimed at prose that suffers the same defect. All four are complaints about style that is *too much*: too inflated, too decorated, too slow, too loud. The trap is that they are not interchangeable insults; the physical image each one comes from determines exactly which fault it names. Knowing the literal sense tells you which stylistic sin is being charged.

- **turgid** — The one whose literal sense is medical/hydraulic — tissue or a river distended with fluid, not something you look at but something you'd sink into. As a style verdict it uniquely charges two things at once, pompous *and* soporific: the reader's complaint is that they couldn't get through it.
- **florid** — The only one whose bodily sense is colour rather than size or weight — a face red with heat, drink, or blood pressure (and, in medicine, a symptom bloomed into full view). Its stylistic fault is therefore surface **decoration**, flourishes crowding out sense — a florid page can be quick and lively, just overdressed.
- **ponderous** — Charges **pace**, not emptiness: the fault is mass without lightness of touch, sentences arriving like furniture dragged across a floor. Alone in this group it's compatible with real substance — a ponderous book may be full of content it simply cannot move.
- **bombastic** — The one with no live physical sense left (its root, *bombast*, was cotton padding) and the one aimed at a **performer** — a speaker, out loud, before an audience. It alone charges hollowness: the listener hears the gap between the volume and the thought, so it's ridiculous rather than boring.

> **On the exam:** Match the clue to the fault — ornament → florid, slowness/tedium → ponderous, inflated *and* wearying → turgid, loud and empty → bombastic; and watch for passages using the literal senses (a flushed complexion, a swollen river, a heavy load) where the style meaning is the wrong answer.


---

## Intensity scales

*One dimension, ordered weakest to strongest. Sentence Equivalence often turns on exactly this.*


<a id="intensity__angry-speeches"></a>
### Angry speeches: from scolding to venom

All three name a speech that is too long, too hot, and no longer persuading anyone. Each is a verdict the audience passes, never a label a speaker claims: they concede that words had force while denying they had reason. What separates them is not how loud but what the anger is made of — moralising, loss of control, or settled bitterness — and who is trapped listening.

- **harangue** — **Harangue** is defined by the captive audience and the corrective intent — it comes *at* people who cannot leave, and it wants to improve them. It is the only one of the three that works comfortably as a verb with an object (*harangued the crowd for an hour*), because the relationship between speaker and trapped listener is the whole point. The anger can be cold and moralising rather than furious.
- **tirade** — **Tirade** is the one that says the speaker *lost control*. It's spontaneous and hot — an eruption at a target who is standing right there, not a prepared position. Where a harangue is delivered from a podium and a diatribe can be typed out, a tirade happens in the moment and is regretted later.
- **diatribe** — **Diatribe** is the coldest and most durable: bitterness that has been composed. It's the only one that is routinely *written* — published, printed, circulated — and the only one that can attack an abstraction (a policy, a movement, a school of thought) rather than the people in the room. Nothing has to be shouted for it to qualify; the venom is on the page.

> **On the exam:** All three fit "long angry speech," so the sentence decides it by target and temperature: captive listeners being scolded → harangue; a speaker who snapped in the moment → tirade; a sustained written attack on an idea → diatribe.


<a id="intensity__argumentative-to-warlike"></a>
### Argumentative to warlike

All four describe hostility as a *trait* rather than a passing mood — a person set up to fight, or a thing set up to be fought over. None of them means merely angry; anger is provoked and passes, while these describe how someone is standing before you say anything. What separates them is how far along the fight is: still an argument, an appetite for one, a scowl daring you to start it, or blows already being exchanged. Register splits them too — one belongs to committee minutes, one to war reporting, one to arrest reports.

- **contentious** — The only one that fits an inanimate thing — a **contentious** clause, border, or nomination is the *object* people fight over, and that use is nearly neutral. Even applied to a person it stays at the level of argument: talk, objections, disputes, never fists. It's the word a performance review or a court opinion would use.
- **pugnacious** — The appetite word. **Pugnacious** is the only one here that can flatter — it implies energy, relish, and a willingness to punch above your weight (the trial lawyer, the small striker who won't be bullied). The fighting is usually verbal, and the speaker is often enjoying the spectacle rather than condemning it.
- **truculent** — The only sullen one. **Truculent** points downward and inward — it's the scowl, the arms folded, the subordinate radiating a dare at authority (the truculent witness, the truculent teenager). No relish, no charm; the aggression is withheld and glowering, waiting for you to supply the excuse. Of prose, it means savagely out to wound.
- **belligerent** — The fight has already started. **Belligerent** is a posture leaning in — voice up, chest out, no sulking held in reserve. Uniquely, it doubles as a technical noun for a state at war, so it swings between the Geneva communiqué and the police report about the man who wouldn't leave the bar.

> **On the exam:** The exam separates these by *what they attach to* and *who is looking*: only contentious takes an issue as its subject, only pugnacious can be admiring, only truculent supplies the sulk, and only belligerent names a warring state.


<a id="intensity__asking-to-abasement"></a>
### Asking to abasement

All three describe asking someone who holds power over you, humbly and with feeling — not a horizontal request between equals. What separates them is how much of the asker's dignity is spent in the asking, and whether the writer approves. The scale runs from a plea that leaves the asker's standing intact, through one that formally surrenders it, to one the observer finds degrading. Choosing wrongly doesn't change the action described; it changes what the sentence says about the person doing it.

- **entreat** — **Entreat** is the only one here that costs the asker nothing in standing — the plea is earnest but composed, and it typically leans on affection, loyalty, or respect rather than on a power gap. A wife entreats her husband, a subject entreats a king, and neither is diminished by it. Its faint archaism makes it the elevated, not the abject, choice.
- **supplicate** — **Supplicate** puts the asker's body into it — kneeling, hands out, position formally surrendered. Unlike the others it has a legitimate ritual home in prayer and formal petition, where the abasement is expected; drag it into ordinary life ("supplicated for a raise") and the incongruity turns witheringly ironic.
- **grovel** — **Grovel** is the observer's verdict, not a description of the plea: it says the self-abasement went further than the situation warranted and was performed for someone with power. No one applies it to their own conduct except as a joke, and it reliably lowers the reader's estimate of the person doing it.

> **On the exam:** The exam hinges these on the sentence's attitude, not its action — a clue like "with quiet dignity" or "without losing composure" forces **entreat**, an explicit power gap or kneeling image forces **supplicate**, and any word of contempt from the narrator forces **grovel**.


<a id="intensity__attacking-a-reputation"></a>
### Attacking a reputation

All five are ways of talking someone down — lowering how they are regarded, by the listener or by the world. They differ on three axes: whether the attack must be **false**, whether it must be **public**, and how **wicked** the target ends up looking. At the low end the victim merely seems small and unimpressive; at the high end they seem evil, and the attacker seems like a liar. Most of these words judge the speaker as much as the target.

- **belittle** — The only one that needs no audience and makes no accusation — **belittle** shrinks, it does not blacken. The target ends up looking minor, not wicked, and the classic scene is one-on-one and perfectly polite: a boss, a parent, a rival. It also uniquely attaches to non-persons — a fear, a grievance, an achievement can be belittled.
- **denigrate** — Where *belittle* can be one condescending remark, **denigrate** is the sustained running-down of someone's worth or reputation, and the word itself rules the attack undeserved. Crucially it requires no lie — unfair emphasis, sneering, faint praise all denigrate. Formal: the verb of editorials and HR complaints.
- **defame** — Falsity and publicity are both mandatory here — **defame** is the legal-technical member, splitting into libel and slander. Truth is a complete defence: however savage the statement, if it is accurate you have not defamed. Note the shift in victim — *belittle* damages how you see yourself, **defame** rewrites how everyone else sees you.
- **vilify** — The only one that specifies the *content* of the attack: **vilify** paints the target as evil, contemptible, someone fit to be hated. It needs a crowd and time — a press campaign, not a courtroom claim — and unlike *defame* it needs no provable lie, only distortion. It usually arrives as "unfairly vilified," the writer taking the target's side.
- **calumny** — The only noun: **calumny** names the lie itself, or the practice of telling it, so it takes articles and plurals — *a calumny*, *spread calumnies*. It out-moralises *defame*: same falsehood, but with deliberate malice and the speaker's disgust attached, and none of the legal machinery. Use it when you want the accusation to sound shameful rather than actionable.

> **On the exam:** The trap is the falsity axis: only **defame** and **calumny** entail a lie, so a sentence stipulating "though every word was true" kills them and rewards **denigrate**/**vilify** — and **calumny**'s noun slot is often the cleanest structural giveaway.


<a id="intensity__barely-visible-to-blatant"></a>
### Barely detectable to brazen

All five rate how strongly something registers on an observer — from the faint trace you have to hunt for, up to the offence nobody could pretend not to see. The scale is not just about brightness, though: as it climbs, the words stop describing the thing and start judging it. At the low end the burden sits on the perceiver's attention; at the high end it sits on the offender's shamelessness.

- **discernible** — The only word here that requires effort from the observer — it marks the threshold of perception, not the loud end of it. It also does its real work negated: **no discernible** difference is a claim about the rigour of the looking, not just the absence of the thing.
- **conspicuous** — About contrast with surroundings — the thing sticks out of its background, so it attaches to people, clothes, spending, a building, in a way the others don't. It's the eye's word, and it carries social awkwardness: to be **conspicuous** is to be clocked, which is why the thing that isn't there can be conspicuous by its absence.
- **manifest** — Formal and institutional: the fact displays itself so openly that inference is unnecessary — a judge's or doctor's word for *manifest error*, *manifest injustice*. Uniquely, it also runs as a verb, tracking something hidden (a disease, a talent) coming out into view.
- **patent** — Obvious plus exasperation. Almost never said of a neutral or pleasant fact — it collocates with *lie*, *nonsense*, *absurdity*, *patently unfair* — and the annoyance is aimed at anyone still arguing. Where **manifest** is grave, **patent** is withering.
- **flagrant** — The obviousness has become moral: the offender didn't even bother to hide. It attaches to a fixed set of wrongs — *violation, breach, abuse, disregard, misconduct* — and unlike everything above it, saying it is an act of condemnation, not description.

> **On the exam:** The exam separates these by collocation, not by brightness — the right answer is the one that fits the noun (a *flagrant* violation, a *patent* lie, a *conspicuous* absence), and "no discernible" is the giveaway for a sentence about careful measurement finding nothing.


<a id="intensity__boredom-to-total-inertia"></a>
### Boredom to total inertia

All three name a settled low-energy state in which nothing gets done — not a mood that passes but one that has set in. None of them is an accusation: in each case the person is described as *afflicted*, not blamed, which is what separates the whole group from laziness, sloth, or indolence. They differ in where the deficit sits — in your interest, in your body, or in your motion at all — and in how far gone you are.

- **ennui** — The only one where the failure is in the **world**, not in you: you have the energy to act, nothing just seems worth acting on. It requires a subject refined enough to be disappointed — an aristocrat, a poet, a bright bored teenager — and never a fever patient or a government agency.
- **lassitude** — The deficit is physical and has usually been *caused*: heat, illness, convalescence, months of grief. Unlike **ennui** the sufferer may want very much to get up and cannot; unlike **torpor** they are still awake to it, and the word keeps a soft melancholy that torpor has burned off.
- **torpor** — The end of the scale: not weary, not disenchanted, simply **not moving**. It is the coldest and most clinical of the three — it drops feeling entirely, which is why it alone stretches to bodies without minds (a hibernating animal) and to institutions (*decades of administrative torpor*).

> **On the exam:** Watch the subject of the sentence: only **torpor** takes an economy, a bureaucracy, or a hibernating animal, and only **ennui** requires someone with tastes to be bored of.


<a id="intensity__brief-to-vanishing"></a>
### Brief to vanishing

All four say a thing does not last, and any of them can be swapped into "a ___ pleasure" without breaking the sentence. What separates them is not how long the thing lasts but what the speaker is pointing at: whether impermanence is a philosophical property, a recorded fact, a lifespan, or an act of disappearing. Register does the rest of the work — one belongs to sermons, one to incident reports, two to poetry. The scale runs from "this will end" to "this is dissolving as you watch."

- **transitory** — The moralist's word: impermanence stated as a truth about the thing, usually an abstraction — power, glory, grief, a boom. It implies a speaker with a lesson (don't get attached), which none of the others carry.
- **transient** — The technician's word: passing through, reported flatly. It takes concrete subjects the others don't — a voltage spike, a fever, a population, a hotel guest — and alone in this group it becomes a noun for a person, which is what makes it sound cold when applied to one.
- **ephemeral** — Points at lifespan: a fixed, tiny span that runs out. It usually implies the brevity is part of the appeal (blossom, a fad, internet fame), and it is the only one with a live engineering sense — short-lived by design, don't rely on it.
- **evanescent** — Points at the fading itself, not the span: the thing is thinning while you look — mist, a scent, a chord dying out. The softest and most rarefied of the four, and it needs a subject delicate enough to dissolve; a fever or a badge cannot be evanescent.

> **On the exam:** Sentence Equivalence loves pairing two of these and rewarding the one whose register matches the sentence — clinical context takes **transient**, aesthetic context takes **ephemeral**/**evanescent**, and a sentence about worldly glory takes **transitory**.


<a id="intensity__broken-word-to-treachery"></a>
### Broken Word to Treachery

All three cover the failure of someone who was trusted — a commitment given, then violated. They differ in how much of the bond is broken and how harshly the speaker judges it: one is a walked-back deal, one is a person handed over, one is a moral verdict. The scale runs from procedural bad faith to condemnation. Note that the middle term also carries a second, quieter sense that has nothing to do with malice at all.

- **renege** — The narrowest and coolest: **renege** breaks a *specific prior undertaking* — a pledge, a contract, an offer — and takes *on*. No person need be harmed and no intimacy need exist; a government reneges on a treaty the way a buyer reneges on a signed bid. It's the transactional end of the scale, more bad faith than treachery.
- **betray** — **Betray** takes a *person, cause, or confidence* as its object, not a clause — you hand someone over to the other side. It also has a sense the others lack entirely: an involuntary leak, where a tremor or a flush **betrays** nerves their owner was working to hide. That sense implies no villain, only a detail that defected.
- **perfidy** — **Perfidy** is the noun of judgment, formal and contemptuous: it names the *violation of a bond by someone who traded on it* — ally, spouse, oath. It presumes calculation, so no accident or slip qualifies, and it's reached for when plain betrayal isn't damning enough. In the laws of war it's a defined crime: feigning surrender to shoot.

> **On the exam:** The trap is sense 2 of **betray** — in a sentence about a face, a voice, or a gesture revealing hidden feeling, the answer is not treachery-flavored at all, and *perfidy* is planted to pull you there.


<a id="intensity__calming-an-angry-party"></a>
### Calming an angry party

Someone is already angry, and you are doing something to bring the temperature down. All four assume a grievance that exists before you act, and all four are transitive — you calm *them*. What separates them is the price of the calm and what it says about the two parties: whether you merely said the soothing thing, handed over something cheap, surrendered outright, or paid tribute upward to a power that outranks you.

- **mollify** — The cheapest option: a soothing word, a reassurance, nothing changes hands. It attaches happily to feelings rather than just people (**mollify** her fears, his outrage), and it is the one word here you routinely see failing — "failed to mollify" is a stock phrase, because talk alone often doesn't work.
- **placate** — Now something is handed over, but it's token — a tweak, a gesture, enough to quiet them. **Placate** carries a faint eye-roll at the person being soothed, treating them as a nuisance to be managed rather than a party with a real claim.
- **appease** — The concession is substantive and the writer disapproves. **Appease** names you as the weaker will: you gave the bully what he demanded and he will be back for more. It's also the only one here that takes appetites (**appease** hunger, curiosity), and the only one whose noun, *appeasement*, works as a straight accusation.
- **propitiate** — The only word that encodes rank. You are the smaller party paying an offering upward — to a god, a king, an inspector, a furious dean. Used of an ordinary person it turns sardonic, casting them as a petty deity who expects tribute.

> **On the exam:** The exam builds a sentence whose blank needs a *cost* or a *power gap* — a diplomat yielding territory, a supplicant before a board — and offers **mollify** as the trap: it fits "calm them down" but carries no concession and no hierarchy.


<a id="intensity__careful-to-nitpicking"></a>
### Careful to Nitpicking

All four describe close attention to small details — the same observable behaviour of not letting anything small slide. What separates them is not how much attention, but the verdict passed on it: whether the detail-work was worth doing, whether it makes the person tiresome to be around, and whether the speaker is admiring, needling, or sneering. The scale runs from care that earns respect to care that reveals a defect in the person doing it.

- **meticulous** — The only one that is straightforwardly praise, and the only one whose focus is the **accuracy of the work itself** rather than the taste or temperament of the person. **Meticulous** attaches to research, records, restoration, notes — output you can check. The faint anxiety is the worker's own, not an imposition on anyone else.
- **fastidious** — Adds a second target the others lack: **being pleased**. Where meticulous judges work, **fastidious** also judges surroundings, food, company, cleanliness — it can describe someone who *produces* nothing and simply finds things beneath him. Praise and needle at once; the care is genuine but has crossed into discomfort, and there is a squeamish, faintly aristocratic edge.
- **finicky** — The domestic, low-stakes fuss — the register is a shrug or an eye-roll, never scorn, and the trifles are trifles (dressing on the salad, the wrong pillow). Uniquely, **finicky** also runs the other direction: a machine, engine, or recipe can be finicky, meaning *it* is temperamental and demands coaxing. No other word in this group can be applied to an object.
- **pedantic** — The only one about **rules, technicalities, and learning** rather than physical detail or cleanliness, and the only one that is purely an insult. **Pedantic** convicts the person of misplaced priorities — right about the semicolon, oblivious to the argument — and usually of enjoying the correction in front of an audience. Fussiness turned outward at other people.
