Each locates that resistance in a different place: in the heart that won't soften, in the will that won't reverse, in the body that won't be quieted. All three are verdicts from the person being blocked — nobody calls themselves any of these.

- **obdurate** — The resistance is **emotional**, not intellectual: what fails to move you is pleading, pity, or the sight of suffering. **Obdurate** implies a moral failing — a hardened heart the speaker is condemning — and lives in near-biblical register (an obdurate sinner, an obdurate creditor). Wrong word for a stain or a lid; it needs someone capable of mercy who withholds it.
- **obstinate** — The resistance is to **argument and evidence**: you've been shown you're wrong and you still won't turn. **Obstinate** says nothing about your feelings, only that your will has outlasted any reason for it — you may be damaging yourself. Uniquely among these, it works on inanimate things: an obstinate cough, an obstinate lid.
- **obstreperous** — The only one that makes **noise**. **Obstreperous** requires both volume and defiance — resistance you can hear from across the room — and it is always spoken downward, by whoever is supposed to be in charge (teacher, judge, flight crew). The others resist silently; this one is a scene.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable "stubborn": check whether the sentence supplies pity being refused (obdurate), a losing argument being continued (obstinate), or actual disruptive noise (obstreperous).


<a id="root__pendere"></a>
### Root: pendere (to weigh, hang, pay)

Latin *pendere* is the merchant's scale: goods hung from a hook, weighed out, paid for. Every word here keeps one frame of that picture — the measured portion handed over, the weight suspended and not yet settled, the pan tipped permanently to one side. They don't overlap in meaning, which is exactly the danger: they share a spelling family and nothing else, so recognizing the root tells you where the image comes from but never what the word does in a sentence.

- **dispense** — The literal weighing-out: an authority releases an allotted amount by rule — pharmacy, court, vending machine — with no warmth in the handover. It's also the only word here that flips on a preposition: **dispense with** cancels the transaction entirely and does so briskly, almost dismissively, as if the thing were beneath bothering with.
- **indispensable** — Literally *cannot be dispensed with* — the negation is the whole word. Alone in this group it's a verdict of necessity, and an absolute one: no degrees, no "fairly." Test it by subtraction, not by praise — remove it and the operation halts.
- **poise** — The hanging sense, not the paying one: weight suspended in balance, nothing wobbling. Uniquely here it's about visible bearing — steady voice, unhurried hands, the composure a stranger can see — with a whiff of grace and breeding. **Poised to** reverses the temperature: not relaxed but coiled, weight already committed toward the leap.
- **propensity** — The scale tipped and left there — *pro-* (forward) + hang, a permanent lean. Alone in this group it describes a person's interior disposition, and it sounds clinical, as though assessed by a lawyer or psychologist. Because it names what people can't help, it attaches to faults far more readily than virtues.

> **On the exam:** The trap is direction, not definition: *dispense* hands out, *dispense with* throws away, and *indispensable* is that second sense negated — so a sentence-equivalence stem can hinge entirely on a two-letter preposition or a prefix.


<a id="root__plicare"></a>
### Root: plicāre (to fold) — folded in, folded open, folds without breaking

Latin *plicāre* is the fold, and this family splits by what the fold is doing. Fold something *in* and it's present but not on the page — meaning carried without being stated. Fold it *open* (ex-) and you've laid the thing out to be worked over, which slides easily from "make use of" to "use up." And a thing that simply takes a fold without cracking is bendable — a quality that is high praise for leather and a wrist, and an insult for a spine. So the group's real question is never "does it bend?" but *who folds it, and what happens after*.

- **exploitative** — The only member describing a relationship rather than a property — and the only one that convicts. Something is unfolded and worked until it's spent, by a party with enough power that the other side can't walk; note that the verb and the noun *exploit* stay neutral or even admiring, and this adjective never does.
- **implicit** — The fold stays shut: the content is fully there, just never unfolded onto the record — which is what makes it the word for arguments people won't own. Alone here it applies to meaning, not matter; and watch sense 2, where nothing folded apart means nothing held back, so *implicit trust* is total, not tacit.
- **pliant** — Takes the fold and keeps it. Of a person that's the charge — no resistance, holding whatever shape the last pair of hands left; not the obedience-to-authority of *docile* or the fawning of *obsequious*, just shapeable. The word a manipulator uses about a mark.
- **supple** — Takes the fold and springs back — the only one here that implies strength inside the bending, which is why it's praise for a gymnast, a wrist, a prose style, or a negotiator. Where the yielding of **pliant** comes from having nothing to push back with, this yielding is control.

> **On the exam:** The root is never the trap — the traps are **implicit** sense 2 (absolute, not partial) and the fact that **pliant** and **supple** describe identical physical behaviour with opposite verdicts about the person.


<a id="root__ponere"></a>
### Root: ponere, positus (to place)

Latin *ponere / positus* means to put or place, and every word here is a different answer to the question *placed where?* — beside the matter, toward the purpose, down from a throne, or into a stance. Two of them place a remark (and are near-twins in sound and sense, which is the whole danger); one removes a person from a position; one holds a position for show. The root is a memory hook, not a meaning: knowing it tells you a placement is involved, never which one.

- **apposite** — Placed *beside* — praises the **aim of the content**, not the moment. An **apposite** quotation would still be apposite if you had produced it a week later or read it in a footnote; it hits the precise nerve of the matter. The critic's written verdict, and it attaches almost only to things said: analogies, examples, comparisons.
- **apropos** — Placed *toward the purpose* — praises the **timing**. The same remark that is **apropos** in the flow of a conversation is merely stale a minute later. It is also the only word here with a prepositional life (*apropos of your last point*), it carries an audible French accent, and it belongs to speech; apposite never does either.
- **depose** — The only word here that acts on a **person, not a remark** — placing someone *down* out of high office. Strictly about rank: kings, presidents, party chiefs, never a clerk. Deliberately colorless about method — a coup, a vote, or a mob all depose equally — which is what separates it from *overthrow* and *oust*. Watch for the unrelated legal sense: to take sworn out-of-court testimony.
- **posturing** — The only pejorative, and the only word about a **position held for display**. The others certify that something genuinely fits; **posturing** certifies that it doesn't — the stance is a costume worn for leverage, with no intention behind it. Cooler and more calculating than *grandstanding*, which just wants the attention.

> **On the exam:** The exam trades on the apposite/apropos overlap — if the sentence stresses *when* the remark came, it wants apropos; if it stresses *how exactly it fit*, apposite — and separately baits *apposite* against *opposite*.


<a id="root__pes"></a>
### Root: pēs, pedis (foot) — freeing the feet vs. shackling them

Latin *pēs, pedis* means "foot," and every word here is a metaphor about feet on a journey. *Ex-ped-* is pulling a foot out of the snare — getting free, getting moving. *Im-ped-* is the foot caught in a shackle — still able to shuffle, but slowed and encumbered. The whole group is therefore about *progress toward a goal* and whether it is being released, dragged on, or (in the last case) merely trudged through on foot instead of taking flight.

- **expedient** — The only member that judges a **motive**. **Expedient** frees the *speaker's own* feet, not the road's — it says the choice worked for whoever made it and quietly cost them a principle. Where *expedite* is something you're thanked for, *expedient* is something you're caught at: *politically expedient*, *merely expedient*.
- **expedite** — The only member that is an **action someone with authority takes**, and the only positively-valued one. **Expedite** frees the *system's* feet — it presupposes a queue, a backlog, a stack of approvals to jump. No moral shading whatever, unlike its adjective cousin; you expedite a visa, never a friendship.
- **impede** — The **verb** of partial drag, and the only member that is typically **agentless and blameless** — fog, red tape, an injury impedes. Note the strength ceiling: to *prevent* is to make impossible, but the thing you **impede** still limps forward. Choosing it over *block* is a claim about degree, not about malice.
- **impediment** — The **noun**, and it names a standing **condition** rather than an act — a *speech* **impediment**, a legal **impediment** to marriage. Where *impede* describes what happened once, an **impediment** is attached to the traveller and stays attached; it gets *removed* or *overcome*, not merely resisted.
- **pedestrian** — The only word using the foot **literally**, and the only one where feet are themselves the insult. **Pedestrian** work isn't obstructed — nothing is in its way; it simply plods when it should have flown. It's a critic's verdict on quality (prose, cooking, an argument), not a comment on progress at all.

> **On the exam:** The exam's favourite trap is **expedient**: the root and the neighbour *expedite* both smell efficient and useful, so test-takers slot it into a blank whose surrounding clause ("...though everyone knew it was wrong") is actually signalling compromised principle.


<a id="root__rapere"></a>
### Root: rapere (to seize, snatch)

Latin *rapere* means to seize or snatch, and each of these words keeps a different piece of that act. One keeps the grabbing hand and the hunger behind it; one keeps the violence of what gets carried off, leaving a stripped landscape; one keeps only the quickness — the snatch done before anyone can look up. Because the root splits three ways, these words are not synonyms and rarely substitute for one another; the confusion is that the shared etymology makes them feel like a scale of the same idea.

- **rapacious** — The only one that describes an **appetite** rather than an act — a standing disposition in the taker, present even before anything is seized. It attaches to agents with power over others (landlords, conquerors, creditors), and the victim survives, merely stripped.
- **ravage** — The only one focused on **aftermath**, and the only one where the agent wants nothing — plague, fire, war, and time carry nothing off, they just leave ruin behind. Where **rapacious** needs a greedy person, **ravage** prefers an impersonal force, and it uniquely doubles as a noun for the wreckage itself (*the ravages of time*).
- **surreptitious** — The only one describing **manner**, not appetite or damage — it modifies how something is done, and the thing done may be trivial or harmless. It is also the only one that requires concealment: **rapacious** and **ravage** are conspicuous by nature, while what is condemned here is the hiding, not the force.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating the shared root as shared meaning — the exam counts on you reasoning "seize" and picking the wrong one; choose by what the sentence emphasizes (the taker's hunger, the wreckage left, or the stealth of the doing).


<a id="root__salire"></a>
### Root: salīre (to leap) — leap at, leap between, leap back

Latin *salīre*, "to leap," survives in all three as a buried physical image, and the prefix decides where the leap goes: *at* a target, *away* from one thing to the next, *back* to the original shape. What unites them is motion under pressure — something springs, and the word records the direction. The confusion isn't that the meanings overlap (they barely do); it's that the shared root makes them feel related when they behave completely differently on the page. Two of the three describe force landing on something; the third describes energy that never lands anywhere at all.

- **assail** — *ad-* + *salīre*, leap **at**: the only one of the three that takes a direct object and names a victim — critics assail a proposal, doubts assail a person. It's the blow being struck, so it demands an aggressor (which can be an emotion), and it's the only word here you can be on the receiving end of.
- **desultory** — *de-* + *salīre*, leap **down and off** — from the *desultor*, the circus rider who vaulted between galloping horses. It's the odd one out: no target, no impact, nothing struck. It rates the *manner* of an effort as scattered and unbothered, and it's the only member that carries a droop of energy rather than force.
- **resilient** — *re-* + *salīre*, leap **back**: the aftermath word, and the only positive one. It doesn't describe the hit or the flailing — it describes returning to form afterward, which is why it quietly concedes that something already went wrong.

> **On the exam:** The root is a memory aid, not an answer key — the GRE tests these in unrelated sentences, and the trap is letting "leap" pull you toward motion words when *desultory* is really about half-heartedness and *resilient* about recovery.


<a id="root__sedere"></a>
### Root: sedere (to sit) — where you sit decides what you mean

Each of these buries Latin *sedere*, "to sit," and none of them means anything like sitting. The work is done entirely by the prefix, which says **where** the sitting happens relative to something else: apart from the group, in wait beside the road, still there after the rest has gone, on top of what came before. So the root is a spelling and memory hook, not a meaning: it tells you a position is being taken toward some other thing, and the prefix tells you which position. Learn the four positions and the words stop blurring.

- **dissident** — *dis-* = apart: the one who refuses the seat assigned to him and sits away from the body. Alone in this group it names a **person** and takes a public stance — the position is deliberate, visible, and costly, whereas the other three describe things that sit where they sit without choosing.
- **insidious** — *in-* = sitting in ambush (Latin *insidiae*, an ambush by the roadside). The only hostile sitting here: it is waiting for you, and waiting is the whole method. **Insidious** requires concealment plus time — remove the camouflage and the word collapses; a slow harm everyone can see is just slow.
- **residual** — *re-* = sitting back, after. Purely retrospective and purely passive: it names what a completed process failed to carry off, and it acts on nothing. Small, measurable, usually unwanted — **residual** is the quantity left in the beaker, not an agent doing anything to anyone.
- **supersede** — *super-* = sitting above. The only one about **rank**: the new thing sits over the old and the old loses its standing, not just its popularity. Bureaucratic and bloodless — no ambush, no leftovers, no defiance, just a memo saying the previous edition no longer counts. Note the spelling: *-sede*, the lone survivor of *sedere* where every look-alike takes *-cede*.

> **On the exam:** The root never picks the answer — these four never compete for one blank; the GRE tests each against its own near-twin (supersede/supplant, insidious/sinister, residual/remaining, dissident/rebel), so use *sedere* for spelling and recall only.


<a id="root__sentire"></a>
### Root: sentire (to feel, to perceive)

Latin *sentire* covers both halves of feeling: the physical registering of a stimulus and the inner emotional response to it. Every word here is a prefix or suffix hung on that stem — feeling *with* others, feeling *apart* from them, feeling *back* at an old wound, the raw *sensation* itself, the tender *sentiment*. The trap is assuming the root guarantees emotion: two of these are about the temperature of a group's agreement, and one is about jolting an audience's nerves rather than moving its heart. Knowing the root gets you into the neighbourhood; it will not tell you which house.

- **consensus** — *Con-* + *sentire*: feeling **together**. The only word here whose feeling is collective property rather than one person's — and it names a settled state, not an act, which is why it can be built, reached, or broken by a body that never voted.
- **dissent** — *Dis-* + *sentire*: feeling **apart**. Occupies the same public arena as consensus but from the losing side — it is an act, on the record, requiring an official position to push against, and it credits the speaker with conscience rather than mere annoyance.
- **resent** — *Re-* + *sentire*: feeling it **again**, and again. The private, inward member of the group — no forum, no audience, just stored bitterness aimed backward at a perceived injustice, and the only one that quietly indicts the person doing the feeling.
- **sensational** — Built on the *perception* half of the root, not the emotion half: it targets the audience's nerves — shock, gasp, thrill — and judges the effect produced, not the feeling held. Uniquely two-faced here: pure praise for a performer, pure accusation for a newspaper.
- **sentimental** — Built on *sentiment*, and restricted to the soft end of it — nostalgia, tenderness, pity, never rage or terror. Where **sensational** overstimulates, this oversweetens; the charge is that the feeling exceeds what the subject earned, which is why it kills a novel but forgives a person keeping old letters.

> **On the exam:** The GRE's favourite move is swapping **sensational** and **sentimental** in criticism of prose — both mean "laid on too thick," but one overdoes shock and the other overdoes tenderness; secondarily it pairs **consensus** and **dissent** in text completions that hinge on consensus *not* meaning unanimity.


<a id="root__solvere"></a>
### Root: solvere (to loosen, dissolve) — dissolving doubt into decision

Latin *solvere* means to loosen or dissolve, and *re-* + *solvere* gives the family its shared move: a knot of doubt is dissolved and something previously unsettled becomes settled. Every word here turns on the same question — has the mind stopped moving? One names the act and the firmness itself, one praises a person in whom that firmness has already hardened, one convicts a person in whom it never formed. The confusion is that they describe the same axis from three different distances: the event, the settled state, and its failure.

- **resolve** — The only member that names the **event** and the substance rather than a character trait — and the only one that takes non-human objects: you **resolve** a dispute, a plot, a doubt, a chord, or a smudge of light into two stars. Its claim is finality (a paused argument isn't resolved), and as a noun it's the raw material the other two measure: what *resolute* people have and *irresolute* people lack.
- **resolute** — Praise, and the deciding is already **over** — this is the settled state holding under pressure, not the effort of deciding. It says as much about the speaker as the subject: identical behaviour gets called **resolute** in an ally and *obstinate* in an opponent. Reserve it for people and their bearing; problems and disputes cannot be resolute.
- **irresolute** — Not merely undecided — **irresolute** indicts the person rather than describing the question, and lands precisely when action was required and none came. The failure is temperamental, not informational, which is why it's a quiet insult and stays literary: a biographer writes it about a general, nobody says it at dinner.

> **On the exam:** The trap is the technical sense of **resolve** — "separate into constituent parts / render distinguishable" (forces, stars, harmonies) — which the GRE prefers over the everyday "settle a dispute"; secondarily, it tests that *irresolute* carries blame while *undecided* does not.


<a id="root__spargere"></a>
### Root: spargere (to scatter, sprinkle)

Latin *spargere* is what you do with a handful of seed or a flick of water: throw so the pieces land apart, thin and separate, each one landing where it will. The root shows up in three grammatical slots — the act of breaking a mass apart, the thin state left behind afterward, and the figurative version where what gets sprinkled is doubt. Confusion comes from the shared picture of "spread out": all three describe things that are present but not concentrated. What separates them is what is being scattered, and whether anyone did the scattering on purpose.

- **aspersion** — The only figurative member, and the only hostile one: what gets sprinkled is doubt, and it lands on a person's character. Note the giveaway grammar — plural, and you *cast* them — and the fact that the word is almost always spoken by someone disclaiming the act ("I cast no aspersions"), which is how the smear gets delivered while staying too vague to answer.
- **disperse** — The verb of the group: it names the *event*, the moment a concentrated mass comes apart. It needs something gathered to begin with — a crowd, a cloud, a beam — and often an agent doing the breaking up, which is why riot police disperse protestors. Nothing is left thin here so much as left *gone from where it was*.
- **sparse** — The adjective, and purely descriptive of a resting state — no event, no agent, no one to blame. It reports density over an area (hair, vegetation, data points) and stays coolly neutral where *meagre* or *paltry* would grumble; a scientist calls a dataset sparse as a measurement, not a complaint.

> **On the exam:** The traps are semantic near-misses: **sparse** is offered where *scarce/meagre* is meant (it's about spacing, not shortage), and **aspersion** is offered where an open *accusation* is meant — GRE contexts usually cue it with a denial or a whispered, unrebuttable slight.


<a id="root__specere"></a>
### Root: specere (to look) — who looks, and what survives a second look

Latin *specere*, "to look," runs through every one of these — but each puts the looking in a different place. Some describe the **thing being looked at** (how visible it is, how well it survives a second look); others describe the **person doing the looking** (how sharp their eye is, how thin the evidence they're reasoning from). The confusion is that all five hover around the gap between how something appears and what it actually is. Sorting them means asking two questions: who is doing the looking, and has a verdict been reached?

- **conspicuous** — Pure visibility, no verdict attached — it says the thing **catches the eye**, not that it's true, false, or dubious. Alone in this group it describes physical or social prominence rather than reasoning, and the discomfort it carries is about being *seen*, not about being *wrong*.
- **perspicacious** — The only one that praises the **looker**. Everything else here is something an observer says about an object; this is what you say about the observer — the person whose second look catches what everyone else's first look missed. Formal, admiring, and aimed at judgement of people and motives.
- **specious** — A **delivered verdict**: you looked twice and the reasoning failed. It attaches almost exclusively to arguments, excuses, and claims — never to a person or an object — and it accuses the thing of being deliberately well-dressed. Where *suspect* withholds judgement, **specious** has already convicted.
- **speculate** — The only **verb**, and the only word about looking *forward* rather than at. Nothing is being deceived or doubted here — the reasoner is simply running ahead of the evidence, and by using the word admits it. Respectable when an analyst does it, insulting when it names how someone handles money.
- **suspect** — **Doubt without a conclusion** — the claim has failed the sniff test but not yet the audit. Strictly passive as an adjective: it describes what *attracts* suspicion, never what feels it. The register is professional understatement — the word an auditor reaches for precisely because *fraudulent* would commit them.

> **On the exam:** Two traps: *perspicacious* (sharp-eyed observer) versus the lookalike *perspicuous* (clearly expressed — a property of the text, not the reader); and *suspect* versus *specious*, where the exam rewards the weaker word when the sentence says "not yet disproven."


<a id="root__stringere"></a>
### Root: stringere (to draw tight, bind)

Latin *stringere* means to draw tight, bind, or squeeze. Every word here involves tension applied — something pulled taut, clamped down, or contracted. The confusion is that the tightening lands in different places: on a rule, on the tongue, or on the thing being squeezed. Two of them also look nearly identical on the page and differ by a single letter.

- **stringent** — The tightening is in **the bar itself** — rules, criteria, controls, protocols. It measures how little slack a standard permits, not how much it hurts to fail it, which is why *stringent testing* reads as praise where *harsh testing* would not. It never attaches to a temperament: a person can be strict, but only a system is stringent.
- **astringent** — The tightening is a **sensation** — literally puckering tissue, figuratively puckering prose or wit. Unlike stringent, it describes tone and taste rather than requirement, and it stings *bracingly* rather than burning; the medicinal undertone makes it a compliment to a writer, and it is never applied to a rule.
- **distressed** — The only one naming **what is being squeezed** rather than the force doing the squeezing — the object under strain, not the standard or the sting. It's the third-party, clinical register (*a vessel in distress*), sits a notch below *distraught*, and carries two GRE-favourite trade senses: cheap because the company is failing, or costly because the denim was battered on purpose.

> **On the exam:** The classic trap is the missing *a-*: check whether the blank governs a rule or requirement (**stringent**) or a taste, tone, or style (**astringent**) — and don't assume **distressed** just means "upset" when the sentence is about assets or furniture.


<a id="root__stare"></a>
### Root: stāre (to stand)

Latin *stāre* gives all of these the image of something holding its position instead of moving, leaking, or falling. The root shows up in four directions: remaining in place over time, refusing to move at all, keeping something from running out, and being solid enough to hold weight. The overlap is structural rather than semantic — they are not synonyms, so the risk is misreading the root, not confusing the definitions.

- **extant** — **Extant** is standing *out* of the wreckage — it describes what physically survives after time has destroyed the rest, so it attaches to counted objects (manuscripts, colonies, letters), never to abstractions or claims. Of the four, it's the only one that is purely an observation about the world, with no agent doing anything.
- **staid** — **Staid** is standing *still* — the sense of stopped motion turned into a character judgement about a person or institution that is respectable and has quit surprising anyone. It's the only word here that carries a verdict; the other three are neutral about their subject.
- **stanch** — **Stanch** makes something *stop* — the only word that acts on a flow, and it requires a leak already running (blood, deposits, defections). It buys containment, not a cure, which is why it names an emergency measure rather than a fix.
- **substantiate** — **Substantiate** puts something *under* — it builds a foundation beneath words, not things, so its objects are always assertions: allegations, rumours, charges. The burden falls on whoever spoke; unlike *corroborate*, no second witness is implied, just evidence from you.

> **On the exam:** Traps are the lookalikes, not the meanings: **stanch** (stop a flow) vs *staunch* (loyal), **staid** vs *stayed*, **extant** vs *extinct* — and in sentence equivalence, **substantiate** is swapped for *corroborate*, which wrongly demands a second independent source.


<a id="root__sub"></a>
### Root: sub- (under, from below)

Every word here puts one thing *under* another — but "under" does different work in each. In one it means beneath in rank; in another, back down to a lower level; in another, filed under a bigger heading; in the last, attacking from underneath. What makes them confusable is that all four describe a loss of height, standing, or independence, so under time pressure the prefix feels like the meaning. The discriminators are **who is doing it** and **what happens to the smaller thing**.

- **subservient** — The only adjective, and the only one describing a *stance* rather than an event — a permanent posture of being under someone. It is also the only one that judges: **subservient** is a sneer, where the others are neutral reports of what occurred.
- **subside** — The only word with no agent at all. Nobody subsides a flood; the flood **subsides** on its own, and only because it had risen first. Where the others need someone to do them to something, this one is what a thing does when everyone stops touching it.
- **subsume** — The smaller thing survives intact — it just loses its own heading and now counts as an instance of the bigger one. Cool and clerical: a ministry **subsumes** a department the way a category swallows an example, with no hostility and nothing damaged.
- **subvert** — Here the "under" is where the *attacker* stands, not where the victim lands — the direction of the prefix flips. The only aggressive word in the set, and the only one that can be praise: **subverting** a genre is a compliment, **subverting** an election is a charge.

> **On the exam:** Sentence-completion items hinge on agency — a blank whose subject acts alone (fever, uproar, swelling) can only be **subside**; if an actor is named, ask whether the smaller thing is filed (**subsume**) or hollowed out (**subvert**).


<a id="root__tacere"></a>
### Root: tacēre (to be silent)

All three descend from Latin *tacēre*, "to be silent," and all three describe something that goes unsaid. The confusion is that they locate the silence in three different places: in a person's choice on one topic, in a person's permanent disposition, and in the agreement itself rather than in any person. Two of them describe speakers; one describes a thing that was never spoken. Getting them right means asking what the silence is *doing* — withholding, characterizing, or communicating.

- **reticent** — The topic-specific one: it takes **about** and points at a subject the speaker could disclose and won't — usually his own affairs. It's a live choice in a particular scene, so it invites a reading (discretion or evasion) in a way a mere personality trait never does.
- **tacit** — The only one that doesn't describe a person at all — it modifies the *understanding*: a tacit agreement, tacit approval, a tacit admission. Here silence carries content and binds two parties; nobody is being characterized as quiet, and a very talkative person can give tacit consent by not objecting.
- **taciturn** — Measures word count, not content: no topic, no withheld secret, just a standing temperament of few words with everyone about everything. Where **reticent** implies there's something specific he isn't saying, **taciturn** implies there was never much to say — hence its faint chill rather than its faint suspicion.

> **On the exam:** Sentence Equivalence loves offering *reticent* and *taciturn* as a "pair" — check for a topic: if the sentence names what he won't discuss, only **reticent** fits; if it describes him across all conversations, only **taciturn** does. **Tacit** is the giveaway distractor whenever the blank modifies a person instead of an agreement.


<a id="root__tangere"></a>
### Root: tangere, tactus (to touch)

Every word here is a metaphor about contact — how much of something is actually touching something else. Full contact means substance you can lay a hand on; a single point of contact means grazing past; contact between people means knowing exactly how hard to press. The root supplies the image, but each word chooses a different amount of touch, and that amount is the whole meaning.

- **tact** — The only one about people rather than things: touch as **pressure applied to another person**, calibrated live. It's a faculty someone possesses, not a property of an object or an argument — and it's almost always invoked in the negative, as a charge laid against whoever just said the unsayable.
- **tangential** — Contact at exactly **one point, then gone**. It concedes the connection in order to dismiss it — the polite blade that *irrelevant* swings bluntly. Attaches to remarks, arguments, evidence, or a person's whole conversational manner; the speaker is ruling something out of scope, not denying it exists.
- **tangible** — **Full contact** — solid enough to be handed over, measured, pointed at. It's the demand word: whoever asks for tangible results is calling the previous offering vapour. Where *tangential* grades relevance, this grades reality, and its opposite is *vague*, not *unrelated*.

> **On the exam:** The trap is that tangible and tangential share a root and their first four letters but sit at opposite ends of the contact scale — check whether the sentence is grading reality or relevance.


<a id="root__tempus"></a>
### Root: tempus, temporis (time)

All four descend from *tempus* — time — but each has drifted somewhere different, and the GRE tests the drift, not the root. Two stay literal (a point in time; a shared moment in time), one turns metaphysical (what exists in time is perishable, therefore worldly rather than eternal), and one wanders off through *tempestas*, "season/weather," into emotional storms. The confusion is that they all look like they should mean "having to do with time," so a test-taker reaches for a chronological reading where the intended sense is secular, or unprepared, or furious.

- **temporal** — The only one whose tested sense **abandons time entirely**: opposed not to *timeless* but to *spiritual*. It attaches to power, authority, rulers, and ambitions — a king's **temporal** sway against a bishop's spiritual one — and carries a faint sneer at the merely earthly.
- **contemporary** — The only **relational** member: it needs a second thing to be simultaneous with, and if none is named, the implied partner is the present. That's the trap — **contemporary** accounts of Waterloo are eyewitness, not modern. It's also the only one that names a person (*a contemporary of Newton*).
- **extemporize** — The only **verb**, and the only word about a live human performing: *ex tempore*, out of the moment, no script. It is quietly complimentary — it credits poise under exposure where "unprepared" would indict. Reserve it for speech and performance before an audience, not for jury-rigging a shelf.
- **tempestuous** — The outlier: its time-sense went through *weather*, so it means emotional storm, never chronology. It's the group's only **negatively charged** word, and the only one implying heat rather than mere instability — a **tempestuous** affair has shouting and reconciliation, not just turbulence. Applied to people and relationships, rarely to actual skies.

> **On the exam:** The GRE baits you with the root: sentences about *temporal* rulers or *contemporary* documents reward the non-chronological or eyewitness reading and punish the reflex "having to do with time."


<a id="root__tendere"></a>
### Root: tendere (to stretch) — which way is it pulling?

Latin *tendere* meant to stretch, strain, or pull taut — and every word here is a different answer to the question *stretched in which direction?* Something can be strained against an opposing force, pushed outward from within, let slack after being pulled tight, stretched forward in time, or pulled steadily toward one conclusion. The root gives you the tension; it never gives you the direction, and the direction is the entire meaning. These are five destinations from one starting point, which is why recognizing the root without pinning the vector is worse than useless.

- **contend** — **Contend** is stretching *against* — the tension runs between you and someone pushing back. Alone in this group it requires an opponent: a rival claim, a rival competitor, a stubborn problem. It's also the only one whose normal subject is a person.
- **distend** — **Distend** is stretching *outward from inside* — pressure within forcing the walls out. The vocabulary of bellies, veins, balloons, and corpses; clinical and faintly repellent. Unlike everything else here it describes a physical shape, never an argument, a mood, or a forecast.
- **détente** — **Détente** is the tension *released* — *dé-* undoes the stretch. The only noun here and the only positive one, it names the moment two hostile parties stop pulling. Note what it withholds: no warmth, no settlement, just lowered weapons. It presupposes the hostility that **contend** enacts.
- **portend** — **Portend** stretches *forward in time* — the present reaching ahead to a future, and nearly always a grim one. Its subjects are things, not people: clouds, silence, a sagging quarterly number. Solemn where *indicate* is flat.
- **tendentious** — **Tendentious** is the steady pull *toward a predetermined conclusion*, hidden under a neutral surface. It attaches only to made things — a study, a footnote, a documentary — never to a person's character and never to a physical object. The charge isn't that the piece argues (that's **contend**, done in the open) but that it pretends not to be arguing.

> **On the exam:** The GRE baits root-spotters: the sentence supplies tension, two *tendere* words match the vibe, and only one matches the vector — fix whether the stretch is against, outward, slackening, forward, or toward before you fill the blank.


<a id="root__tenuis"></a>
### Root: tenuis (thin) — attenuate, extenuating, tenuous

Latin *tenuis* means thin, and every word here is about something stretched thin rather than cut off. Each one reduces force — of a signal, of blame, of an argument's support — while leaving the thing itself standing. None of them means *remove*, *disprove*, or *clear*, and that surviving remnant is the whole family trait. They split by what gets thinned and by whether the word names an act, an excuse, or a verdict.

- **attenuate** — The only one that is an act performed on something: an agent (a filter, a lab, a distance, a passing year) deliberately or measurably dials a force down along a scale. Its objects are physical or quantitative — signals, viruses, shock, effect sizes — and it carries no judgment of the thing being weakened.
- **extenuating** — Thins one thing only: **blame**. The facts stay fully intact — the act happened, and you did it — but the surrounding context argues for a lighter penalty, which is why it's the vocabulary of pleas, HR files and sentencing, not of denial. It almost never travels alone; it modifies *circumstances*.
- **tenuous** — Not an act but a resulting state, and the only word here that is an insult. Someone else applies it to your link, evidence, claim or grip on power to say the support underneath it is nearly nothing — polite in register, damning in substance.

> **On the exam:** Traps swap these for words of elimination — *nullify* for **attenuate**, *exonerating* for **extenuating**, *false* or *fabricated* for **tenuous** — but all three only thin; the thing survives.


<a id="root__tenere"></a>
### Root: tenēre (to hold) — holding back, holding on, holding up

All four descend from Latin *tenēre*, "to hold," and each keeps a different piece of that grip. The prefix decides the direction: *abs-* holds yourself away from something, *per-* holds all the way through to the thing that matters, and the bare stem holds a position against pressure. The trap is that a shared root guarantees nothing about shared meaning — two of these come from the same prefix and stem and still land in opposite parts of a sentence, one describing a person who won't let go and one describing a fact that belongs on the table.

- **abstain** — The only member where the holding points backward at the self: you are gripping your own hand to keep it off the glass, the ballot, the argument. It is also the only verb here, the only one with a moral or institutional flavor (principle, health, procedure), and the only one with a technical sense — present in the room, counted, voting neither way.
- **pertinacious** — The grip is on a purpose and it will not open — and the speaker resents it. Alone in this group it is a complaint: it attaches to the creditor, the cough, the rumour that keeps coming back, and it says the persistence has outlived its welcome. Note it describes a holder, not a thing being held.
- **pertinent** — Same prefix and stem as pertinacious, but the reaching-through is a fact's reach toward the question at hand, not a person's refusal to let go. It attaches to information, and it is a verdict delivered by whoever runs the room — a chair, a judge, an examiner — that this deserves the floor. Nothing to do with stubbornness.
- **tenable** — The passive of the family: not who holds, but whether a thing can be held when something pushes against it. It is the weakest praise here — a tenable claim has merely survived attack, which is not the same as being right or persuasive, and *pertinent* would be a genuine compliment where this is barely one.

> **On the exam:** Pertinent and pertinacious are the whole game — one is a compliment to a fact, the other a complaint about a person — and tenable is baited with answer choices meaning "true" or "convincing" when it only means "not yet demolished."


<a id="root__trahere"></a>
### Root: trahere, tractus — to drag, pull (abs-, de-, -able)

Every word here is a different answer to the question *what gets pulled, and which way?* Latin **trahere/tractus** means to drag or draw, so each member describes a pull: something drawn off an object, something drawn away from its worth, or something that can be drawn along by whoever holds the lead. They look alike and they all involve subtraction or traction, which is exactly why the prefixes do the real work — **abs-/ab-** (away from), **de-** (down from), and the bare stem plus **-able** (capable of being pulled).

- **abstract** — The pull is **upward and away from the particular** — the idea is lifted off the object, and nothing is lost or damaged in the process. It is the only word here that is not a criticism by default: math is maximally **abstract** and perfectly rigorous. The complaint version ("too abstract") is about distance from cases, never about imprecision — do not let the GRE sell you *vague* as a synonym.
- **detract** — The pull is **downward off a value**, and it is always a loss to someone's credit — a shaving, not a demolition. Unlike the others it is grammatically bound: things **detract from** a reputation, a performance, an effect; you never detract a thing. It also names the person doing the pulling — a **detractor** — which neither abstract nor tractable can do.
- **tractable** — The only passive one: it describes what **can be pulled**, not what does the pulling. Of people it is faint, condescending praise from whoever holds the reins — steerable, not eager. Of problems it goes coldly technical — it yields to method. Expect the negative, **intractable**, far more often than this form.

> **On the exam:** Two traps: **abstract** baited with *vague/imprecise* (wrong — abstraction is distance from the concrete, not fuzziness), and **detract** offered in a sentence-equivalence answer missing its obligatory *from*; also expect **intractable** rather than tractable, and check whether the noun it modifies is a person (stubborn) or a problem (unsolvable).


<a id="root__unda"></a>
### Root: unda (wave), via abundāre (to overflow)

All three come from water rising past its edge, and all three describe a quantity that exceeds what the situation requires. What differs is where the excess sits: whether it simply *exists* in profusion, whether it *arrives* at someone who can't absorb it, or whether it's *already there twice*. They also differ in grammar and blame — one takes no object and assigns no fault, one needs a victim, and one is a verdict.

- **abound** — The only one with no target and no victim — things simply exist in profusion, and nobody is being done to. Strictly intransitive (things abound, or a place abounds *in/with* them), and it passes no judgement: *wildflowers abound* and *errors abound* use the identical word.
- **inundate** — Requires someone on the receiving end and casts them as the shore: the excess pours in from outside and exceeds their capacity to process it. The complaint is volume, never difficulty — a hundred routine emails inundate you, one hard problem doesn't — and it usually shows up passive: *inundated with*.
- **redundant** — Doesn't count a mass at all; it's a verdict on one item that it duplicates what's already present. *Superfluous* says extra, **redundant** says extra *because repeated* — hence the editor's sting of "you didn't notice you'd already said it." Uniquely, it flips positive in engineering (a deliberate backup) and means laid off in British usage.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating them as interchangeable "too much": the GRE picks sentences where only one grammar works (abound takes no object, inundate needs a recipient) and loves redundant's positive engineering sense — deliberate duplication as a safeguard, not a flaw.


<a id="root__vadere"></a>
### Root: vadere (to go) — out of, into, through

Latin *vadere* means "to go," and each of these words is that going plus a direction: out of (e-), into (in-), through (per-). All four involve something crossing a line it either shouldn't cross or is trying not to be caught behind — a duty, a boundary, a habitat, a whole atmosphere. Three of them carry the implication of a violation; the confusion comes from mistaking which way the motion runs and whether a boundary is being fled, breached, or already dissolved.

- **evade** — The only verb here — the act, not the description. **Evade** needs a specific thing with a claim on you (a subpoena, a tax bill, a pursuer) and a moment of successful dodging; you can evade capture once. It cannot describe an atmosphere or a spread, only an escape.
- **evasive** — The habit or manner, not the act — **evasive** characterizes *how* someone behaves across a whole answer or interview, which is why it works as an accusation where *evaded* would need proof. Uniquely double-lived: damning about speech, entirely blameless about movement (*evasive action*), where no duty is being shirked at all.
- **invasive** — Reverses the direction — going *in*, not out. **Invasive** requires a boundary and a thing on the wrong side of it now establishing itself: a species in a habitat, a tumour past its tissue, a question inside your private life. It always implies a territory with an owner, which is why it neutralizes completely in medicine and ecology, where the boundary is just anatomy or an ecosystem.
- **pervasive** — The boundary is gone — **pervasive** describes the end state after something has soaked through everything, with no intruder to point at and no moment of entry. It attaches to diffuse things (smoke, dread, bias, an aesthetic) rather than agents, and it's the only one here that can be neutral or even admiring: *his influence was pervasive*.

> **On the exam:** The trap is **invasive** vs **pervasive**: invasive needs a violated boundary and something identifiable doing the violating; pervasive needs total saturation and no agent — so a sentence about corruption "throughout every ministry" wants pervasive, while one about questions "into her marriage" wants invasive.


<a id="root__valere"></a>
### Root: valēre (to be strong, to be well)

Latin *valēre* covers two overlapping ideas — to have physical force, and to be in good health — and its English descendants split that inheritance three ways. One tracks strength returning to a body, one tracks strength proving itself against opposition, one tracks strength as a virtue of character. All three assume a contest with weakness, sickness, or danger; the difference is where in that contest the word sits and whether it describes a condition, an outcome, or a quality worth honoring.

- **convalescent** — The only one that describes strength *absent and returning* rather than possessed or proven — it names a condition, not an act, and it can't be done well or badly. It also carries a duration the others don't: valor is a moment, prevailing is an outcome, but **convalescent** is weeks of armchair and blanket, and the clinical register (sanatorium, nursing home) comes with it.
- **prevail** — The only one that requires an opponent — **prevail** is strength measured relationally, against resistance, and it's intransitive: you prevail *over* or *against*, never prevail someone. It's also the only one that describes strength as slow attrition rather than a flash: nothing prevails in ten seconds. And it alone drifts away from the contest entirely, so *prevailing* just means "in force everywhere now."
- **valor** — Strength as a moral property of a person, not a bodily state or a result — and the only one of the three that praises. **Valor** is the language of citations and eulogies, so it presumes combat or a heroic rescue; applied to office life it reads as mock-heroic, which the other two never do.

> **On the exam:** The exam almost never tests **prevail** as "win" — it tests *prevailing* meaning "currently dominant" (where the winning is forgotten) and *prevail upon* meaning "persuade"; and it uses **convalescent** figuratively for markets and institutions, where "recovering but still weak" is the whole answer.


<a id="root__vertere"></a>
### Root: vertere / versus (to turn) — the prefix decides the direction

Every word here is a turning, and the prefix says which way: turned against you, turned away from, turned apart, turned back (an argument), turned to many uses. Because the root image is the same, the words look like relatives and get swapped — especially the two that both mean "turn from/against." The real differences are grammatical and directional: who does the turning (a force outside you, or you yourself), what the turning attaches to (conditions, feelings, evidence, skills), and whether the turn is a fault or a virtue.

- **adverse** — The turning is done **to** you by something outside: conditions, effects, rulings, markets. It never names a feeling — a person is not adverse to broccoli, and **adverse** takes no human subject at all.
- **aversion** — The only word in the group that lives inside a person's head: a settled dislike that wants distance rather than damage. Where *adverse* is a force pressing on you, **aversion** is you backing away — and it takes **to**, never *of*.
- **divorced** — The only one that presupposes a bond that existed and should still hold, so the separation reads as an accusation of failure, not a neutral fact. Passive, always with **from**, and on the GRE almost never about marriage.
- **incontrovertible** — The turning here is purely rhetorical — an argument that cannot be turned back. It grades *evidence*, not danger, feeling, or importance: an **incontrovertible** fact can be completely trivial, and the word wants documents and data, not charm.
- **versatile** — The lone compliment: turning your hand to many things and being good at each. Unlike *adaptable* (you cope with change) or *flexible* (you yield to others), **versatile** claims skills already in hand — and it applies to tools and fabrics as readily as to people.

> **On the exam:** The classic trap is adverse/averse: the exam offers "adverse to risk" where only *averse* (or *aversion*) fits, banking on the shared root to hide the fact that one describes a force and the other a feeling.


<a id="root__via"></a>
### Root: via (road, way)

Latin *via* is a road, and each of these words freezes a different moment on it: leaving the road, taking a crooked one, standing in the road to block it, and the crossroads where everybody walks. The trap here is not meaning but shape — three of them start with a *-vi-* cluster and get mixed up on sight, and the fourth hides its road entirely. Once you can name which relation to the road each one encodes, they stop bleeding into each other.

- **deviate** — *de-* "off" + road: the road stays intact, you step off it. Alone in this group it demands a stated baseline — a flight plan, a protocol, the mean — so it is a measurement verb before it is an accusation. Where **devious** describes a whole crooked route, **deviate** marks a single, locatable departure from a line someone else drew.
- **devious** — Here the road itself winds. It rates *method*, not morals, and it attaches to a person or a scheme rather than to a quantity — the loops, the cover story, the friend who "happened" to mention it. That's why it carries a flicker of admiration for the cleverness, an attitude **deviate** (clinical) and **obviate** (bloodless) never have.
- **obviate** — *ob-* "in the way" + road: to stand across the path so the thing never arrives. The only forward-facing member — it acts on what hasn't happened yet, and almost always on an abstraction (*the need, the objection, the difficulty*). Note the resemblance to *obvious* is a coincidence of sound: obviating removes a requirement, it does nothing to visibility.
- **trivial** — *tri-* + *via*: the three-road junction, the public corner where anyone can overhear — hence commonplace, hence beneath notice. It's the group's only adjective of *worth*: the others describe direction or timing, this one delivers a verdict that something has none. Saying an objection is trivial dismisses it rather than sizes it.

> **On the exam:** The GRE's favourite here is **obviate**, baited by *obvious* — sentences reward "make unnecessary" and punish "make clear"; secondarily it swaps **deviate** and **devious** in answer pairs, where only one can take *from*.


<a id="root__vocare"></a>
### Root: vocāre (to call)

Latin *vocāre*, "to call," and every word here is a species of calling — but they differ in who is called, by whom, and how hard. One calls *to* an audience on someone's behalf, one calls something *out* of a listener's memory gently and unbidden, one calls a reaction *forth* on purpose. The prefix does all the work: *ad-* (toward), *e-* (out of), *pro-* (forth). The confusion is that all three describe a stimulus producing a response, so they look interchangeable until you ask whether the response was pleaded for, quietly summoned, or deliberately baited.

- **advocate** — The only one requiring a **speaker with a position** — and typically a third party being spoken *for*. **Advocate** is calling toward an audience on behalf of a cause or a person too weak to plead for itself; it is also the only member that names a human being (an advocate), not just an effect. You advocate reform; you never advocate a mood.
- **evoke** — The gentlest and the only one with **no intent required and no adversary**. What is **evoked** was already dormant inside the listener — the smell, the chord, the photograph only stirs it; nothing is argued and no one is targeted. Its objects are atmospheres, memories, images, never people or policies, which is why it is the house verb of art criticism.
- **provocative** — Intent is the whole point, and the reaction is meant to be **strong and outward** — argument, anger, or desire, not private reverie. **Provocative** is the only adjective here and the only one whose connotation flips with context: praise in a book review, an accusation at a dinner table, sexual suggestion applied to a look. If it wasn't aimed, it isn't provocative.

> **On the exam:** The exam's favourite trap is swapping **evoke** for **provoke/provocative** — a passage that quietly summons nostalgia is not one that deliberately picks a fight; watch also for **provocative** in a tone question, where it can be the credit or the charge.


<a id="root__verus"></a>
### Root: vērus (true) — asserting it, having it, faking it

All three descend from Latin *vērus*, "true," but each fastens onto a different link in the chain between a fact and the person reporting it. One is the act of putting a claim forward as true; one is the property of being true (and of being the kind of source that tells the truth); one is the mere look of truth, which can sit on something entirely false. All three are formal enough that they signal courtroom, criticism, or reportage rather than ordinary speech.

- **aver** — The only verb here — an **act**, not a quality. **Aver** is the moment a speaker stakes their own credibility on a statement, usually against doubt: it says nothing about whether the claim is true, only that the person refuses to hedge. Its object is always a proposition (*averred that…*), never a text or a performance.
- **veracity** — The **actual** truth-value, and the trait of a habitual truth-teller. Alone in this group it can be predicated of a person as a standing virtue, and it is the only one that presumes real correspondence to fact — which is why it lives in the negative: what gets *questioned* or *disputed* is whether the claim is genuinely true, not whether it sounds true.
- **verisimilitude** — Appearance only, and deliberately silent about fact — a forgery or a lie can have plenty of it. It attaches to **made things** (a novel, a set, a performance, an alibi) and is critics' cool praise for craft; you cannot verisimilitude a claim or possess it as a character trait.

> **On the exam:** The trap is treating **verisimilitude** as a synonym for truth — in sentence equivalence it pairs with *plausibility* and *lifelikeness*, and a context conceding something is fabricated still supports it, where **veracity** would be wrong.
